會試錄序

我皇上統天建極，臨照九有，如日月之明，無遠弗徹；恩則雨露霑洽庶類，威則雷霆震耀，罔不讋伏。四十四年於茲，道化洋溢光天之下，至於海隅蒼生，萬邦黎獻，咸切帝臣之願焉。歲乙丑，復當會試天下士。屆期，禮部尚書臣李春芳、侍郎臣秦鳴雷、臣高儀，以考試官請。
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Our Emperor, uniting with Heaven and establishing the supreme standard, presides over and illuminates the nine regions. Like the light of the sun and moon, his radiance reaches even the remotest places. His beneficence, like rain and dew, moistens and nourishes all beings; his majesty, like thunder, shakes and dazzles them, leaving none who do not submit in awe. Forty-four years have now passed. The transforming influence of his Way spreads abundantly beneath radiant Heaven, reaching even the common people at the shores of the seas. The worthy men of the myriad lands all fervently desire to serve as his subjects.

In the yichou year [1565], the time came once again to hold the Metropolitan Examination for scholars throughout the realm. When the appointed time arrived, your servant Li Chunfang, Minister of Rites, and your servants Qin Minglei and Gao Yi, Vice Ministers, requested the appointment of Examiners.

厥事臣方總校
大典乃輟館事
陛辭以往臣伏自思念經術淺
薄行能無異乃數蒙
拔擢超躐恒格以至今茲臣受

殫精盡慎思所自効者乎既
入院臣乃諗諸眾曰茲舉也
為求賢也今即以賢進後或

translation_en: His Majesty commanded your servant Gong and your servant Zhengmeng, Academician Reader-in-waiting, to take charge of this undertaking. I was then overseeing the collation of the Great Compendium (Dadian), so I suspended my work at the compilation office, took leave of His Majesty, and proceeded to my assignment. I humbly reflected: my learning in the Classics is shallow, and my conduct and abilities are unexceptional; yet I have repeatedly received promotions beyond the established rules, down to the present occasion. The favors I have received from Your Majesty are exceedingly generous, far beyond my due. Often I have considered how I might exert all my strength to repay them fittingly, but I have had no means of doing so. Now, appointed for want of someone better and graciously entrusted with evaluating the examination essays, I feared that I could not bear the responsibility. Yet I also rejoiced inwardly, saying: “Perhaps this will allow me to repay even a ten-thousandth of those favors!” How could I dare fail to devote all my energies and exercise the utmost care, considering how best to render service? title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
未可知也乃即以不肖進後
其謂何是故代者有罰挾冊
者有罰羣聚而通者有罰茲
惟我
聖天子明命諸執事敬之哉罔或
弗覈俾我校文者罔攸據既
入簾臣又諗諸眾曰茲試言
===
也為覘所存也即良於言存
或未可知也乃即弗良於言
存其謂何是故浮夸者黜險
僻者黜曼衍而無當者黜茲
亦惟我
聖天子明命我諸執事敬之哉罔
固舊見俾或售於淫辭於是

punctuated: 未可知也。乃即以不肖進，後其謂何？是故代者有罰，挾冊者有罰，羣聚而通者有罰。茲惟我聖天子明命，諸執事敬之哉！罔或弗覈，俾我校文者罔攸據。」既入簾，臣又諗諸眾曰：「茲試言也，為覘所存也。即良於言，存或未可知也；乃即弗良於言，存其謂何？是故浮夸者黜，險僻者黜，曼衍而無當者黜。茲亦惟我聖天子明命，我諸執事敬之哉！罔固舊見，俾或售於淫辭。」於是
translation_en:
…what they will prove to be later may still be unknown. But if we recommend the unworthy at the outset, what can be said of the consequences? Therefore, those who take the examination for others are punished; those who smuggle in books are punished; and those who gather together and communicate answers are punished. These are the explicit commands of our sagely Son of Heaven. All you officials must heed them reverently! Let nothing go uninvestigated, leaving us who assess the compositions without a basis on which to proceed.”

After entering the examiners’ inner enclosure, I again addressed the assembled officials: “This examination of their words is intended to discern what they hold within. Even if their words are good, what they hold within may remain unknown; but if even their words are poor, what can be said of what they hold within? Therefore, compositions that are superficial and boastful are rejected; those that are abstruse and eccentric are rejected; and those that ramble without substance are rejected. These too are the explicit commands of our sagely Son of Heaven. All of us officials must heed them reverently! Do not cling to established views and thereby allow anyone to gain acceptance through extravagant language.” Thereupon …

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
羣多士三試之士凡四千六
百有奇遵
宸斷取中式者四百人以其名氏
及文之純者爲錄以
獻臣乃諗諸多士曰於戲諸士
出而事
君也自今日始也乃亦知所以事
===
君乎夫
君尊如
天勢相去至遠乃仕者率知義而
弗知恩不知
天至尊遠也乃曰惟天萬物父母
恩則若斯焉故曰天弗可欺
報本弗可以已也夫

translation_en:
…the assembled scholars who sat the three examination sessions numbered over four thousand six hundred. In accordance with the imperial decision, four hundred were selected as successful candidates. Their names and the finest of their compositions were compiled into a record for presentation to the throne.
Your servant then addressed the scholars, saying: “Ah! Scholars, your entry into service of the ruler begins today. But do you also understand how to serve him? The ruler is as exalted as Heaven, and the distance separating you from him in station is immense. Yet those who enter office generally recognize their duty but fail to recognize his grace. Do they not understand that Heaven is supremely exalted and remote, yet it is said, ‘Heaven is the father and mother of all things’? Such is its beneficence. Thus it is said, ‘Heaven must not be deceived, and one must never cease repaying the source of one’s blessings.’ Now, …

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
君上誠至尊遠然生成則
天也矧又以為才焉而拔之而爵
祿之則所尤厚也是可弗知
恩乎可弗思所以報乎可欺乎故
曰臣事君以忠蓋不可弗忠
也雖然亦知所謂忠乎夫忠
也者心之自盡者也無遠近
===
無彼此無隱顯而純然者也
是故利於公亦利於私者從
而盡心焉非忠也其事在公
其心乃在私也有利於公弗
利於私而盡心焉者乎非純
臣弗能也有其實亦有其名
者從而盡心焉非忠也其事

君上誠至尊遠，然生成則天也。矧又以為才焉，而拔之，而爵祿之，則所尤厚也。是可弗知恩乎？可弗思所以報乎？可欺乎？故曰：「臣事君以忠。」蓋不可弗忠也。雖然，亦知所謂忠乎？夫忠也者，心之自盡者也，無遠近，無彼此，無隱顯，而純然者也。
是故利於公亦利於私者，從而盡心焉，非忠也，其事在公，其心乃在私也。有利於公弗利於私而盡心焉者乎？非純臣弗能也。有其實亦有其名者，從而盡心焉，非忠也，其事
translation_en:
…the ruler is indeed supremely exalted and distant, yet in giving life and nurturing it he is Heaven itself. Moreover, when he recognizes a man's talent, promotes him, and grants him rank and emoluments, his generosity is especially great. Can one fail to acknowledge this favor? Can one fail to consider how to repay it? Can one deceive him? Thus it is said: “A minister serves his ruler with loyalty.” One cannot but be loyal. Yet do you also understand what loyalty means? Loyalty means giving one's heart to the utmost, without distinction between near and far, this and that, hidden and manifest, and with undivided sincerity.
Thus, to devote oneself wholeheartedly to something that benefits both the public interest and one's private interest is not loyalty: the undertaking concerns the public good, but one's heart is set on private advantage. Are there those who devote themselves wholeheartedly to something that benefits the public interest but not their private interest? Only a minister of undivided integrity can do so. To devote oneself wholeheartedly to something that brings both substantive achievement and reputation is not loyalty: the undertaking…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
在實其心乃在名也有有其
實無其名而盡心焉者乎非
純臣弗能也
主上所可知所可見者從而盡心
焉非忠也其事在
主上其心乃在
知見也有於所弗知弗見而盡
===
心焉者乎非純臣弗能也蓋
臣嘗見人之理家也乃不惟
才士即中人亦罔弗臧脫不
幸有弗臧也乃厥究亦多臧
也何者心誠求之故不遠也
至其理國事也不直中人即
才士亦罔或臧脫幸有臧也

蓋臣嘗見人之理家也，乃不惟才士，即中人亦罔弗臧。脫不幸有弗臧也，乃厥究亦多臧也。何者？心誠求之，故不遠也。至其理國事也，不直中人，即才士亦罔或臧。脫幸有臧也，
translation_en:
…lies in actual accomplishment, but his heart is set on reputation. Are there those who devote themselves wholeheartedly when there is actual accomplishment but no reputation to be gained? Only a minister of unmixed loyalty can do this. To devote oneself wholeheartedly to what the sovereign can know and see is not loyalty: one’s work concerns the sovereign, but one’s heart is set on being noticed. Are there those who devote themselves wholeheartedly to what the sovereign neither knows nor sees? Only a minister of unmixed loyalty can do this.
Your servant has observed how people manage their households. Not only talented men but even ordinary people invariably manage well. If, by misfortune, something goes badly, the ultimate outcome is nevertheless usually good. Why? Because they sincerely seek it in their hearts, they do not fall far short. When it comes to managing affairs of state, however, not only ordinary people but even talented men scarcely ever manage well. If, by good fortune, something goes well, …

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
乃厥究亦多弗臧也何者弗
既厥心也故曰不誠無物夫
苟既厥心則一為而一成百
為而百成敬斯謂之敬勤斯
謂之勤也苟弗既厥心也則
百為無一有焉即祗畏戰慄
非敬也即夙夜無息胼胝手
===
足非勤也何者非其心也非
其心則謀不審謀不審則不
當事機事不當機而能無僨
焉者寡矣矧克有濟是故曰
無物也夫無物之謂欺欺之
謂負而況可言報乎臣之道
必不可若斯也茲多士之進

punctuated: 乃厥究亦多弗臧也。何者？弗既厥心也。故曰：「不誠無物。」夫苟既厥心，則一為而一成，百為而百成；敬斯謂之敬，勤斯謂之勤也。苟弗既厥心也，則百為無一有焉；即祗畏戰慄，非敬也；即夙夜無息，胼胝手足，非勤也。何者？非其心也。非其心則謀不審，謀不審則不當事機。事不當機而能無僨焉者寡矣，矧克有濟！是故曰「無物」也。夫無物之謂欺，欺之謂負，而況可言報乎？臣之道必不可若斯也。茲多士之進
translation_en: …yet in the end, most such efforts likewise turn out badly. Why? Because they have not put their whole hearts into them. Thus it is said: “Without sincerity, there is nothing.” If one puts one’s whole heart into an undertaking, one action will bring one success, and a hundred actions a hundred successes. Only then does reverence deserve to be called reverence, and diligence deserve to be called diligence. If one does not put one’s whole heart into it, a hundred actions will yield not a single accomplishment. Even fearful trembling is no reverence; even ceaseless labor from dawn to night, until hands and feet are calloused, is no diligence. Why? Because one’s heart is not in it. If the heart is not in it, plans will not be carefully considered; if plans are not carefully considered, they will not fit the circumstances of affairs. Few undertakings that fail to fit the circumstances can avoid ruin, much less achieve success! This is why it is said, “There is nothing.” To produce nothing in this way is to deceive; to deceive is to betray one’s trust. How, then, could one speak of repaying the sovereign? The way of a minister must never be like this. Now, as these many scholars advance…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
也猶尚如未汩之泉而未斲
之璞也故臣惓惓焉以人臣
之所以為心者相戒勉冀有
所先入而弗以巧宦之說投
也諸士誠聽臣言終其身弗
改庶可少裨於用而於臣圖
報之心亦可少償焉厥或弗
===
聽或聽亦罔終卒致僨事則
臣之心有欲盡而弗得者矣
然亦可如何矣雖然
皇上之明日月也既厥心或弗既
厥心弗能逃也既厥心
雨露之弗既厥心
雷霆之亦弗能逃也諸士固宜

punctuated: 也，猶尚如未汩之泉而未斲之璞也。故臣惓惓焉，以人臣之所以為心者相戒勉，冀有所先入，而弗以巧宦之說投也。諸士誠聽臣言，終其身弗改，庶可少裨於用，而於臣圖報之心亦可少償焉。厥或弗聽，或聽亦罔終，卒致僨事，則臣之心有欲盡而弗得者矣。然亦可如何矣！雖然，皇上之明，日月也。既厥心或弗既厥心，弗能逃也。既厥心，雨露之；弗既厥心，雷霆之，亦弗能逃也。諸士固宜
translation_en:
…are still like springs not yet muddied and jade not yet hewn. Thus your servant earnestly admonishes and encourages them concerning the disposition that should guide a minister, hoping that this teaching may take root first, before doctrines of cunning advancement in office are offered to them. If these gentlemen truly heed your servant’s words and remain steadfast throughout their lives, they may render some small service in office, and your servant’s desire to repay imperial favor may likewise find some small fulfillment. Should they fail to listen, or listen but fail to persevere, and ultimately bring affairs to ruin, then your servant’s wish to give his utmost will remain unfulfilled. Yet what could be done?

Nevertheless, Your Majesty’s discernment is like the sun and moon. Whether they devote themselves wholeheartedly or fail to do so cannot escape it. Those who devote themselves wholeheartedly receive your rain and dew; those who do not receive your thunder and lightning, which likewise cannot be escaped. These gentlemen surely ought to…

translation_en:
…know to exercise caution in their own conduct. What need, then, is there for your servant’s words?

For this examination, the following servants of Your Majesty served as Associate Examiners. Tang was Assistant Supervisor of Instruction. Min was Expositor. Jin was Rectifier. Tai, Ziqiang, Dashou, and Shimei were Senior Compilers. Hao, Gui, Siwei, and Youding were Junior Compilers. Shouting was Chief Supervising Secretary. Yijing was Left Supervising Secretary. Shi was Supervising Secretary. Qidi was a Bureau Director. Jin and Sansheng were Vice Directors.

The Censors Bangzhen and Chengyin served as examination monitors. Together they brought the work to completion. Responsibility for guarding and inspecting outside the examination compound fell to the Censors Gu Tingdui and Zhou Hongzu; these additional appointments were instituted this year. Previously, the conduct of the scholars had somewhat exceeded proper bounds, becoming conspicuous enough to draw criticism. An imperial edict expressly required stricter controls, and these appointments were therefore added. I record them all here out of respect for …

translation_en:
Yu Youding, a Compiler in the Hanlin Academy, held the civil rank chengshi lang. His courtesy name was Bingzhong; he was from Yin County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the renxu year (1562).

Xing Shouting, Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for War, held the civil rank chengshi lang. His courtesy name was Shaonan; he was from Linying County, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the bingchen year (1556).

Ouyang Yijing, Left Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Revenue, held the civil rank congshi lang. His courtesy name was Sizhi; he was from Pengze County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiwei year (1559).

Zhou Shi was a Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Personnel. His courtesy name was Xingshu; he was from Qiantang County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the bingchen year (1556).

Lin Qidi, a Secretary acting as Director of the Guizhou Bureau in the Ministry of Revenue, held the civil rank chengde lang. His courtesy name was Minjiao; he was from Putian County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiwei year (1559).

Wu Jin, a Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Merit Titles in the Ministry of Personnel, held the civil rank chengde lang. His courtesy name was Lifu; he was from Jingxing County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Chang Sansheng, a Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of the Arsenal in the Ministry of War, held the civil rank chengde lang. His courtesy name was Xilu; he was from Sizhou, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the bingchen year (1556).

Examination Monitoring Officials:

Li Bangzhen, an Investigating Censor for the Henan Circuit, held the civil rank wenlin lang. His courtesy name was Zihuai; he was from Feicheng County, Shandong, and became a metropolitan graduate in the gengxu year (1550).

Bao Chengyin, an Investigating Censor for the Zhejiang Circuit, held the civil rank wenlin lang. His courtesy name was Zichuan; he was from Changzhi County, Shanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the bingchen year (1556).

Proctors:

Yu Li was a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites. His courtesy name was Jili; he was from Maping County, Guangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1562).

Ming Xi, a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the civil rank chengzhi lang. His courtesy name was Bo'an; he was from Lanxi County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiwei year (1559).

Officials Responsible for Printing Examination Papers:

Pang Yuan, Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the civil rank fengyi dafu. His courtesy name was Weiming; he was from Wujiang County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1553).

Qi Yuanzuo, a Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the civil rank chengzhi lang. His courtesy name was Xizhong; he was from Jiaxing County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1562).

Yang Wan, a Central Secretariat Drafter, held the civil rank zhengshi lang. His courtesy name was Ziquan; he was registered in Anning Subprefecture, Yunnan, and was a native of Dantu County, Zhili. He was a student admitted by virtue of an official's status.

punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

綏之斯來，動之斯和。

人道敏政，地道敏樹。夫政也者，蒲盧也。

詩曰：「天生蒸民，有物有則。民之秉夷，好是懿德。」孔子曰：「爲此詩者，其知道乎！故有物必有則，民之秉夷也，故好是懿德。」

易

上九：視履考祥，其旋元吉。象曰：「元吉在上，大有慶也。」

大壯，大者壯也。剛以動，故壯。大壯利貞，大者正也。正大而天地之情可見矣。

與天地相似，故不違。

說萬物者，莫說乎澤。

書

簫韶九成，鳳凰來儀。

夾右碣石，入于河。

文王惟克厥宅心，乃克立兹常事，司牧人
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“If he brings them peace, they come to him; if he rouses them, they live in harmony.”

“The way of human beings brings government swiftly to fruition; the way of earth brings plants swiftly to growth. Government is like rushes.”

“The Book of Poetry says: ‘Heaven gives birth to the multitude of people; wherever there is a thing, there is a principle. The people hold fast to their constant nature and love this excellent virtue.’ Confucius said: ‘The author of this poem surely understood the Way! Thus, wherever there is a thing, there must be a principle; because the people hold fast to their constant nature, they love this excellent virtue.’”

Book of Changes

“Nine at the top: Examine your conduct and assess its auspices. On its completion, supreme good fortune. The Image says: ‘Supreme good fortune at the top: there is great cause for celebration.’”

“Great Strength means that the great is strong. Firmness combined with movement produces strength. ‘Great Strength benefits from correctness’ means that the great is correct. Through correctness and greatness, the true nature of Heaven and Earth can be seen.”

“It resembles Heaven and Earth and therefore does not run counter to them.”

“Of all that delights the myriad things, nothing is more delightful than the marsh.”

Book of Documents

“When the Xiao Shao music had been performed nine times, phoenixes came to display their stately bearing.”

“Passing Jieshi on their right, they entered the Yellow River.”

“King Wen was able to set his heart aright, and thus could establish these regular offices and oversee and shepherd the people …”

translation_en:
…thereby being able to employ men of outstanding virtue. King Wen did not assume concurrent responsibility for the various pronouncements, lawsuits, and matters requiring care; he instructed the officials charged with governing the people. Whether their conduct was proper or improper, and in the various lawsuits and matters requiring care, King Wen did not presume to take direct cognizance of these affairs.
May you, Duke, thus complete the establishment of Zhou and lay a foundation without end.

Book of Odes
They dye some black and some yellow; our vermilion is brilliantly bright.
The multitudes became fish; the tortoise-and-snake banners became falcon banners. The diviner interpreted it: “The multitudes becoming fish means a year of abundant harvests; the tortoise-and-snake banners becoming falcon banners means households will be numerous and flourishing.”
At the Biyong ceremonial college in Haojing, from the west and from the east, from the south and from the north, none thought of withholding submission.
Profoundly wise was Shang; long had its auspicious signs appeared.

Spring and Autumn Annals
Autumn, the seventh month. Sixth year of Duke Yin.
The army of Song attacked Chen; men of Wei came to Chen’s aid. Twelfth year of Duke Xuan.
Spring. The lord of Jin sent Han Chuan to come and convey instructions concerning the lands of Wenyang: they were to be returned to Qi. Eighth year of Duke Cheng.
Jin attacked Xianyu. Twelfth year of Duke Zhao. Autumn. Xun Wu of Jin led an army to attack Xianyu. Fifteenth year of Duke Zhao.

Book of Rites

text:

誠若有美而文而誠若
德者性之端也樂者德之華也金石絲竹

動其容也三者本於心然後樂器從之

三年耕，必有一年之食；九年耕，必有三年之食。

君子之於禮也，有所竭情盡慎，致其敬而誠若；有美而文而誠若。

德者，性之端也；樂者，德之華也；金石絲竹，樂之器也。詩，言其志也；歌，咏其聲也；舞，動其容也。三者本於心，然後樂器從之。是故情深而文明，氣盛而化神，和順積中而英華發外。

盡其道，端其義，而教生焉。

第貳場

明君恭己而成功。

translation_en:
Three years of cultivation must yield a reserve of food sufficient for one year; nine years of cultivation must yield a reserve sufficient for three years.

In observing ritual, the gentleman sometimes exhausts his feelings and exercises the utmost care, expressing his reverence with an air of sincerity; sometimes he displays beauty and refinement, likewise with an air of sincerity.

Virtue is the manifestation of human nature; music is the flowering of virtue. Metal, stone, silk, and bamboo are the instruments of music. Poetry expresses one's aspirations; singing gives voice to one's sounds; dancing sets one's bodily form in motion. These three originate in the heart, and musical instruments then accompany them. Thus, when feelings are deep, their patterned expression is brilliant; when vital energy is abundant, its transforming influence is wondrous. Harmony and accord accumulate within, and their splendid flowering manifests itself outwardly.

Fully realize its Way and set its principles right, and teaching arises from them.

The enlightened ruler holds himself in reverence and achieves success.

Question: Portents signifying the imperial mandate have a very ancient origin. The Book of Odes speaks of “receiving the mandate,” and the Book of Documents of “perpetuating the mandate.” Although neither explicitly sets forth a doctrine of such portents, are not the ode “Dark Swallow” and the chapter “Presentation of Grain” concerned with them? When Heaven intends to bestow abundant aid upon an extraordinary sage, so as to favor and pacify the four quarters, there must be a portent of receiving the mandate to herald his advent. When a sage king grandly establishes extraordinary achievements and thereby wins Heaven’s favor, there must likewise be a portent of perpetuating the mandate to manifest Heaven’s response. Such is certainly the principle, without delay or deviation [?].

Chao and Sui belong to the distant past. By the age of the Five Emperors and Three Kings, the portents clearly recorded in charts and chronicles were resplendent indeed. Have you examined them and come to understand them? Truly, they equaled the Five Emperors and Three Kings in greatness. Our Emperor, supremely divine and supremely sage, has responded to the fortunes of the age and brought about a restoration, magnificently establishing achievements worthy of Heaven. title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
天庥之隆渥而綏
景祐於無疆者固必有道也亦能仰窺而頌述
歟夫觀天莫繪遊聖難言固矣然
玄貺集而弗彰
洪業成而弗贊非臣子之心也諸士其極思而
恭陳之固未能盡闡其
盛庶或得一二焉
問孔子云可與共學未可與適道可與適
道未可與立可與立未可與權則是權
===
者聖人之事而學聖人者所當知也自
今言之權固一物也而以之言道何取
義歟且聖人直言權耳後儒乃以經權
並稱果一事歟抑二事歟彼反經合道
之說其謬固不足辯獨謂常則守經而
變則行權然歟否歟夫權以達變固也
至於居常之時其人倫物理雖至纖細
莫不各有當然不易之則然所以各當
其則而無過不及之差者果孰使之然歟

今言之權固一物也而以之言道何取

並稱果一事歟抑二事歟彼反經合道

punctuated:
天庥之隆渥，而綏景祐於無疆者，固必有道也。亦能仰窺而頌述歟？夫觀天莫繪，遊聖難言，固矣。然玄貺集而弗彰，洪業成而弗贊，非臣子之心也。諸士其極思而恭陳之，固未能盡闡其盛，庶或得一二焉。
問：孔子云：「可與共學，未可與適道；可與適道，未可與立；可與立，未可與權。」則是權者，聖人之事，而學聖人者所當知也。自今言之，權固一物也，而以之言道，何取義歟？且聖人直言權耳，後儒乃以經權並稱，果一事歟？抑二事歟？彼反經合道之說，其謬固不足辯。獨謂常則守經，而變則行權，然歟？否歟？夫權以達變，固也。至於居常之時，其人倫物理，雖至纖細，莫不各有當然不易之則。然所以各當其則，而無過不及之差者，果孰使之然歟？
translation_en:
…Heaven’s abundant and generous protection, and secure its great blessings without end: there must assuredly be a way to accomplish this. Can you also discern it reverently and recount it in praise? To contemplate Heaven is to confront what cannot be depicted, and to approach the sage is to confront what is difficult to express [?]: this is certainly so. Yet to leave divine gifts unproclaimed when they gather, and great achievements unpraised when they are accomplished, is contrary to the sentiments of a subject. You candidates should apply your utmost thought and respectfully set forth your answers. Though you surely cannot fully expound this splendor, perhaps you may capture one or two aspects of it.
Question: Confucius said: “Those with whom one can study are not necessarily those with whom one can proceed toward the Way; those with whom one can proceed toward the Way are not necessarily those with whom one can stand firm; those with whom one can stand firm are not necessarily those with whom one can exercise discretionary judgment.” Thus discretionary judgment (quan) is the work of the sage, and something that those who would learn to become sages ought to understand. Speaking in present-day terms, quan is certainly a physical object—a weighing weight. What meaning is drawn from it when it is used to discuss the Way? Moreover, the sage spoke simply of quan, whereas later Confucian scholars paired constant principle (jing) with discretionary judgment (quan). Are these really one thing, or two? The error in the claim that one “departs from constant principle to accord with the Way” scarcely merits refutation. But is the claim that one preserves constant principle in ordinary circumstances and exercises discretion in changing circumstances correct or not? That discretion serves to respond to changing circumstances is certain. Yet in ordinary circumstances, human relationships and the principles of things, down to their finest details, each have their own proper and unchanging standard. What, then, enables each to conform to its standard, without erring through excess or deficiency?

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
歟且善用權者莫若孔子今觀其動靜
語黙孰非權者果何分於常變歟程子
謂權即是經是矣而朱子則云經權亦
當有辨果孰為定論歟乃世又有所謂

歟夫權信難言然聖人之權既所當求
非聖人之權又所當擇則不可以無言

歟？且善用權者莫若孔子。今觀其動靜語黙，孰非權者？果何分於常變歟？程子謂權即是經，是矣；而朱子則云經權亦當有辨，果孰為定論歟？乃世又有所謂權謀權術者，其為害甚大，亦可謂之權歟？夫權信難言，然聖人之權既所當求，非聖人之權又所當擇，則不可以無言也。諸生誦法孔子，或有得其說者焉，其明著於篇，用觀所見。

問：局曲之士難與立功，利巧之人難與任事。自古濟天下之務者，固非豪傑不能也。乃豪傑所為，則有甚可疑者。如周公佐周，不免東征之舉；孔子相魯，先行兩觀之事。何乃遠人情若是歟？此聖人事，吾不敢議。後代乃有天下甫定而即為治未央者，有率軍討逆而先試以左右袒者，有身處偽朝至與嬖倖博陸者，有叛卒投虜，報至弗答，且以為吾固遣之
translation_en:
…? Moreover, none excelled Confucius in exercising discretionary judgment (quan). Looking now at his activity and repose, his speech and silence, which did not involve such judgment? What distinction, then, was there between ordinary and exceptional circumstances? Master Cheng said that discretionary judgment is itself the constant norm (jing), and this is correct; yet Master Zhu said that the constant norm and discretionary judgment must also be distinguished. Which, then, should be taken as the definitive view? Furthermore, there are what people call expedient schemes and manipulative techniques. These do very great harm: can they too be called discretionary judgment? Discretionary judgment is indeed difficult to discuss. Yet, since we ought to seek the discretionary judgment of the sages and discriminate concerning that of those who are not sages, we cannot leave it undiscussed. You students recite the teachings of Confucius and take him as your model; some among you may have grasped the explanation. Set it forth clearly in your essays, so that we may see your understanding.

Question: It is difficult to accomplish great deeds with narrow-minded scholars, and difficult to entrust affairs to those who are crafty in pursuing their own advantage. Since antiquity, only men of outstanding ability have been capable of successfully managing the affairs of the realm. Yet some deeds of such men are deeply open to question. For example, the Duke of Zhou, in assisting the Zhou dynasty, could not avoid undertaking an eastern campaign; Confucius, serving as chief minister of Lu, first carried out the affair at the two gate towers [the execution of Shaozheng Mao]. Why were their actions so far removed from ordinary human feelings? These were the affairs of sages, which I dare not criticize. In later ages, however, there was one who, when the realm had only just been pacified, immediately undertook the construction of Weiyang Palace; one who led troops to suppress rebellion but first tested them by having them bare their left or right arms; one who served at an illegitimate court and even played liubo with an influential favorite; and one who, when rebellious soldiers defected to the enemy, made no response upon receiving the report, and moreover maintained, “I myself had sent them…”

text:
者夫數子者皆當時所謂豪傑也而所
爲若是初蓋有疑之者焉然卒以濟事
而天下賴之豈倖成歟抑豪傑所見自
有異乎人者歟傳云非常之原黎民懼
焉及臻厥成天下晏如也夫臻厥成焉

者。夫數子者，皆當時所謂豪傑也，而所爲若是，初蓋有疑之者焉。然卒以濟事，而天下賴之，豈倖成歟？抑豪傑所見，自有異乎人者歟？傳云：「非常之原，黎民懼焉；及臻厥成，天下晏如也。」夫臻厥成焉，固可自表著矣；不知黎民懼焉之際，果何以用之歟？且未用之先，靡所嘗試，或有假之者焉，抑何以辨歟？夫今兹之舉，誠願得豪傑爲世用也。諸士無有因而自見者乎？其各以意對，無徒勦說焉也。

問：昔人有言：「立治有體，論治者貴識體。」則夫人臣欲以佐太平之業者，不可不審也。嘗觀漢宋二史所記載，佐元祐者，於新法之害民而更張之，可謂得善治之體矣。而佐元康者，則好觀故事，數條奏請施行之，何歟？乃若當以德化民之君，而陳治安之策；輔深仁厚澤之主，而答手詔條陳十事，其果論治而識體，如所
translation_en:
…These men were all regarded as outstanding figures in their day. Yet their actions were such that, at first, some surely doubted them. In the end, however, they accomplished their purposes, and all under Heaven benefited. Did they succeed by luck? Or do outstanding men possess insights different from those of others? The commentary says: “At the inception of an extraordinary undertaking, the common people are afraid; when it reaches completion, all under Heaven are at ease.” Once such men have achieved success, their worth can certainly become manifest of itself. But while the common people are still afraid, on what grounds should they actually be employed? Moreover, before they have been employed, when they have never been tested, there may be some who falsely assume this character. How are they to be distinguished? In this examination, we sincerely hope to find outstanding men for service to the age. Are there none among you candidates who will take this opportunity to make yourselves known? Let each answer according to his own judgment, without merely repeating borrowed arguments.

Question: A man of former times said: “Establishing good government has its essential principles; in discussing government, what matters is to understand those principles.” Thus, those who wish, as ministers, to assist in the work of bringing about great peace must examine them carefully. I have read the accounts in the histories of the Han and Song. Those who served during the Yuanyou reign period altered the New Policies because they harmed the people; they may be said to have grasped the essential principles of good government. Yet one who served during the Yuankang reign period delighted in examining precedents and repeatedly submitted itemized memorials requesting their implementation. Why was this? Then there was one who, serving a ruler who transformed the people through virtue, presented proposals for securing good government and peace; and another who, assisting a sovereign of profound benevolence and abundant beneficence, responded to an edict in the emperor’s own hand by setting forth ten matters. In discussing government, did they truly understand its essential principles, as they were described …

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
稱通達國體老練世事者歟然一則悉
采用之一則畧施行焉其所遇不同又
何歟不知二賢之言亦有可裨於今時
者否歟願詳言之以觀識治體之學
問山澤之儲民生之利用存焉自太公立
圜法以權百貨之中管仲煮東海以佐
一匡之業而後世之言鹽筴錢幣者宗
之要以經制斯民通利上下法之不可
以已也漢唐而下其制盖益密矣以言
===
鹽筴則有官給器而募民煮之法有官
自貸而總其利之法有召商人貨中引
之法是孰為適宜歟以言錢幣則有兩
銖四銖八銖之異其品亦仄比輪公式
之異其名當五當十當千之異其用是
孰為折衷歟我
朝參酌往古設鹽運司鹽課司以榷鹽筴設
寶源局以鑄錢幣制易而不煩法信而
可守視歷代最稱善矣廼邇者淮鹾底

問：山澤之儲，民生之利用存焉。自太公立圜法，以權百貨之中，管仲煮東海，以佐一匡之業，而後世之言鹽筴錢幣者宗之。要以經制斯民，通利上下，法之不可以已也。漢唐而下，其制盖益密矣。以言鹽筴，則有官給器而募民煮之法，有官自貸而總其利之法，有召商人貨中引之法，是孰為適宜歟？以言錢幣，則有兩銖、四銖、八銖之異其品，亦仄比輪公式之異其名，當五、當十、當千之異其用，是孰為折衷歟？我朝參酌往古，設鹽運司、鹽課司以榷鹽筴，設寶源局以鑄錢幣，制易而不煩，法信而可守，視歷代最稱善矣。廼邇者淮鹾底
translation_en:
…those described as thoroughly understanding the principles of state and being seasoned in worldly affairs? Yet in one case his proposals were adopted in full, while in the other they were implemented only in part. Why, again, did they meet with different receptions? Might the words of these two worthies also offer something beneficial for the present day? Explain in detail, so that we may assess your understanding of the essentials of government.
Question: The resources stored in mountains and marshes provide useful things upon which the people's livelihood depends. Taigong established monetary regulations to balance the values of all commodities, and Guan Zhong boiled seawater from the eastern sea to support his achievement of unifying the realm. Later writers on salt administration and coinage took them as their models. The essential purpose is to order the people's economic affairs and allow benefits to circulate between those above and below; these are arrangements that cannot be dispensed with. From the Han and Tang onward, the regulations presumably became increasingly detailed. In salt administration, there was a method whereby the government supplied equipment and recruited people to boil salt; a method whereby the government itself made loans [?] and controlled all the profits; and a method whereby merchants were invited to supply goods in exchange for salt certificates. Which of these is most appropriate? As for coinage, denominations differed in weight—two zhu, four zhu, and eight zhu; their names also differed, as in the doubtful sequence “ze bi lun gong shi” [?]; and their circulating values differed, with coins worth five, ten, or a thousand. What should serve as the proper standard among these? Our dynasty considered the practices of antiquity and established Salt Distribution Commissions and Salt Tax Offices to administer the salt monopoly, and the Coinage Service to cast coins. Its arrangements are simple and uncomplicated, and its regulations dependable and capable of being maintained. Compared with successive dynasties, these may be judged the best. title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
滯邊餉告詘制錢沮塞市闤生疑若是
者何故說者謂工本之鹽增則正課壅
私鑄之錢盛則制寶淆其亦然歟停工
本斷私鑄果可使泉貨阜通公私兼濟
歟且鑄錢利重而私鑄則其奸微故察
之為難工本之增度支專為足邊計也
茲而損之將安所取盈歟夫授握算而
不知縱橫非適用之器也多士於茲二
者諒有成畫試為我陳之

punctuated: 滯，邊餉告詘，制錢沮塞，市闤生疑。若是者何故？說者謂工本之鹽增，則正課壅；私鑄之錢盛，則制寶淆。其亦然歟？停工本，斷私鑄，果可使泉貨阜通，公私兼濟歟？且鑄錢利重，而私鑄則其奸微，故察之為難。工本之增，度支專為足邊計也，茲而損之，將安所取盈歟？夫授握算而不知縱橫，非適用之器也。多士於茲二者，諒有成畫，試為我陳之。
translation_en: …has become stagnant, funds for provisioning the frontier are reported insufficient, the circulation of officially minted coins is obstructed, and doubts arise in the marketplaces. Why is this so? Some say that when the quantity of salt allocated to cover production costs increases, the regular salt revenue is impeded; and when privately minted coins proliferate, the official currency becomes debased. Is this indeed the case? Would ending the production-cost allocation and suppressing private minting truly make currency abundant and freely circulating, meeting both public and private needs? Moreover, minting coins is highly profitable, but illicit private minting is concealed and therefore difficult to detect. The fiscal authorities increased the production-cost allocation specifically to provide adequately for the frontier. If it is now reduced, where will the shortfall be made up? Someone given counting rods to hold who does not know how to arrange them vertically and horizontally is no suitable instrument for practical service. You candidates surely have well-developed plans concerning these two matters. Set them forth for me.

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

綏之斯來，動之斯和。

陳棟

同考試官左給事中歐陽批：「場中作此義者，類多牽滯。此作辭不費，而發揮神化之妙，不啻躬逢其盛，亦可謂善言聖人者。」

同考試官都給事中邢批：「此題作者，篇篇活套，種種陳言，殊多可厭。沉着古雅，獨見此篇，宜錄以式。」

同考試官編修李批：「體認精切，結構渾成，聖人神化之妙，宛然在目，可式多士矣。錄之。」

同考試官修撰丁批：「語義場中襲用陳套，令人厭觀。此作不事造語，而會意成章，蓋文之以理勝者。錄之。」

同考試官右中允陳批：「說理渾融，措詞雅健，且斯字發得尤切，語義之最佳者。」

考試官侍讀學士胡批：「醇雅中有精思，可錄。」

考試官學士高批：「平正。」
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“When he brings them peace, they come to him; when he moves them, they become harmonious.”

Chen Dong

Comment by Associate Examiner Ouyang, Left Supervising Secretary: “Most essays on this passage in the examination are strained and labored. This essay wastes no words, yet elucidates the marvel of the sage’s numinous transforming influence so vividly that it is as though one personally witnessed it at its height. Its author may indeed be said to speak well of the sage.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Xing, Chief Supervising Secretary: “Among essays on this topic, piece after piece uses stock formulas and every sort of stale expression; much of it is quite tiresome. This piece alone displays depth and composure, with classical elegance. It should be included as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Hanlin Compiler: “Its understanding is precise and penetrating, its structure a seamless whole. The marvel of the sage’s numinous transforming influence appears vividly before one’s eyes. It can serve as a model for the many candidates. Include it.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Ding, Hanlin Senior Compiler: “The essays on the Analects passage in this examination repeat worn-out formulas, making them tiresome to read. This piece does not labor at contriving phrases; rather, it grasps the meaning and forms it into a coherent composition. It is an essay that excels through its reasoning. Include it.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Right Assistant Director of Instruction: “The exposition of principle is thoroughly integrated, and the wording elegant and vigorous. Its development of the word si (‘then’) is especially apt. It is the best of the essays on the Analects passage.”

Comment by Examiner Hu, Hanlin Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: “Within its purity and elegance there is penetrating thought. It merits inclusion.”

Comment by Examiner Gao, Hanlin Academician: “Balanced and correct.”

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
□者擬聖人之治有神於得民者有神於化民
者盖民心難得而尤難以化也聖人有以感之
而效可立致焉非至神其孰能如此哉子貢曉
子禽之意如此盖謂有德者必有業然德之未
至者以形用而德之至者以神用夫子天下之
至聖也設見諸行事豈但所謂立斯立道斯行
而已乎民罔常懷固必綏之而後来也然有未
必來者况斯來耶夫子弗綏則已苟於既立而
加惠焉亦為之懷保云爾而非若是其幾也然
===
===
有是懷保之仁即有是歸附之義近孰與被已
相招矣遠孰與聞已相應矣有不疾而自速者
焉何也綏之神故也所以潛為之格者非惟天
下弗知而聖人亦弗知也民心罔中固必動之
而後和也然有未必和者况斯和耶夫子弗動
則已苟於既道而振德焉亦為之鼓舞云爾而
非若是其幾也然有是鼓舞之機即有是變化
之妙以章百姓既昭明矣以協萬邦既時雍矣
有不行而自至者焉何也動之神故也所以默

…[illegible] considers the sage’s government: there is something numinous in his winning over the people, and something numinous in his transforming them. For the people’s hearts are difficult to win, and still more difficult to transform. The sage has the means to move them, and the effects can be achieved at once. Who but one supremely numinous could accomplish this? Such was the meaning of Zigong’s explanation to Ziqin. His point was that one who possesses virtue must have achievements; yet those whose virtue is not perfected act through outward forms, while those whose virtue is perfected act through numinous influence. The Master was the supreme sage of the world. Had his qualities been manifested in government, would the outcome have been merely what is meant by “when he establishes them, they take their stand; when he guides them, they proceed”?

The people are not constant in their affections, so they must indeed be brought peace before they will come. Yet even then some may not come; how much less can they be expected to come immediately! If the Master did not bring them peace, that would be the end of it. But if, having established them, he further bestowed his bounty upon them, he would merely be cherishing and protecting them, without anticipating such results [?]. Yet wherever there is this benevolence that cherishes and protects, there is a corresponding sense of rightness that leads people to attach themselves to him. Those nearby—who has yet received his bounty?—already summon one another; those far away—who has yet heard of it?—already respond to one another [?]. Things become swift of themselves, without haste. Why? Because of the numinous power of his bringing them peace. The means by which he imperceptibly reaches them are unknown not only to all under Heaven, but even to the sage himself.

The people’s hearts do not hold steadily to the mean, so they must indeed be stirred before they become harmonious. Yet even then some may not become harmonious; how much less can they be expected to become harmonious immediately! If the Master did not stir them, that would be the end of it. Yet wherever there is this impulse that rouses and inspires, there is the wondrous efficacy of transformation. 為之運者，非惟天下相忘，而聖人亦自忘也。夫子至神之用，一至於此，是豈人之所能測乎？測之不能，而可及耶？子乃謂「豈賢於我」，謬矣！抑夫子嘗云：「王者必世而後仁。」而子貢於夫子則極言其治效之速，何歟？盖夫子以成功言，所謂高厚悠久者也；子貢以感應言，所謂過化存神者也。然必世之仁，其感應未嘗不速，而綏來動和，亦必愈久而愈極其盛也。故不觀子貢之言，無以知聖德之為神；不觀夫子之言，無以知王道之為大。合之則備矣。

translation_en:
…what silently sets this in motion is such that not only does all under Heaven forget its operation, but the sage himself also forgets it. The Master's supremely numinous efficacy reaches such a height: how could anyone fathom it? If one cannot even fathom it, how could one equal it? Yet you say, “How is he superior to me?” You are mistaken!
Yet the Master once said, “Even with a true king, it would take a generation before benevolence prevailed.” Why, then, did Zigong speak so emphatically of how swiftly the Master's government would achieve its effects? The Master was speaking of completed achievement—what is described as lofty, profound, enduring, and lasting. Zigong was speaking of influence and response—what is described as transforming wherever one passes and exerting a numinous influence wherever one abides. Yet the benevolence that requires a generation has never been slow in eliciting a response; and bringing people to come through reassurance and to harmony through inspiration must likewise grow ever more flourishing with time. Thus, without considering Zigong's words, one cannot understand the numinous character of sagely virtue; without considering the Master's words, one cannot understand the greatness of the kingly Way. Taken together, the two accounts are complete.
“In the way of human beings, government flourishes readily; in the way of earth, trees flourish readily. Government is like reeds and rushes.”
Chen Jingbang
Associate Examiner Lin, Acting Bureau Director, comments: “People readily bring government into effect, and government itself is readily brought into effect. Writers generally fail to develop this point. This essay grasps the meaning closely and clearly, and its language is also refined and elegant. It is among the very best compositions and should be recorded as a model.”
Associate Examiner Zhang, Compiler, comments: “Throughout, the essay very clearly distinguishes and analyzes the meanings concerning people and government. Its language and spirit are elegant, vigorous, ample, and fluent. Among essays on the meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean, none equals this one. Record it.”

The sage explains that people are inherently capable of readily putting government into effect, and that government itself is readily put into effect. Establishing government through people is like planting trees in the earth: it is already easy. How much more so when government is as readily brought forth as reeds and rushes! In telling this to the ruler of Lu, the sage expressed the highest expectations of him. The government of Kings Wen and Wu can certainly be examined and understood. But why must its implementation or cessation depend upon people? It is truly because of the way people work: when an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers share the same virtue, they can establish a generous and capacious framework of government; when they rise and rejoice with one heart [?], they can achieve the results of enlightened and vigorous government. When their spiritual energies are brought to bear, it takes only the execution of a measure for everything from rectifying the court to reaching the myriad people to become effective. When their resolve is applied, it takes only a change of direction for everything extending from households and the state to all within the Four Seas to be reached. This may be compared to the earth’s readiness to grow trees. Transformed by its abundant virtue and nourished by its rich fertility, could anything planted there fail to grow quickly? Such is people’s readiness to bring government into effect. If only the right people are obtained, there will naturally be no measure of government that cannot be implemented.
Moreover, government is what the sages have planned and ordered. The spirit of “The Ospreys” (Guanju; transcribed here as 關睢 [?]) and “The Qilin’s Hoofs” (Linzhi), applied in laws and institutions, is wholly good and has demonstrable effects. Government is also what the reigning kings have modified through subtraction and addition. 商，又宜民而不悖。惟弗立耳，而立之斯立，初無俟於積累也；惟弗行耳，而行之斯行，非有待於更張也。又譬則樹中之蒲盧然，其生也勃焉，其成也忽焉，凡植焉者有能先之者乎？噫！地道敏樹矣，而蒲盧又易生，苟得地以種之，豈不尤速乎？不然，雖易生之物，有不能自生者也。人道敏政矣，而王政又易舉，苟得人以舉之，豈不尤速乎？不然，雖易舉之政，有不能自舉者也。政之繫乎人也如此夫！抑此夫子憲章文武而欲行周公之道者也。周禮在魯，文獻既存，而俗有先王之遺，則至道又無難者，故於魯君特惓惓耳。然論政莫備於此，言固在也。有其舉之，則蒲盧之易，百世無不然者，豈特魯哉？

translation_en:
…Shang, and they also suit the people without going against what is right. It is merely a matter of not establishing them: once established, they stand, without any initial need for gradual accumulation. It is merely a matter of not putting them into practice: once put into practice, they operate, without awaiting reform. They are also like reeds among growing plants: their growth is vigorous, and they reach maturity swiftly. Can any other planted thing outstrip them? Ah! The way of earth brings rapid growth to plants, and reeds are particularly easy to grow. If suitable ground is found in which to plant them, will they not grow still faster? Otherwise, even things that grow easily cannot grow of themselves. The way of humanity brings government rapidly to fruition, and kingly government is particularly easy to implement. If the right people are found to implement it, will it not take effect still faster? Otherwise, even forms of government that are easy to implement cannot implement themselves. Such is government’s dependence upon people!

Moreover, this expresses the Master’s purpose in taking Kings Wen and Wu as his models and wishing to put the Duke of Zhou’s Way into practice. The rites of Zhou remained in Lu; both written records and worthy men survived, and its customs retained the legacy of the former kings. Thus even the highest Way would present no difficulty, and this was why he addressed the ruler of Lu with such particular earnestness. Yet no discussion of government is more comprehensive than this, and his words remain. Given someone to put it into practice [?], it will be as easy as growing reeds: this holds true for a hundred generations. How could it apply only to Lu?

The Book of Odes says: “Heaven gives birth to the multitude of the people; where there are things, there are their principles. The people hold fast to their constant nature and love this excellent virtue.” Confucius said: “The author of this ode surely understood the Way! Thus, wherever there are things, there must be their principles; because the people hold fast to their constant nature, they love this excellent virtue.”

Yi Zaiting

大賢引詩及聖人贊詩之辭所以明性善也盖
物則各具而懿德同好則人性之善明矣非大
賢引詩及聖言以證之何以知其然哉想其答
公都子之意若謂以情善而徵性善吾之論性
固若此矣然非獨吾言之也古人亦有言之者
也詩云天生蒸民有物有則謂生理之出諸天
者然也民之秉彝好是懿德謂良心之在於人
者然也孔子讀而贊之曰為此詩者其知性情
□□何則器形而下道形而上固未始□□

難在點撥聯絡。是作辭不費，而肯綮如見，妙解者。
同考試官編修佘批：融會孔子言詩之意，而屬詞嚴密，闡理詳明，是邃於性學者。
同考試官編修萬批：辭確意盡，知道之文也。

大賢引詩及聖人贊詩之辭，所以明性善也。蓋物則各具，而懿德同好，則人性之善明矣。非大賢引詩及聖言以證之，何以知其然哉？想其答公都子之意，若謂：以情善而徵性善，吾之論性固若此矣。然非獨吾言之也，古人亦有言之者也。《詩》云：「天生蒸民，有物有則。」謂生理之出諸天者然也。「民之秉彝，好是懿德。」謂良心之在於人者然也。孔子讀而贊之曰：「為此詩者，其知性情之道乎！」何則？器形而下，道形而上，固未始□猶
translation_en:
…The difficulty lies in bringing out the crucial points and connecting them. This composition wastes no words, yet makes the essential joints seem visible: a subtle understanding.
Associate Examiner She, a Hanlin Editor, comments: It integrates the meaning of Confucius’s remarks on the ode; its wording is tightly constructed, and its exposition of principle detailed and clear. This is the work of someone deeply versed in the study of human nature.
Associate Examiner Wan, a Hanlin Editor, comments: Precise in wording and exhaustive in meaning—a composition by someone who understands the Way.
Associate Examiner Zhu, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: Those who write on this topic generally ramble without hitting the mark. This essay alone probes to the root of the essential principles, expressing its meaning fully in concise language. Only someone of profound attainment could accomplish this. It should be recorded as a model.
Examiner Hu, a Hanlin Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: Ample in expression and complete in meaning.
Examiner Gao, a Hanlin Academician, comments: It vividly brings out the meaning of Confucius’s remarks on the ode.
The great worthy’s quotation of the ode and of the sage’s words praising it serves to illuminate the goodness of human nature. For things each possess their governing principles, while beautiful virtue is what all alike love; thus the goodness of human nature becomes clear. Had the great worthy not cited the ode and the sage’s words as evidence, how could one know that this is so? We may imagine the intent of his reply to Gongduzi as follows: “To establish the goodness of human nature through the goodness of the feelings—such indeed is my account of human nature. Yet I am not alone in saying this: the ancients also spoke of it. The Book of Odes says, ‘Heaven gives birth to the multitude of the people; where there is a thing, there is a governing principle.’ This describes how the principle of life issues from Heaven. ‘The people hold fast to their constant nature, loving this beautiful virtue.’ This describes how the innate good heart resides in human beings. Confucius read the ode and praised it, saying, ‘The author of this ode must surely have understood the Way of human nature and the feelings!’ Why is this? Concrete things lie below the realm of form; the Way lies above the realm of form. Indeed, they have never [illegible] …” [?]

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
□□其有情效其動亦未始不相符也使
□物而無則是器之離乎道也而何以為器乎
使秉彛而不好德是情之拂其性也而何以為
情乎所以天之生人有是物必具是則乃其所
為主者也有是則斯成是物乃其所主者也盖
天非此無以生人而賦則惟均人非此無以為
人而分則有定其謂民之秉彛非與夫秉彛即
物則也以在民而謂之彛然懿德即秉彛也以
可好而謂之懿惟為秉彛所以根於心者悅諸
===
心而好此懿德者達之天下而無間焉盖有不
容自已者也勉强云乎哉所同具者所同然而
好此懿德者揆之百世而如一焉盖有不能自
知者也矯飾云乎哉信乎有物之必有則也秉
彛之必好德也乃其道固如是也而詩人其知
之乎夫知有物之有則則吾所謂仁義禮知者
可識也知秉彛之好德則吾所謂惻隱羞惡辭
讓是非者可識也而情之可為善也不既明乎
情善則性可知矣彼三說者奚待辯焉大抵孔

translation_en: …[?] its having feelings and the manifestation of its activity likewise have never failed to correspond. If there were things [?] without their governing principles, this would mean that concrete entities were divorced from the Way; how, then, could they be concrete entities? If people possessed their constant moral endowment yet did not love virtue, this would mean that their feelings ran counter to their nature; how, then, could these be their feelings? Thus, when Heaven brings human beings into existence, wherever there is a thing, it necessarily possesses its governing principle: this is what acts as its master. Only with this principle does the thing take form: it is what the principle governs. Without this, Heaven could not bring human beings into existence, and its bestowal is uniform; without this, human beings could not be human, and their allotted endowment is fixed. Is this not what is meant by the people's possession of a constant moral endowment? This constant endowment is precisely the principle inherent in things. Because it resides in the people, it is called their constant endowment. And excellent virtue is precisely this constant endowment. Because it is worthy of love, it is called excellent. Precisely because it is their constant endowment, what is rooted in the heart delights the heart, and love of this excellent virtue extends throughout the world without exception. There is something in it that cannot be restrained. How could this be called forced effort? What all possess, all alike affirm; and love of this excellent virtue, measured across a hundred generations, remains the same. There is something in it of which people themselves cannot be conscious. How could this be called affectation? Truly, wherever there are things, there must be governing principles; whoever possesses the constant moral endowment must love virtue! This is inherently how the Way operates. Did not the poet understand it? If one understands that things have their governing principles, one can recognize what I call benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom. If one understands that possessing the constant moral endowment entails loving virtue, one can recognize what I call compassion, shame and aversion, deference and yielding, and the sense of right and wrong. Is it not already clear, then, that the feelings can lead to goodness? Once the goodness of the feelings is established, human nature can be understood. What further refutation do those three theories require? Generally speaking, Confucius…

translation_en:
…Confucius seldom spoke of human nature, so his students could not hear his teaching on it. Yet Mencius alone discussed it in detail. Why? Human nature is indeed difficult to discuss, but when miscellaneous doctrines obscure the truth, disputation becomes indispensable. In the end, the goodness of human nature was clarified and the various doctrines refuted, keeping human hearts from sinking to the level of birds and beasts. Was this not the power of disputation? Alas! Despite this teaching handed down to posterity, later thinkers still advanced doctrines that human nature has three grades or that good and evil are mixed within it.

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
理備於君子而察乎天地者也明於此義而大
壯之名辭居可知矣夫子彖傳之意若謂天下
無常勝之勢而有常勝之理故君子雖得其勢
尤必以理御之夫勢難乎其為壯也卦之所以
名大壯者何也蓋陽大陰小易之分也卦體四
陽居中則是際道長之會而疇離其大來之祉
合志尚往莫能禦矣茲非所謂壯乎乾剛震動
卦之德也此卦以乾遇震則是本自勝之強而
固執其信道之果率作興事無所疑矣茲非所
===
由壯乎夫勢之勝者在我而才足以濟之宜無
不可為者卦辭復有利貞之云何也盖德有小
大之異而類之邪正從之其宅心之廣者則豫
諸內者必直無妄思也其執德之弘者則制乎
外者必方無僻行也大自無不正矣固壯之所
以利也極而言之而天地之情有不可見乎盖
天地之大也究其道雖運於無窮要其情不外
於正大健順無私而至易至簡以貞其運高厚
不測而兼覆兼載以弘其功其所以妙合于一

punctuated: 理備於君子而察乎天地者也。明於此義，而大壯之名辭居可知矣。夫子彖傳之意若謂天下無常勝之勢，而有常勝之理，故君子雖得其勢，尤必以理御之。夫勢難乎其為壯也，卦之所以名大壯者何也？蓋陽大陰小，易之分也。卦體四陽居中，則是際道長之會，而疇離其大來之祉，合志尚往，莫能禦矣。茲非所謂壯乎？乾剛震動，卦之德也。此卦以乾遇震，則是本自勝之強，而固執其信道之果，率作興事，無所疑矣。茲非所由壯乎？夫勢之勝者在我，而才足以濟之，宜無不可為者。卦辭復有利貞之云，何也？盖德有小大之異，而類之邪正從之。其宅心之廣者，則豫諸內者必直，無妄思也；其執德之弘者，則制乎外者必方，無僻行也。大自無不正矣，固壯之所以利也。極而言之，而天地之情有不可見乎？盖天地之大也，究其道，雖運於無窮，要其情，不外於正大。健順無私，而至易至簡，以貞其運；高厚不測，而兼覆兼載，以弘其功。其所以妙合于一
translation_en: …the principle is fully embodied in the gentleman and manifest in Heaven and Earth. Once this meaning is understood, the name and statement of Great Strength (Dazhuang) can be understood [?]. The Master's meaning in the Commentary on the Judgments seems to be that, under Heaven, no position of advantage ensures constant victory, but there is a principle that does. Thus, even when the gentleman enjoys such an advantage, he must above all govern it through principle. Now, a position of strength is difficult to attain. Why is this hexagram named Great Strength? Yang is great and yin small: this is a distinction made in the Book of Changes. With four yang lines occupying the middle of the hexagram's structure, it marks a time when the Way is growing; together they partake of the blessing of the great coming forward [?]. United in purpose and intent on advancing, they cannot be resisted. Is this not what is meant by strength? Qian is firm and Zhen moves: these are the virtues of the trigrams. In this hexagram, Qian encounters Zhen. Thus, grounded in the strength of self-mastery and holding firmly to the resolve born of faith in the Way, one undertakes work and initiates affairs without hesitation. Is this not the source of strength? When the advantage lies with us and our abilities suffice to carry it through, it would seem that there is nothing we cannot do. Why, then, does the hexagram statement also say, “It is beneficial to be correct and firm”? Virtue differs in its smallness or greatness, and the corresponding distinction between the deviant and the correct follows from this. For one whose disposition is broad, what is established within [?] must be upright, without wayward thoughts; for one whose grasp of virtue is expansive, conduct governed outwardly must be square, without aberrant actions. Greatness is naturally correct in every respect: this is precisely what makes strength beneficial. To extend the argument to its utmost, can the true nature of Heaven and Earth remain unseen? Such is the greatness of Heaven and Earth that, though their Way operates without limit, their essential nature does not go beyond correctness and greatness. Vigorous and compliant, impartial, supremely easy and supremely simple, they thereby maintain the correctness of their operation. Immeasurably high and deep, sheltering all and bearing all, they thereby extend their achievement. That whereby they wondrously unite as one…

punctuated:
而散見於兩者，胥在是矣。天地且然，而況于君子之動乎？是知一正大也，君子得之以成其德業，天地得之以昭其化工。處大壯者，尚亦是務哉！觀聖人係臨之辭，亦曰利貞；而其於夬也，則告之以自治。盖勢之盛者不可常恃，聖人既幸其盛，而過中之防毎惓惓焉，所以致慎於天人交勝之際，而欲其以人定也。噫！聖人為世道計、為君子謀也深哉！
說萬物者莫說乎澤。
沈楩

translation_en:
…and are manifested separately in the two: all this lies herein. If even Heaven and Earth are thus, how much more must this apply to the gentleman’s actions? Thus we know that uprightness and greatness are one and the same principle: the gentleman attains it to perfect his virtue and achievements; Heaven and Earth attain it to manifest their transforming work. Should not those situated in Great Strength (Dazhuang) likewise make this their concern? Consider the words the sage appended to Approach (Lin): these too say, “It is beneficial to be steadfast and correct.” In Breakthrough (Guai), he admonishes one to govern oneself. For flourishing power cannot always be relied upon. While the sage welcomes its flourishing, he is ever solicitous about guarding against going beyond the mean. Thus he urges caution at the juncture where Heaven and human action contend for ascendancy, wishing human effort to bring stability. Ah! How profound are the sage’s plans for the course of the world and his counsels for the gentleman!
“Of that which delights the myriad things, nothing is more delightful than the marsh.”
Shen Pian
Associate Examiner Zhou, Supervising Secretary, comments: “He grasps the mysteries of the Five Phases and the four seasons beyond what is explicitly expressed, and brings them forth with brilliance.”
Associate Examiner Yu, Compiler, comments: “His exposition of the vital energies associated with the hexagrams is orderly, elegant, refined, and concise. This is among the finest essays on the meaning of the Book of Changes.”
Associate Examiner Wan, Compiler, comments: “He develops the meaning of delighting things with authenticity and precision.”
Associate Examiner Zhu, Senior Compiler, comments: “The language and reasoning are clear and clean. This is how essays on the meaning of the Book of Changes should be written.”
Examiner Hu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “Pure and orthodox; worthy of inclusion.”
Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: “The reasoning is clear and the flow of expression smooth.”

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
大傳舉造化之遂乎物者而歸諸後天之兌
盖物必得所說而後有以遂其生也然而莫有
說於兌焉兌之為用大矣哉大傳發後天圖學
之蘊盖謂立萬物之命者神也統於神而生成
乎萬物者六子也六子之於物豈惟動撓與燥
而已哉乃若涵美利以育羣生而形色之不同
者各有以全其性之所宜斂太和以陶庶類而
小大之不齊者皆有以得其情之所適是之謂
說萬物也夫孰有說於兌澤者乎盖前乎兌者
===
為離焉火之所燥盛陽方舒而物猶俟於休養
未可以言說也後乎兌者為坎焉水之所潤純
陰方肅而物已厎於歸藏非所以言說也惟夫
兌之位則西也陰陽之氣於是乎始凝正美利
順成之候兌之時則秋也水火之用於是乎相
濟正太和保合之初離得是以制乎燥而滋息
之機隨分而咸足物至於此有不充然自全其
性者乎坎由是以委乎潤而涵濡之化隨材而
各成物至於此有不油然自得其情者乎是盖

punctuated: 大傳舉造化之遂乎物者，而歸諸後天之兌。盖物必得所說，而後有以遂其生也。然而莫有說於兌焉，兌之為用大矣哉！大傳發後天圖學之蘊，盖謂立萬物之命者，神也；統於神而生成乎萬物者，六子也。六子之於物，豈惟動撓與燥而已哉？乃若涵美利以育羣生，而形色之不同者，各有以全其性之所宜；斂太和以陶庶類，而小大之不齊者，皆有以得其情之所適：是之謂說萬物也。夫孰有說於兌澤者乎？盖前乎兌者為離焉，火之所燥，盛陽方舒，而物猶俟於休養，未可以言說也；後乎兌者為坎焉，水之所潤，純陰方肅，而物已厎於歸藏，非所以言說也。惟夫兌之位則西也，陰陽之氣於是乎始凝，正美利順成之候；兌之時則秋也，水火之用於是乎相濟，正太和保合之初。離得是以制乎燥，而滋息之機隨分而咸足，物至於此，有不充然自全其性者乎？坎由是以委乎潤，而涵濡之化隨材而各成，物至於此，有不油然自得其情者乎？是盖
translation_en:
The Great Commentary identifies that aspect of creation and transformation which brings things to fulfillment and attributes it to Dui in the Later Heaven arrangement. For things must obtain that in which they delight before they can fulfill their lives. Yet nothing delights them more than Dui. Great indeed is Dui’s operation!

The Great Commentary reveals the profound meaning of the teaching of the Later Heaven Diagram. Its point is that spiritual efficacy establishes the allotted lives of the myriad things, while the six offspring trigrams, governed by that efficacy, generate and complete them. In their action upon things, do these six offspring merely set them in motion, stir them, and dry them? They also harbor beautiful benefits to nurture all living beings, so that things differing in form and color can each fulfill what befits their nature. They gather Supreme Harmony to mold the many kinds of beings, so that things unequal in size can all attain what suits their inherent dispositions. This is what is meant by delighting the myriad things. What, then, delights them more than Dui, the marsh?

Before Dui comes Li: as fire dries things, abundant yang is just unfolding, and things still await rest and nourishment. One cannot yet speak of delight. After Dui comes Kan: as water moistens things, pure yin is becoming stern, and things have already reached the stage of returning to storage. This is not what is meant by delight. Dui’s position alone is in the west, where the vital forces of yin and yang first begin to coalesce: precisely the season when beautiful benefits reach their fulfillment in due course. Dui’s season is autumn, when the operations of water and fire complement one another: precisely the beginning of the preservation and union of Supreme Harmony.

Through this, Li gains the means to regulate its drying, and the workings of nourishment and growth become sufficient for all things according to their respective allotments. When things reach this stage, is there any that does not abundantly fulfill its own nature? Through this, Kan gives itself over to moistening [?], and the transforming action of saturation and nourishment brings each thing to completion according to its endowment. When things reach this stage, is there any that does not spontaneously find satisfaction in its inherent disposition? This, indeed, is…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
一神之妙用本無為也而所以說乎物者非兌
無以分其職六子之造物各有司也而所以使
之說者惟兌有以專其功吁知兌之為說者其
知神之所為乎抑甞論之自不測而言謂之神
自主宰而言謂之帝帝以神用而六子並效其
能是可以觀君道矣君之道專而逸臣之義分
而勞帝王所以澤被天下而民說無疆者用此
術也是故致治莫大乎法天法天莫大乎體易

簫韶九成鳳凰來儀

punctuated:
一神之妙用，本無為也，而所以說乎物者，非兌無以分其職。六子之造物，各有司也，而所以使之說者，惟兌有以專其功。吁！知兌之為說者，其知神之所為乎？抑甞論之，自不測而言謂之神，自主宰而言謂之帝。帝以神用，而六子並效其能，是可以觀君道矣。君之道專而逸，臣之義分而勞。帝王所以澤被天下而民說無疆者，用此術也。是故致治莫大乎法天，法天莫大乎體易。

translation_en:
… the wondrous operation of the single spiritual power is fundamentally without deliberate action; yet its function of bringing joy to things could not be apportioned without Dui. The six children [the six derivative trigrams] each have their charge in bringing things into being; yet only Dui can take sole credit for making them joyful. Ah! Might one who understands how Dui brings joy also understand what spiritual power does? I have also considered this: viewed in its unfathomability, it is called spiritual power; viewed in its ruling authority, it is called the Supreme Ruler. The Supreme Ruler operates through spiritual power, and the six children all exercise their capacities. Here one can discern the Way of the sovereign. The sovereign’s Way is unified and at ease; his ministers’ duties are divided and laborious. It is by employing this method that emperors and kings extend their beneficence throughout the world and bring the people boundless joy. Thus nothing is greater for achieving good government than modeling oneself on Heaven, and nothing is greater for modeling oneself on Heaven than embodying the Book of Changes.

Book of Documents

“When the Xiao Shao music had been performed nine times, phoenixes came in stately array.”

Yuan Zunni

Associate Examiner Lu, Senior Compiler, comments: “This composition expounds principles with depth and subtlety, and its phrasing is precise and apt. Reading it, one can envision the splendor of Shun’s Shao music.”

Associate Examiner Wang, Left Admonisher, comments: “Serene and understated, balanced and harmonious: an excellent composition.”

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
考試官侍讀學士胡批是善言韶樂之感者錄之
考試官學士高批平順
聖樂備而盛瑞臻其所感深矣甚矣和之能召
和也今聖樂備作而鳳凰之瑞即臻焉則樂其
可知矣乎后夔形容帝舜之德如此蓋謂帝之
為德雖有作而弗可及故其為樂雖甚盛而蔑
以加樂者何簫韶是已成有九是天子之所用
也名曰成是治功之所象也今也不徒上下之
翕如而已有始有卒而所以自為一成者各盡
===
其律呂之變亦不徒詠間之皦如而已再始復
亂而所以合為九成者備舉其條理之詳播九
德而揚九功雍然其鳴蓋盡善而盡美也舞九
韶而協九奏至矣其大如天覆而地載也樂至
於是其所感何如哉吾知聲與氣相通也今和
氣充乎宇宙而靈秘已開然氣與聲相應也故
和聲詔於兩間而神幾自動鳳凰非常之瑞豈
人所能致乎時則先得氣而來焉集止有容於
□煥文明之氣象鳳凰非時不出豈世可得見

punctuated:
考試官侍讀學士胡批：是善言韶樂之感者，錄之。
考試官學士高批：平順。
聖樂備而盛瑞臻，其所感深矣甚矣！和之能召和也，今聖樂備作而鳳凰之瑞即臻焉，則樂其可知矣乎？后夔形容帝舜之德如此，蓋謂帝之為德，雖有作而弗可及，故其為樂，雖甚盛而蔑以加。樂者何？簫韶是已。成有九，是天子之所用也；名曰成，是治功之所象也。今也，不徒上下之翕如而已，有始有卒，而所以自為一成者，各盡其律呂之變；亦不徒詠間之皦如而已，再始復亂，而所以合為九成者，備舉其條理之詳。播九德而揚九功，雍然其鳴，蓋盡善而盡美也；舞九韶而協九奏，至矣其大，如天覆而地載也。樂至於是，其所感何如哉？吾知聲與氣相通也，今和氣充乎宇宙而靈秘已開；然氣與聲相應也，故和聲詔於兩間而神幾自動。鳳凰非常之瑞，豈人所能致乎？時則先得氣而來焉，集止有容，於□煥文明之氣象。鳳凰非時不出，豈世可得見
translation_en:
Examiner Hu, Academician Reader-in-waiting, comments: “This is an excellent account of the responsive influence of the Shao music. Include it.”
Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: “Smooth and fluent.”
When the sage’s music is complete, a magnificent auspicious sign arrives: profound indeed, and powerful, is the response it evokes! Harmony can summon harmony. Now that the sage’s music is fully performed and the auspicious phoenix immediately appears, may we not understand the nature of this music? Thus did Kui describe the virtue of Emperor Shun. His meaning was surely that, although others might arise, none could equal the emperor’s virtue; hence, magnificent though his music was, nothing could be added to it. What music was this? It was the Xiao Shao. Its movements number nine: this is the music used by the Son of Heaven. They are called “completions,” for they represent the accomplishments of his government. Now it is not merely that the higher and lower tones blend harmoniously. There is a beginning and an end, and each movement, complete in itself, exhausts the variations of the pitch standards. Nor is it merely that the singing and its intervals [?] are clear and distinct. Beginning anew and returning to the concluding passage, the nine movements together fully display every detail of their ordered structure. Proclaiming the nine virtues and celebrating the nine achievements, their sound is harmonious: truly perfect in goodness and perfect in beauty. With the dancing of the nine Shao movements and the harmonizing of the nine musical performances, their grandeur reaches its utmost, like Heaven sheltering and Earth sustaining all things. When music reaches this level, what response does it evoke?
I know that sound and vital force communicate with one another. Now harmonious vital force fills the cosmos, and its numinous mysteries have already opened. Yet vital force and sound respond to each other; thus harmonious sound makes itself heard between Heaven and Earth, and the mysterious workings of the spirit move of themselves. The phoenix is an extraordinary auspicious sign: how could human effort bring it here? At such a time it is the first to receive this vital force and comes accordingly. It alights with graceful bearing, thereby [?] displaying the radiant aspect of cultivated order. The phoenix does not emerge except at the proper time: could the world behold it …

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
乎時則覽德輝而下焉翩躚可覩於以呈盛世
之光華來者鳳凰也而胡為乎來鳳凰弗得而
知也固有感之者也感者簫韶也而所以為感
簫韶弗得而與也猶有本之者也則夫神人之
胥懌不益可知而鳥獸之蹌蹌又何待言矣乎
吁帝之德其可為至德也已矣大抵咸章而下
作者亦多而古今獨稱舜樂何歟盖其得位於
揖遜而致治於無為樂以象之故若此其盛也
厥後孔子在齊聞之至於三月不知肉味千載
===
而下所感且若此矣而況后夔之親典其事者
乎雖然聖人之樂亦惟聖人能知之否則端冕
而聽古樂惟恐臥者豈謂其不能感哉
公其惟時成周建無窮之基
周子義
同考試官署郎中林批體裁峻整詞氣端莊得命誥
之意是留心經學者

知也固有感之者也感者簫韶也而所以爲感

胥懌不益可知而鳥獸之蹌蹌又何待言矣乎

作者亦多而古今獨稱舜樂何歟蓋其得位於
揖遜而致治於無爲樂以象之故若此其盛也
厥後孔子在齊聞之至於三月不知肉味千載
===
而下所感且若此矣而況后夔之親典其事者
乎雖然聖人之樂亦惟聖人能知之否則端冕
而聽古樂惟恐臥者豈謂其不能感哉
公其惟時成周建無窮之基
周子義

之意是留心經學者
同考試官編修張　批融會經旨而詞致明淨可錄
同考試官修撰陸　批莊嚴典雅宛若康王告戒畢

乎？時則覽德輝而下焉，翩躚可覩，於以呈盛世之光華。來者鳳凰也，而胡為乎來？鳳凰弗得而知也，固有感之者也。感者簫韶也，而所以為感，簫韶弗得而與也，猶有本之者也。則夫神人之胥懌，不益可知，而鳥獸之蹌蹌，又何待言矣乎？吁！帝之德，其可為至德也已矣！大抵咸章而下，作者亦多，而古今獨稱舜樂，何歟？盖其得位於揖遜，而致治於無為，樂以象之，故若此其盛也。厥後孔子在齊聞之，至於三月不知肉味，千載而下，所感且若此矣，而況后夔之親典其事者乎？雖然，聖人之樂，亦惟聖人能知之。否則，端冕而聽古樂，惟恐臥者，豈謂其不能感哉？
公其惟時成周建無窮之基
周子義

translation_en:
…? At such a time, the phoenix beholds the radiance of virtue and descends; its graceful flight can be seen, displaying the splendor of a flourishing age. It is the phoenix that comes, but why does it come? The phoenix itself cannot know: there is certainly something that moves it. What moves it is the music of the Xiao Shao; yet the reason for its power to move lies beyond the music itself: there is still an underlying source. Is it not then all the more evident that spirits and men alike rejoice? And what need is there to speak of birds and beasts dancing in measured steps? Ah! The emperor’s virtue may indeed be called consummate virtue!
From the Xianzhang onward, there were many makers of music. Why, then, have people throughout the ages singled out Shun’s music for praise? It is because he attained the throne through courteous yielding and brought about good government through nonaction. His music gave expression to this, and thus attained such magnificence. Later, when Confucius heard it in Qi, for three months he did not know the taste of meat. Even a thousand years later its moving power was such—how much more so for Kui, the Director of Music, who personally presided over its performance! Nevertheless, only a sage can understand a sage’s music. Otherwise, when someone listens to ancient music in ceremonial robes and cap and fears only that he will fall asleep, can one say that the music lacks the power to move him?
“Duke, lay at this Chengzhou a foundation that will endure without end.”
Zhou Ziyi

賢王期大臣惟在于立可久之功焉夫立功莫
大于可久也畢公治成周而康王以此期之所
以尊敬之者至矣其意若謂大臣以體國為忠
則必以善後為務公之治成周也吾固以成終
期之矣然其地密邇王室所係匪輕公則有世

道之責而為慮不可以不長任國家之重而為
計不可以不遠其惟是成周仰承祗命之意而
遠猷是念以貽繼述之謀益篤弼亮之忠而永

之皆修而成功運于不息化民而易俗務期餘
風之皆殄而大業衍于無疆剛柔並用旌別之
政舉焉不特為今日之休而要諸恒久足以恢
百代之宏規保釐並施德義之訓敷焉非止于

賢王期大臣，惟在于立可久之功焉。夫立功莫大于可久也。畢公治成周，而康王以此期之，所以尊敬之者至矣。其意若謂：大臣以體國為忠，則必以善後為務。公之治成周也，吾固以成終期之矣。然其地密邇王室，所係匪輕。公則有世道之責，而為慮不可以不長；任國家之重，而為計不可以不遠。其惟是成周，仰承祗命之意，而遠猷是念，以貽繼述之謀；益篤弼亮之忠，而永圖是懷，以弘康乂之烈。興道以致治，務期厥德之皆修，而成功運于不息；化民而易俗，務期餘風之皆殄，而大業衍于無疆。剛柔並用，旌別之政舉焉，不特為今日之休，而要諸恒久，足以恢百代之宏規；保釐並施，德義之訓敷焉，非止于一世之近，而垂諸將來，足以樹萬年之偉績。式
translation_en:
〔…the tone of his address to the Duke.〕
Associate Examiner Wang, Left Mentor, comments: 〔The wording is concise, yet the meaning is complete. Accept it.〕
Examiner Hu, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: 〔Grounded in the classics and substantial.〕
Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: 〔Refined and elegant.〕
What a worthy king expects of his great ministers is simply that they establish achievements capable of enduring. For in establishing achievements, nothing is greater than ensuring their endurance. When the Duke of Bi governed Chengzhou, King Kang held this expectation of him: the respect and esteem he thereby showed him were utmost. His meaning was as though he said: A great minister regards devotion to the state as loyalty; he must therefore make provision for its future his task. In your governance of Chengzhou, my lord, I have certainly expected you to bring the work to completion. Yet this place lies very close to the royal house, and what depends upon it is no small matter. You bear responsibility for the moral order of the age, and your concerns must therefore extend far into the future; you carry the weight of the state, and your plans must therefore reach far ahead. In this Chengzhou, reverently uphold the intention of the charge you have respectfully received, and give thought to far-reaching counsels, leaving plans for those who will continue your work. Deepen still further your loyalty in assisting the ruler, and cherish enduring designs, extending the achievements of peace and good government. Promote the Way to bring about good order, striving to ensure that all cultivate their virtue, so that accomplished good continues without ceasing. Transform the people and change their customs, striving to ensure that every lingering pernicious influence is extinguished, so that the great undertaking extends without limit. Employ firmness and gentleness together, putting into effect policies that distinguish and recognize merit. Seek not merely the blessings of today, but enduring results sufficient to enlarge the grand design for a hundred generations. Apply protection and good governance together, spreading instruction in virtue and righteousness. Look beyond the short span of a single age and transmit these benefits to the future, sufficient to establish magnificent achievements lasting ten thousand years. Take as a model…

化于始周公之所以克慎也而于以成終長
治久安之道此其基矣惟公茂建之非予之所
望耶有容于中君陳之所以克和也而于是以
成終悠遠高厚之功其基之矣惟公肇立焉非
予之所願耶由是觀之賢王圖治之切老臣經

之隆自能輔成盛治而康王告戒懇至惟若不

化于始，周公之所以克慎也，而于以成終，長治久安之道，此其基矣。惟公茂建之，非予之所望耶？有容于中，君陳之所以克和也，而于是以成終，悠遠高厚之功，其基之矣。惟公肇立焉，非予之所願耶？由是觀之，賢王圖治之切，老臣經國之遠，咸可想見矣。抑畢公四世元老，其勳德之隆，自能輔成盛治，而康王告戒懇至，惟若不足，而復以無窮事業望之。蓋其保大圖艱，深思遠慮，故言之不覺其詳也。噫！若《畢命》數語，真足以對揚文武之光烈，比隆堯舜之都俞矣。周家德澤深長，曆數久遠，有由然哉！

詩

鎬京辟廱，自西自東，自南自北，無思不服。

同考試官都給事中邢 批〔建都立學義不平，此作得〕
translation_en:
…transformation at the outset: this was how the Duke of Zhou exercised due care. By bringing it through to completion, the foundation for lasting good government and enduring peace would be laid. That you, my lord, should establish it abundantly—is this not what I hope for? Having forbearance within: this was how Jun Chen achieved harmony. By bringing this through to completion, the foundation would be laid for achievements enduring and far-reaching, lofty and profound. That you, my lord, should inaugurate them—is this not what I desire? Viewed thus, both the worthy king’s earnest pursuit of good government and the veteran minister’s far-reaching plans for governing the realm can readily be imagined.

Moreover, the Duke of Bi was a senior statesman who had served four generations of rulers. His eminent achievements and virtue naturally enabled him to assist in perfecting flourishing government. Yet King Kang admonished him with utmost earnestness, as though this were still insufficient, and further looked to him for undertakings without limit. Intent on preserving greatness and anticipating difficulties, the king thought deeply and planned far ahead; thus, without realizing it, he spoke at such length. Ah! These few words in the Charge to Bi truly suffice to acknowledge and extol the glorious achievements of Kings Wen and Wu, and rival in grandeur the exchanges of counsel and assent between Yao and Shun and their ministers. There was indeed a reason why the Zhou house’s beneficent influence was so profound and enduring, and its allotted dynastic span so long!

Book of Odes

“At Haojing’s royal academy, from the west and from the east, from the south and from the north, none thought of withholding submission.”

Chen Dong

This, too, is well worth contemplating. Truly, this is the voice of the Greater Odes, not merely skill in literary composition.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Xing, Chief Supervising Secretary: “The significance of establishing a capital and founding schools is extraordinary [?]. This composition captures …”

Associate Examiner Chen, Right Rectifier, comments: “Its understanding is outstanding, and its writing adequately expresses it. Worth selecting.”

The sage established a capital and instituted instruction, thereby winning the hearts of all under Heaven. Indeed, moral transformation through instruction is a great undertaking of the state. When King Wu established his capital, he immediately gave this priority; fitting indeed was it that he won the hearts of all under Heaven! This is what the poet recounts and celebrates in singing of King Wu’s deeds. His meaning is that those who possess a state rightly value gathering the people together, but value still more bringing their moral transformation to completion. Surely our King Wu understood this! He considered that Feng could no longer accommodate the multitudes who had gathered there, while Hao was foremost among places where flourishing vital energies converged. Thus he determined the cardinal directions and established the center, broadening the foundation for laying out his realm; he planned on a grand scale and took up residence at its center, securing the basis for unified rule. Yet he did not say, ‘In this initial period of foundation, there is as yet no time for moral instruction.’ Instead, the Biyong royal academy was built. There he expounded [two illegible characters; ?]; there the four disciplines were continually honored and the four teachings established. There he performed…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
禮則凡習射上功習鄉上齒恒於斯也盖於樂
辟廱兹焉益大而譽髦斯士兹焉益廣矣然何
以遂得天下之心與夫京邑四方之樞風聲所
出而國學首善之地教化所倡是以自東自西
地固遠矣而仰文命之敷者莫不傾心以嚮化
其在於東猶其在於西也自南自北人固衆矣
而孚皇極之訓者莫不丕應而徯志其在於南
猶其在於北也盖養人以善既非力驅勢迫之
為則順德以誠夫豈笑貌聲音之末聖人之化
===
其被之溥而入之深也有若此哉旴武王信其
克君也已雖然武王得民匪專此也盖其敬義
交脩而洪範丹書復相翊賛所以端本原者固
自有在所謂神道設教而天下服者也噫戡亂
以武矣而復以文德綏之姬籙八百寔基於此

…rites: archery practice, which honored achievement, and the district drinking ceremony, which honored seniority, were regularly conducted here. Thus the joy of the Biyong, the royal academy, grew still greater here, and the cultivation of these outstanding scholars became still more extensive. But how did this win the hearts of all under Heaven? The capital is the hub of the four quarters, from which the influence of exemplary conduct spreads; the state academy is the foremost seat of goodness, where moral instruction originates. Thus, from east and west, though the lands were distant, all who looked up to the spread of his civil ordinances inclined their hearts toward his transforming influence. Those in the east were like those in the west. From south and north, though the people were numerous, all who trusted the teachings of the August Ultimate responded wholeheartedly and awaited his wishes. Those in the south were like those in the north. Nurturing people through goodness did not involve driving them by force or compelling them through power; their sincere submission to virtue could hardly have been a superficial matter of smiles, expressions, and words. Such was the breadth of the sage’s transforming influence and the depth to which it penetrated! Ah [?]! King Wu truly proved himself capable of being a ruler.
Nevertheless, King Wu did not win the people through this alone. He cultivated reverence and righteousness together, further assisted by the Great Plan and the Cinnabar Writing. His means of rectifying the root and source thus had a firm foundation. This is what is meant by establishing instruction through the numinous Way and bringing all under Heaven into submission. Ah! Having quelled disorder through military force, he then pacified the people through civil virtue. The Ji house’s eight hundred years of dynastic rule were indeed founded on this. Hence the saying: “Employing civil and military means together is the art of lasting peace and enduring good government.” Is this not true?
“Profoundly wise was Shang; long had its auspicious signs appeared.”
Tang Yilin.
