商人頌世德之隆，而原其受命之久焉。盖德之所在，天命之所歸也。商人既以世德而受命，則其祥之所發，不亦久哉？此祫祭宗廟而追言之也。意謂創業者人也，而命則係乎天；申命者天也，而感則由乎人。我商何如哉？彼濬焉而深，而沉幾之莫測；哲焉而明，而旁燭之無疆。君德莫盛乎此也，而有者鮮矣，矧世有乎？惟我商也，天命有歸，將啟興王之運，故天心純佑，迭生聖德
translation_en:
…in recitation, it truly sounds like bronze bells and stone chimes: among the finest essays on the meaning of the Classics.
Associate Examiner Xing, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “Its composition is balanced and correct, its language ample and unhurried. Moreover, its grasp of the meaning of enduring duration is especially true and precise. It can serve as a model for all under Heaven.”
Associate Examiner Li, Compiler, comments: “It elucidates receiving the Mandate through virtue. Without needing ornamental embellishment, it achieves an admirable wholeness and elegance. It should be recorded as a model.”
Associate Examiner Ding, Senior Compiler, comments: “Its elucidation of the meaning of ‘long manifested’ is supremely lucid. The author clearly has a profound understanding of the Book of Odes.”
Associate Examiner Chen, Right Mentor, comments: “The language and ideas are clear and precise. Record it.”
Examiner Hu, Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “The language is harmonious yet dignified.”
Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: “Elegant and vigorous.”
The people of Shang praised the abundance of their ancestral virtue and traced how long ago they had received the Mandate. For wherever virtue resides, there the Mandate of Heaven comes to rest. Since the people of Shang received the Mandate through virtue accumulated over generations, had not their auspicious signs likewise been manifest for a long time? This is what they recalled at the collective sacrifice to the ancestors in the ancestral temple. The meaning is this: those who establish a dynasty are human, but the Mandate depends upon Heaven; it is Heaven that renews the Mandate, but the influence that elicits its response comes from human beings. How was it with our Shang? Profound and deep, its rulers’ subtle discernment was unfathomable; wise and luminous, their illumination reached everywhere without limit. No ruler’s virtue could surpass this, yet few possessed it—how much rarer, then, that it should be possessed generation after generation! Only in our Shang did the Mandate of Heaven find its destination. Heaven was about to inaugurate the destined rise of a king; therefore, in its purpose it bestowed its wholehearted aid and successively brought forth rulers of sagely virtue…

之君遡湯而上肇基非一世也而濬哲之德則
咸有之耿光大烈蓋奕葉之相承也纘緒非一
君也而濬哲之德則世濟之重明繼照蓋後先
之相望也夫德之與命相為感孚者也世有聖
君則世篤其慶久膺天命則久發其祥故正域
四方人以為帝命所屬也而不知簡在之意已
殷於立國之初所以開一代之昌祚者其来蓋
亦遠矣奄有九有人以為受命不殆也而不知
定保之徵屢見於歷世之際所以拓一統之洪
===
業者其積蓋有漸矣夫然則天命雖集於今而
休祥實肇于古天之眷商厥惟舊哉宜禘祭者
之所為頌美也雖然垂裕者祖宗之澤也繼述
者子孫之責也商人禘祭登歌而首言祖德蓋

至于高宗賢聖之君六七作焉夫既多濬哲以
開之復多賢聖以繼之所以祈天永命者可知
矣商祚之益久也宜哉

之君。遡湯而上，肇基非一世也，而濬哲之德則咸有之，耿光大烈，蓋奕葉之相承也；纘緒非一君也，而濬哲之德則世濟之，重明繼照，蓋後先之相望也。夫德之與命，相為感孚者也。世有聖君，則世篤其慶；久膺天命，則久發其祥。故正域四方，人以為帝命所屬也，而不知簡在之意已殷於立國之初，所以開一代之昌祚者，其来蓋亦遠矣；奄有九有，人以為受命不殆也，而不知定保之徵屢見於歷世之際，所以拓一統之洪業者，其積蓋有漸矣。夫然則天命雖集於今，而休祥實肇于古。天之眷商，厥惟舊哉！宜禘祭者之所為頌美也。雖然，垂裕者祖宗之澤也，繼述者子孫之責也。商人禘祭登歌，而首言祖德，蓋欲以修德保業啓後王之繹思焉耳。是以自湯至于高宗，賢聖之君六七作焉。夫既多濬哲以開之，復多賢聖以繼之，所以祈天永命者可知矣。商祚之益久也，宜哉！

春秋
translation_en:
…rulers of sagely virtue. Tracing back beyond Tang, the foundations were laid over more than one generation, and all possessed the virtue of profound wisdom. Their brilliant glory and great achievements were handed down through successive generations. More than one ruler carried on this heritage, and each generation sustained that virtue of profound wisdom. Their successive radiance shone on, as later rulers followed their predecessors.

Virtue and Heaven’s mandate respond to and accord with one another. When every generation has a sage ruler, every generation enjoys abundant blessings; when Heaven’s mandate has long been received, its auspicious signs likewise manifest themselves over a long span. Thus, when Shang ordered the lands of the four quarters, people thought that the Supreme Lord’s mandate had devolved upon it, without realizing that his intention to choose it had already been strong at the founding of the state. The origins of what inaugurated a dynasty’s flourishing fortunes were indeed remote. When Shang possessed all the Nine Regions, people thought that its receipt of the mandate was secure, without realizing that signs of Heaven’s assurance and protection had repeatedly appeared through successive generations. What expanded the great enterprise of unified rule had indeed accumulated by degrees.

Thus, although Heaven’s mandate came to fruition in the present, its auspicious signs had truly begun in antiquity. How longstanding was Heaven’s favor toward Shang! It was fitting that those performing the di ancestral sacrifice should praise this. Nevertheless, bequeathing prosperity is the ancestors’ beneficence; carrying on their work is the descendants’ responsibility. When the people of Shang performed the di sacrifice and sang in the ancestral hall, they spoke first of ancestral virtue, surely wishing to prompt later kings to reflect continually on cultivating virtue and preserving their inheritance. Thus, from Tang to Gaozong, six or seven worthy and sagely rulers arose. With so many rulers of profound wisdom to establish the enterprise, and so many worthy sages to carry it on, we can understand how they sought from Heaven an enduring mandate. How fitting that Shang’s dynastic fortunes should endure ever longer!

Spring and Autumn Annals

translation_en:
“Autumn, the seventh month.” 〔The sixth year of Duke Yin.〕
Han Ji

Comment by Associate Examiner Chang, Acting Vice Director: Recording the seasons and months proceeds fundamentally from attaching weight to both Heaven and humanity, thereby revealing their unity of principle. The intention that the ruler should model himself on Heaven should therefore remain implicit. Of the essays submitted at this examination, this alone grasps that point. Its language is also exceptionally refined and elegant, worthy of imitation; hence its inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Senior Compiler: Language and meaning blend seamlessly, capturing the purport of the unity of Heaven and humanity.

Comment by Examiner Hu, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: It ably elucidates the meaning of the commentary.

Comment by Examiner Gao, Academician: Precise and fitting.

The Spring and Autumn Annals records the seasons and months in full to reveal the single principle shared by Heaven and humanity, intending that rulers should model themselves on Heaven. For Heaven and humanity do not possess two different principles. Looking simply at how the Spring and Autumn Annals records the opening of each season and its month, how could rulers refrain from modeling themselves on Heaven in establishing their government? The Spring and Autumn Annals is a book that records events; thus events are attached to months, and months to seasons. Yet in the sixth year of Duke Yin, although there was no event, it records “Autumn, the seventh month.” Why is this taken to reveal the single principle shared by Heaven and humanity?

Heaven has four seasons, whose successive changes complete the year. If the seasons were incomplete, the work of the year would be deficient. Could this be the august and unceasing Way of Heaven? Therefore, a season must not go unrecorded merely because there is no event. The king establishes the Monthly Ordinances, adapting and regulating transformations so as to achieve good government. If the months were incomplete, the work of government would be deficient. Could this be the utterly sincere and unremitting Way of the king? Therefore …

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
不可以書時而不繫月也用是見上下位殊均
之有不容間之理而天人事異均之有不可缺
之功春以生之夏以長之秋以收之冬以藏之
惟循環無端而後天之所以盡萬物者有全德
矣正月施惠四月遂賢七月斷刑十月固封惟
並行不悖而後聖人之所以盡萬民者有全能
矣雖時序為在天自然之運而示之自然者天
固未始不為人也人君繼天立極者也而可不
求端於天乎雖月令為在人當然之政而盡其
===
當然者人固未始不為天也人君代天理物者
也而可不克肖於天乎故春秋雖無事而書時
又書月若曰著不息者是天道也亦王道也法
天道之運而後盡王道之極聖人垂訓之義深
哉雖然有本焉四德是也易曰乾元亨利貞天
德也又曰君子行此四德者故曰乾元亨利貞
體天德也苟無其德即月令亦虛文耳故中和
之致始可收位育之功而賛化育參天地非盡
性不能也君子論王道而必本之於天德有以

也而可不克肖於天乎故春秋雖紀事而書時
又書月若曰著不息者是天道也亦王道也法
天道之運而後盡王道之極聖人垂訓之義深
哉雖然有本焉四德是也易曰乾元亨利貞天

punctuated: 不可以書時而不繫月也。用是見上下位殊，均之有不容間之理；而天人事異，均之有不可缺之功。春以生之，夏以長之，秋以收之，冬以藏之，惟循環無端，而後天之所以盡萬物者有全德矣。正月施惠，四月遂賢，七月斷刑，十月固封，惟並行不悖，而後聖人之所以盡萬民者有全能矣。雖時序為在天自然之運，而示之自然者，天固未始不為人也。人君繼天立極者也，而可不求端於天乎？雖月令為在人當然之政，而盡其當然者，人固未始不為天也。人君代天理物者也，而可不克肖於天乎？故春秋雖無事而書時，又書月，若曰：著不息者，是天道也，亦王道也。法天道之運，而後盡王道之極。聖人垂訓之義深哉！雖然，有本焉，四德是也。易曰：「乾，元亨利貞。」天德也。又曰：「君子行此四德者，故曰乾，元亨利貞。」體天德也。苟無其德，即月令亦虛文耳。故中和之致，始可收位育之功，而賛化育、參天地，非盡性不能也。君子論王道而必本之於天德，有以
translation_en:
…one cannot record the season without also attaching the month. From this we see that, although those above and below occupy different positions, both possess a principle that admits no interruption; and although Heaven and humanity differ in their affairs, both have accomplishments in which nothing may be lacking. Spring brings things forth, summer nurtures their growth, autumn gathers them in, and winter stores them away. Only through this endless cycle does Heaven possess the complete virtue by which it brings all things to fulfillment. In the first month, bestow favors; in the fourth, advance the worthy; in the seventh, adjudicate punishments; in the tenth, strengthen the borders. Only when these measures all proceed without conflict does the sage possess the complete capacity by which he brings all the people to fulfillment.

Although the succession of seasons is Heaven’s spontaneous movement, in manifesting this spontaneity Heaven has never failed to act for humanity. The ruler of men succeeds Heaven and establishes the supreme standard: can he fail to seek his guiding source in Heaven? Although the Monthly Ordinances prescribe the governance proper to humanity, in fully performing what is proper, humanity has never failed to act for Heaven. The ruler of men orders things on Heaven’s behalf: can he fail to conform fully to Heaven? Thus, even when nothing happened, the Spring and Autumn Annals records the season and also the month, as if to say: what is manifested in this unceasing activity is the Way of Heaven and also the Way of kings. Only by modeling oneself upon the movement of Heaven’s Way can one fully realize the highest standard of the kingly Way. How profound is the meaning of the sage’s instruction handed down to posterity!

Yet this has a foundation: the four virtues. The Book of Changes says, “Qian: origination, flourishing, benefit, and steadfastness.” These are Heaven’s virtues. It also says, “The gentleman practices these four virtues; hence it is said, ‘Qian: origination, flourishing, benefit, and steadfastness.’” This is to embody Heaven’s virtues. Without these virtues, even the Monthly Ordinances are merely empty writing. Thus only by bringing equilibrium and harmony to their utmost can one achieve the proper positioning of Heaven and Earth and the nurturing of all things. To assist their transforming and nurturing activity and stand alongside Heaven and Earth is impossible without fully realizing one’s nature. There is a reason why the gentleman, when discussing the kingly Way, invariably grounds it in Heaven’s virtues…

春秋於大國之討貳必托詞以罪之焉于以見
宋之伐陳省己謀國兩失之春秋於衛書救而

夫！
「宋師伐陳，衛人救陳。」宣公十有二年。
麻永吉。
同考試官署員外郎常批：「重責宋，良得書救之義，且對待敏整，精確，當非苟作者。」
同考試官修撰馬批：「重責宋，誠是傳意，而詞復雅健，錄之。」

春秋於大國之討貳，必托詞以罪之焉，于以見宋之伐陳，省己、謀國兩失之。春秋於衛書救，而所以罪宋者深矣。宋衛清丘有盟，好惡同之，乃宋討陳之附楚也，而衛救焉，宜以失信貶衛矣。而得書救者何？君子曰：「衛以救書，所以罪宋也。」盖省己者，非脩怨之貴，而自厚以遠怨之難。陳之亂也，楚討之，而宋不能，陳是以南向而受盟。宋欲服陳，豈無德禮可以招携乎？而加之兵也，是徒知責陳不當背己以從楚，而不思栗門之
translation_en:
…indeed!
“The army of Song attacked Chen; men of Wei came to Chen’s rescue.” Twelfth year of Duke Xuan.
Ma Yongji.
Associate Examiner Chang, Acting Vice Director, comments: “By placing heavy blame on Song, this truly grasps the significance of recording the action as a ‘rescue.’ Moreover, its paired arguments are deft, orderly, and precise. Surely this is no carelessly composed work.”
Associate Examiner Ma, Compiler, comments: “Placing heavy blame on Song indeed accords with the commentary’s meaning, and the language is also elegant and vigorous. Include it.”
Examiner Hu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “Rigorous, orderly, and appropriate in form.”
Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: “The interpretation is refined, and the language conveys it clearly.”
When the Spring and Autumn Annals records a great state’s punitive attack on one whose allegiance has wavered, it invariably uses its wording to condemn the attacker. Thus we see that, in attacking Chen, Song failed both in examining itself and in planning for its state. By recording Wei’s action as a ‘rescue,’ the Spring and Autumn Annals condemns Song all the more profoundly. Song and Wei had covenanted at Qingqiu to share their friendships and enmities. Yet when Song attacked Chen for adhering to Chu, Wei came to Chen’s rescue. It would seem that Wei should have been censured for breaking faith. Why, then, was its action accorded the designation ‘rescue’? The gentleman says: “Wei’s action is recorded as a rescue in order to condemn Song.”
For one who examines himself, pursuing old grievances is not what deserves esteem; the difficult thing is to strengthen one’s own virtue so as to keep resentment at a distance. When disorder arose in Chen, Chu took punitive action, whereas Song could not. Chen therefore turned south and accepted a covenant. If Song wished to secure Chen’s submission, were there no means of attracting an estranged state through virtue and ritual propriety? Yet it attacked Chen with troops. This was merely to reproach Chen for turning its back on Song and following Chu, without reflecting on what happened at Limen [?] …

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
轉在楚仗義有足多者要之雖縣焉復封焉陳
之德楚宜也而無罪之邦非宋人執言之利矣
惟干戈省厥躬書之訓也宋之伐陳其無乃昧
省躬之訓矣乎謀國者非禦敵之難而能固本
以待敵之貴陳之貳也華棄之而夷是即楚是
以北圖而益橫宋欲禦楚豈無德政可以強國
乎而攻其與也是徒知伐陳或可立威以撓楚
而不思蒲胥之車在楚重怒有足虞者卒之既
伐焉復圍焉楚之仇宋深也而無已之師固宋
===
人自詒之戚矣惟甲胄起戎書之戒也宋之伐
陳其無乃犯起戎之戒矣乎故春秋於伐陳之
下書衛人救陳盖托以罪宋之非義而失圖也
若衛之背盟豈待貶而後見哉抑宋之伐陳晉
之意也清丘載書要言討貳不獨宋志明矣辰
陵遺義而夷釁輕挑夫豈制禦之畧乎伯宗之
對晉不能宗諸侯矣隳世伯之業以成楚莊之
伯果天授楚耶抑晉授之耶士會諸臣不得而
辭其咎矣

punctuated: 轉，在楚仗義有足多者。要之，雖縣焉，復封焉，陳之德楚宜也，而無罪之邦，非宋人執言之利矣。「惟干戈省厥躬」，書之訓也。宋之伐陳，其無乃昧省躬之訓矣乎？謀國者，非禦敵之難，而能固本以待敵之貴。陳之貳也，華棄之而夷是即，楚是以北圖而益橫。宋欲禦楚，豈無德政可以強國乎？而攻其與也，是徒知伐陳或可立威以撓楚，而不思蒲胥之車，在楚重怒有足虞者。卒之，既伐焉，復圍焉，楚之仇宋深也，而無已之師，固宋人自詒之戚矣。「惟甲胄起戎」，書之戒也。宋之伐陳，其無乃犯起戎之戒矣乎？故春秋於伐陳之下書「衛人救陳」，盖托以罪宋之非義而失圖也。若衛之背盟，豈待貶而後見哉？抑宋之伐陳，晉之意也。清丘載書，要言討貳，不獨宋志明矣。辰陵遺義，而夷釁輕挑，夫豈制禦之畧乎？伯宗之對，晉不能宗諸侯矣。隳世伯之業，以成楚莊之伯，果天授楚耶？抑晉授之耶？士會諸臣不得而辭其咎矣。
translation_en:
…the reversal at Limen [?]: Chu’s upholding of righteousness had much that deserved praise. In any event, although Chu had made Chen a county, it subsequently restored it as a fief. Chen was therefore right to feel gratitude toward Chu, and a blameless state offered the men of Song no advantageous pretext for their attack. “When there are weapons of war, examine yourself”: this is the instruction of the Book of Documents. In attacking Chen, was Song not blind to this instruction to examine oneself?

For those who plan a state’s affairs, the crucial achievement is not the difficult task of resisting an enemy, but the ability to strengthen the foundations in readiness for that enemy. When Chen became divided in its allegiance, the states of the Chinese heartland abandoned it, and it turned to the foreign peoples. Chu consequently pursued designs to the north and grew increasingly overbearing. If Song wished to resist Chu, could it not have strengthened its state through virtuous government? Yet it attacked Chu’s ally. This was merely to recognize that attacking Chen might establish its prestige and thwart Chu, without considering the chariot at Puxu [?] and the grounds for fearing Chu’s intensified anger. In the end, Chu first attacked Song and then besieged it. Chu’s enmity toward Song was deep, and the unending warfare was truly an affliction that the men of Song had brought upon themselves. “Armor and helmets give rise to warfare”: this is the warning of the Book of Documents. In attacking Chen, did Song not transgress this warning against provoking warfare?

Thus, beneath its account of the attack on Chen, the Spring and Autumn Annals records: “The men of Wei came to Chen’s aid.” Through this wording it condemns Song’s unrighteousness and faulty planning. As for Wei’s breach of the covenant, did that need explicit censure before it became apparent? Moreover, Song’s attack on Chen reflected Jin’s intentions. The covenant document at Qingqiu stipulated the punishment of those divided in their allegiance: clearly this was not Song’s purpose alone. Righteous duty was neglected at Chenling, while conflict with the foreign peoples was lightly provoked. How could this be a strategy for keeping them in check? Bo Zong’s reply shows that Jin could no longer serve as leader of the feudal lords. By destroying its inherited hegemony, it brought about the hegemony of King Zhuang of Chu. Was it really Heaven that bestowed this upon Chu, or was it Jin? Shi Hui and the other ministers cannot evade their responsibility.

Record of Rites
“For every three years of cultivation, there must be food sufficient for one year; for every nine years of cultivation, there must be food sufficient for three years.”
Gao Qiyu
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Acting Vice Director: “The phrasing is refined and pure, and the thought especially comprehensive. This truly grasps the essentials of governing a state and certainly deserves inclusion.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Lü, Reader-in-waiting: “This composition expounds almost fully the sages’ intention to provide abundance for the state and prosperity for the people. Its language is also elegant and accomplished. It is among the finest essays on the meaning of the Classics.”
Comment by Examiner Hu, Academician Reader-in-waiting: “Precise and apt; worthy to serve as a model.”
Comment by Examiner Gao, Academician: “Substantial and practical.”
Under the former kings’ system of accumulating reserves, a surplus was invariably required when reckoned over a span of years. Accumulating reserves is a major affair of state, yet it cannot be accomplished hastily. The former kings always ensured a surplus over a span of years: was this not how they kept the people from hardship while making resources sufficient? Such is the account in “Royal Regulations.”
The people regard food as Heaven; thus government takes ensuring sufficient food as its essential task. How, then, should the Grand Steward regulate the state’s expenditure? If reserves are not accumulated in advance, the granaries will not be full, and there will certainly be nothing with which to prepare for future needs. Yet if reserves are accumulated too abruptly, the people’s strength will not bear the burden, and there will instead be nothing with which to meet present needs. title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
之舒焉而經制得劑量之宜三年耕與必使有
一年之食夫三而有一可謂多矣而何可必乎
盖每歲所入均析為四而每歲所出皆取其三
雖或年不順成亦寧詘吾所舉而已而贏羡者
固在也則一分之餘既得於三分之外而一年
之食自裕於三年之中有可備以無患也已否
則耕以三年固用以三年也而何有於一年者
哉九年耕與必使有三年之食夫九而有三則
尤多矣而何可必乎盖其析也以四分為恒規
===
而其用也以三分為定則是雖年有久近亦惟
守吾成計而已而異同者無有也則一年之食
既裕於三年之中而三年之餘自得於九年之
外尤可恃以不恐也已否則耕以九年固用以
九年也而何有於三年者哉是知自一年而言
則所積既不為多合九年而言則所積已不為

…consume it slowly, so that established arrangements achieve the proper balance in apportionment. For three years of cultivation, they invariably ensured a reserve of one year’s food. To have one year’s reserve from three years may be called abundant; but how could this be assured? Each year’s receipts were divided equally into four portions, and each year’s expenditures took only three of them. Even if a year failed to yield a good harvest, they would simply curtail their undertakings, leaving the surplus intact. Thus, one portion remained beyond the three expended, and a year’s food naturally accumulated within three years. With such provision, there need be no anxiety. Otherwise, what was cultivated over three years would simply be consumed over three years: how could there be a year’s reserve?

For nine years of cultivation, they invariably ensured a reserve of three years’ food. To have three years’ reserve from nine years was still more abundant; but how could this be assured? Dividing receipts into four portions was their constant rule, and expending three portions was their fixed standard. Whether the span of years was long or short, they simply adhered to their established plan without variation. Thus, once a year’s food had accumulated within three years, a three-year surplus naturally became available beyond the needs of nine years. This afforded still greater assurance against fear. Otherwise, what was cultivated over nine years would simply be consumed over nine years: how could there be three years’ reserve?

From this we know that, considered over a single year, the amount stored was not large; considered over nine years together, it was no longer small. How much more would this be so if the practice continued still longer! This was why public and private resources alike were sufficient in the age of the former kings. I have read the Rites of Zhou and thereby understood how well the Zhou dynasty managed its finances. 内、職外、職幣之類，以理其事，纖悉委曲，無不周備。所以使計年而有餘者，固即由此歟？雖然，制用存乎法，而所以善其法者存乎人。苟非以為國之實心而行其實事，則法何為乎？司國計者，其審諸！

translation_en:
…[officials responsible for] receipts, expenditures, and surplus funds, and others of this kind, to administer these affairs. Every minute detail and complexity was fully provided for. Surely it was through this that annual accounts showed a surplus? Nevertheless, regulating expenditure depends on laws, while making those laws work well depends on people. Unless they carry out practical measures with a sincere concern for the state, what use are laws? Those who manage the state's finances should consider this carefully!

Virtue is the manifestation of one's nature; music is the flowering of virtue. Metal and stone, silk strings and bamboo pipes are the instruments of music. Poetry expresses one's aspirations; singing gives voice to them; dance expresses them in bodily movement. These three have their root in the heart; only then do musical instruments follow. Thus, when feeling is deep, its patterned expression is luminous; when vital energy is abundant, its transforming power is wondrous. Harmony and accord accumulate within, and their flowering radiance appears without.

Huang Caimin.

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
記者原樂之所由作著樂之所由盛盖樂必由
本以及文非徒作也則夫本之盛者其文豈有
不盛哉樂記之意若曰樂之爲道也無本不立
無文不行善觀樂者亦惟於其本焉求之何則
樂所以象德也以言乎德乃性之渾然者呈諸
端緒是樂之本也以言乎樂乃德之粹然者顯
於聲容是德之華也若夫金石絲竹不過其器
焉耳而本豈在是乎何也樂之始而有詩焉志
動於內而情見乎辭所以言其志也言之不足
===
而宣之於歌非咏其聲以成方乎歌之不足而
形之於舞非動其容以盡變乎夫是三者根心
而生詩歌之發舞蹈之容皆無聲無形者為之
本也然後從之以器被諸八音飾以干羽而有
聲有容樂斯作焉使無是心則將無所謂詩歌
舞者矣而况於器乎此可見情其本也文其著
也是故情之所感者深則文之所著自明不然
未有能明者也猶之天地之氣盛則及物之化
自神不然未有能神者也故夫美在其中而和

The recorder traces the origins of music’s creation and makes clear how it comes to flourish. Music must proceed from its root to its patterned expression; it does not simply arise without a basis. Thus, when its root flourishes, how could its patterned expression fail to flourish? The meaning of the Record of Music may be expressed thus: as a Way, music cannot be established without a root, nor can it be put into practice without patterned expression. Those skilled in observing music seek understanding precisely in its root. Why? Music serves to represent virtue. Speaking of virtue, it is the undivided wholeness of human nature manifesting itself in particular expressions: this is the root of music. Speaking of music, it is the purity of virtue becoming visible in sound and movement: this is the flowering of virtue. As for metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments, these are merely its implements. How could its root lie in them?

Why is this so? At music’s inception there is poetry. The intent stirs within, and feelings appear in words, thereby giving voice to that intent. When words are insufficient and one gives expression through song, is this not chanting sounds to form musical patterns? When song is insufficient and one gives embodiment through dance, is this not moving the body to exhaust the possibilities of variation? These three arise from roots in the heart. The utterance of poetry and song and the movements of dance all have their root in what is soundless and formless. Only then are instruments added, expression given through the eight classes of musical sound, and embellishment supplied with shields and feathers. With sound and movement, music thus comes into being. Without this heart, there would be no poetry, song, or dance to speak of—how much less any instrumental music! From this we can see that feeling is its root, and patterned expression its outward manifestation.

Thus, when feeling is deeply stirred, its patterned manifestation naturally becomes clear; otherwise, it can never become clear. This is like the vital energy of Heaven and Earth: when it flourishes, its transforming influence upon things naturally becomes wondrous; otherwise, it can never become wondrous. Thus, when beauty resides within and harmony…

…when the virtue of the harmonious heart has accumulated to the utmost fullness, its patterned expression must become manifest outwardly; the radiance of its blossoming excellence cannot be concealed. Does not the flourishing of music’s outward forms arise from the flourishing of its root? Thus, through the performance of music one can observe virtue: is this not why the gentleman must not delay the work of returning to his true feelings and harmonizing his intentions? Yet, granted that music manifests virtue, why must its root necessarily be traced to human nature? Human nature is ordained by Heaven and endowed within the heart. The gentleman nurtures his nature in stillness to recover the foundation of Heaven’s endowment. Thus, realized in his person it becomes virtue; expressed through instruments it becomes music. Its accomplished efficacy suffices to order Heaven and Earth and assist their transforming and nurturing work. Otherwise, what issues outwardly would have no root: how could it constitute virtue? Hence the saying: “Only when the thoughts of the heart comprehend human nature and Heaven’s mandate can one discuss rites and music.” True indeed!

===
聖人所以端拱而成天下之治者其必有道焉
天下至大也而人君臨御於上則其務誠繁矣
苟惟其繁也而遂竭力以圖之則事無窮而吾
力有限將愈勞而治愈不幾矣聖王則不然以
爲吾既以一身任天下之重使非自持其體則
何以裕吾力而優於天下矧事務雖繁而所以
分理者自有其人吾惟隨事以用其人隨用以
責其效則事務自理而天下有餘治亦奚俟乎
用吾勞者是故臣集其能君總其功端拱九重

不事馳騁而文采充蔚，眞邁古之作，老生佳士。

同考試官修撰丁批：「格古而思精，是能力去虚浮、敦崇大雅者，取之。」

同考試官右中允陳批：「議論層出，而浩博之學、圓融之思、俊逸之才具見，可録。」

考試官侍讀學士胡批：「體格正大，思致精深，議論閎博，積學之士也，取之。」

考試官學士高批：「雄渾暢健，有曲折而無痕迹，論之佳者。」

聖人所以端拱而成天下之治者，其必有道焉。天下至大也，而人君臨御於上，則其務誠繁矣。苟惟其繁也，而遂竭力以圖之，則事無窮而吾力有限，將愈勞而治愈不幾矣。聖王則不然，以爲吾既以一身任天下之重，使非自持其體，則何以裕吾力而優於天下？矧事務雖繁，而所以分理者自有其人。吾惟隨事以用其人，隨用以責其效，則事務自理而天下有餘治，亦奚俟乎用吾勞者？是故臣集其能，君總其功，端拱九重
translation_en:
…Without indulging in rhetorical flights, the writing abounds in literary brilliance. Truly a work surpassing the ancients, by a mature scholar of outstanding quality.

Associate Examiner Ding, Senior Compiler, comments: “Its style is antique and its thought refined. This is someone capable of vigorously rejecting superficiality and firmly honoring the highest literary standards. Accept it.”

Associate Examiner Chen, Right Mentor, comments: “Arguments emerge layer upon layer, fully displaying extensive learning, well-integrated thought, and outstanding literary talent. Worthy of inclusion.”

Examiner Hu, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Its form is correct and grand, its thought refined and profound, and its argument wide-ranging. This is a scholar of accumulated learning. Accept it.”

Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: “Powerful and full-bodied, fluent and vigorous; its turns leave no trace of artifice. An excellent discourse.”

There must be a Way by which the sage brings order to all under Heaven while sitting upright with hands folded. All under Heaven is vast indeed, and when a ruler presides over it from above, his duties are truly numerous. If, merely because they are numerous, he exhausts his strength in attending to them, affairs will remain inexhaustible while his strength is limited. The more he labors, the further he will be from achieving order. The sage king acts otherwise. He reasons: ‘Since I bear in my single person the weight of all under Heaven, unless I maintain the proper bearing of my position, how can I conserve my strength and govern all under Heaven with ease? Moreover, although affairs are numerous, there are people to administer their respective portions. I need only employ the appropriate person for each affair and hold each accountable for the results of his service. Affairs will then be managed of themselves, and all under Heaven will enjoy ample good order. What need will there be to expend my own labor?’ Thus ministers contribute their abilities, and the ruler brings their achievements together, sitting upright with hands folded within the ninefold palace…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
而化自成焉盖得其道也嗚呼非天下之至明
其孰能與於此明君恭己而成功此宋儒范氏
之言也請為之明其意天以四海之廣兆民之
眾付之乎君任若是其大也而禮樂賴以修明
刑政賴以振舉蒸黎賴以乂安九夷八蠻賴以
鎮撫天地賴以平成鬼神賴以格享草木鳥獸
賴以咸若責若是其重也以如彼之任而萃乎
如此之責亦難乎其治之矣而況可恭己以治
乎故有兢兢業業者焉猶曰下民其咨也有亹
===
亹翼翼者焉猶曰民其如傷也而何以云恭己
乎於戲此皆聖人憂勤惕勵之心不能自已者
也而其所以為治則固有為之為者而非其身
自為也夫豈不欲身自為哉而其理固不可也
不觀之天乎夫於穆不已者天也然易知而大
生焉何也吾見其暄以日月鼓以風霆潤以雨
露斂以霜雪而百物生焉且成焉天弗與也乃
論生成者不歸諸日月風霆雨露霜雪而歸之
天則天寔主之也而日月風霆雨露霜雪則皆
alt_text:
而化自成焉蓋得其道也嗚呼非天下之至明
其孰能與於此明君恭已而成功此宋儒范氏
之言也請爲之明其意天以四海之廣兆民之
衆付之乎君任君是其大也而禮樂賴以修明
刑政賴以振舉蒸黎賴以乂安九夷八蠻賴以
鎮撫天地賴以平成鬼神賴以格享草木鳥獸
賴以咸若責君是其重也以如彼之任而萃乎
如此之責亦難乎其治之矣而況可恭已以治
乎故有兢兢業業者焉猶曰下民其咨也有亹
===
亹翼翼者焉猶曰民其如傷也而何以云恭已
乎於戲此皆聖人憂勤惕勵之心不能自已者
也而其所以爲治則固有爲之爲者而非其身
自爲也夫豈不欲身自爲哉而其理固不可也
不觀之天乎夫於穆不已者天也然易知而大
生焉何也吾見其暄以日月鼓以風霆潤以雨
露歛以霜雪而百物生焉且成焉天弗與也乃
論生成者不歸諸日月風霆雨露霜雪而歸之
天則天寔主之也而日月風霆雨露霜雪則皆
punctuated:
而化自成焉，盖得其道也。嗚呼！非天下之至明，其孰能與於此？「明君恭己而成功」，此宋儒范氏之言也，請為之明其意。

天以四海之廣、兆民之眾付之乎君，任若是其大也。而禮樂賴以修明，刑政賴以振舉，蒸黎賴以乂安，九夷八蠻賴以鎮撫，天地賴以平成，鬼神賴以格享，草木鳥獸賴以咸若，責若是其重也。以如彼之任，而萃乎如此之責，亦難乎其治之矣，而況可恭己以治乎？故有兢兢業業者焉，猶曰「下民其咨也」；有亹亹翼翼者焉，猶曰「民其如傷也」。而何以云恭己乎？

於戲！此皆聖人憂勤惕勵之心不能自已者也，而其所以為治，則固有為之為者，而非其身自為也。夫豈不欲身自為哉？而其理固不可也。不觀之天乎？夫於穆不已者，天也；然易知而大生焉，何也？吾見其暄以日月，鼓以風霆，潤以雨露，斂以霜雪，而百物生焉且成焉，天弗與也。乃論生成者，不歸諸日月風霆雨露霜雪，而歸之天，則天寔主之也，而日月風霆雨露霜雪則皆
translation_en:
…and transformation comes about of itself, for he has grasped the proper Way. Ah! Who but the most discerning person under Heaven could attain this? “An enlightened ruler holds himself in reverent composure and achieves success”: these are the words of Master Fan, the Song Confucian scholar. Allow me to elucidate their meaning.

Heaven entrusts to the ruler the vast lands within the Four Seas and their teeming people: so great is his charge. Rites and music depend upon him for their cultivation and clarification; punishments and government, for their vigorous implementation; the common people, for peace and good order; the Nine Yi and Eight Man peoples, for pacification; Heaven and Earth, for harmony and fulfillment; spirits, for coming to receive offerings; and plants, birds, and beasts, for all to flourish in accordance with their natures. So weighty are his responsibilities. With such a charge and so many responsibilities concentrated upon him, governing is indeed difficult. How much less could he govern merely by holding himself in reverent composure? Thus there were those who were ever cautious and diligent, yet still said, “The people below are lamenting”; there were those who labored tirelessly and watchfully, yet still regarded the people “as though they were injured.” How, then, can one speak of reverent composure?

Ah! These are all expressions of the sage’s anxious, diligent, vigilant, and striving heart, which cannot restrain itself. Yet in his conduct of government, there are indeed others who act on his behalf; he does not personally perform everything. Could it be that he does not wish to perform it himself? The underlying principle simply does not permit it. Have you not observed Heaven? Profound and unceasing in its workings is Heaven; yet it governs through ease and brings forth life abundantly. Why is this? I see it warm things through the sun and moon, stir them through wind and thunder, moisten them through rain and dew, and gather them in through frost and snow. The myriad things are born and brought to maturity, while Heaven takes no direct part. Yet those who discuss their birth and maturation attribute these not to the sun and moon, wind and thunder, rain and dew, or frost and snow, but to Heaven. This is because Heaven truly presides over them, while the sun and moon, wind and thunder, rain and dew, and frost and snow are all…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
爲之生爲之成者也而天何爲哉是故曰於穆
而已也夫人君則天也其於天下也是統之者
也而非所統者也兼之者也而非所兼者也如
必自用其力以爲治則是不以日月也而自爲
之晅不以風霆也而自爲之鼓不以雨露也而
自爲之潤不以霜雪也而自爲之斂非所謂統
也且晅則直日月耳而何以鼓鼓則直風霆耳
而何以潤潤則直雨露耳而何以斂非所謂兼
也而所統者所兼者則何爲乎聖王知其然以
===
爲天下之事吾既不可以獨理而才賢之士固
所以亮采惠疇而弼吾之治者也吾惟知所以
用之而何有於治者是故始之以籲俊之誠繼
之以迪知之實而終之以器使之宜燮理寅亮
托之乎公孤率屬阜成付之乎卿士藩宣屏翰
寄之乎岳牧分繁理劇委之乎諸司而聖王在
上則爲之董正而已矣訓迪而已矣專責以盡
其才久任以需其成而已矣而事弗親也其猷
爲謀力輻輳並進畢効於吾前則爲之省成而

translation_en:
…bring things to life and bring them to completion on Heaven’s behalf. Yet what does Heaven itself do? Thus it is said: “It is simply profound and majestic.” The ruler takes Heaven as his model. In relation to all under Heaven, he is the one who unifies, rather than one of those unified; he is the one who encompasses, rather than one of those encompassed. If he insists on governing through his own exertions, this is like dispensing with the sun and moon and himself providing their warmth; dispensing with wind and thunder and himself stirring things into motion; dispensing with rain and dew and himself moistening things; dispensing with frost and snow and himself bringing things into repose. This is not what is meant by unifying. Moreover, if he provides warmth, he is merely the sun and moon: how can he also stir things into motion? If he stirs things into motion, he is merely wind and thunder: how can he also moisten things? If he moistens things, he is merely rain and dew: how can he also bring things into repose? This is not what is meant by encompassing. And what, then, would those whom he unifies and encompasses have to do?

The sage king understands this and considers: “I cannot manage the affairs of all under Heaven alone. Worthy and talented men are precisely those who can assist in carrying out duties, bring harmony to their various spheres, and aid my government. If I only know how to employ them, what difficulty will there be in governing?” Thus he begins with sincerity in summoning outstanding men, proceeds with the actual work of guiding and understanding them, and concludes by employing each appropriately according to his capacity. He entrusts harmonization and reverent assistance to the Three Dukes and Three Junior Dukes; assigns the direction of subordinates and the advancement of prosperity to the ministers; commits the work of serving as protective bulwarks and extending his influence to the regional governors; and delegates the division of manifold tasks and the management of demanding affairs to the various offices. The sage king above them need only supervise and correct them, instruct and guide them, assign them clear responsibility so that they fully exercise their talents, and keep them in office long enough to await their achievements. He does not personally undertake their duties. When their plans, actions, counsel, and efforts converge like spokes at a hub and advance together, and all render their service before him, he then reviews their accomplishments and…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
已矣明賞罰而已矣而用弗擾也夫是之謂有
要有要之謂有體是故耳無煩聽目無煩視心
無煩慮手足無煩動而志定神固弗可撓也無
煩聽則有餘聽乃以兼天下之聽無煩視則有
餘視乃以兼天下之視無煩慮則有餘慮乃以
兼天下之慮無煩動則有餘動乃以兼天下之
動而洞徹高朗弗可窺也夫然後是非莫眩其
度輕重莫溷其量操縱莫測其機威福莫移其
柄超然獨運之理得而所以宰制役使者裕如
===
而不窮由是百官勸務而不懈百職兼舉而不
偏以燮以亮公孤既爲之矣以率以阜卿士既
爲之矣以宣以翰岳牧既爲之矣以分以理諸
司既爲之矣是故以禮樂則修明以刑政則振
舉以蒸黎則乂安以九夷八蠻則嚮風以天地
則平成以鬼神則格享以草木鳥獸則咸若而
聖王獨饗其成焉爲其事者臣也然而弗有也
有其功者君也然而弗爲也豈必竭精畢力勞
役心體哉拱手垂衣裳而化已神矣海內已服

役心體哉拱手垂衣裳而化已神矣海内已服
punctuated: 已矣，明賞罰而已矣，而用弗擾也。夫是之謂有要，有要之謂有體。是故耳無煩聽，目無煩視，心無煩慮，手足無煩動，而志定神固，弗可撓也。無煩聽則有餘聽，乃以兼天下之聽；無煩視則有餘視，乃以兼天下之視；無煩慮則有餘慮，乃以兼天下之慮；無煩動則有餘動，乃以兼天下之動，而洞徹高朗，弗可窺也。夫然後是非莫眩其度，輕重莫溷其量，操縱莫測其機，威福莫移其柄。超然獨運之理得，而所以宰制役使者裕如而不窮。由是百官勸務而不懈，百職兼舉而不偏。以燮以亮，公孤既爲之矣；以率以阜，卿士既爲之矣；以宣以翰，岳牧既爲之矣；以分以理，諸司既爲之矣。是故以禮樂則修明，以刑政則振舉，以蒸黎則乂安，以九夷八蠻則嚮風，以天地則平成，以鬼神則格享，以草木鳥獸則咸若，而聖王獨饗其成焉。爲其事者臣也，然而弗有也；有其功者君也，然而弗爲也。豈必竭精畢力，勞役心體哉？拱手垂衣裳而化已神矣，海內已服
translation_en:
…and nothing more; he need only make rewards and punishments clear, without interfering in the employment of his officials. This is what it means to grasp the essentials; grasping the essentials means possessing the proper framework of rule. Thus his ears are not wearied by listening, his eyes by looking, his mind by deliberation, or his hands and feet by movement. His purpose is settled and his spirit firm, beyond disturbance. With no wearisome listening, he has hearing to spare and can encompass all the listening done throughout the realm; with no wearisome looking, he has sight to spare and can encompass all the looking done throughout the realm; with no wearisome deliberation, he has thought to spare and can encompass all the deliberation done throughout the realm; with no wearisome movement, he has energy to spare and can encompass all the activity throughout the realm. His understanding is penetrating, lofty, and luminous, beyond others’ scrutiny. Only then can questions of right and wrong no longer confound his standards, nor considerations of relative importance confuse his judgment. None can fathom the workings by which he tightens or loosens control, and none can wrest from him the authority to punish and reward. Having grasped the principle of directing affairs independently from above, he commands and employs others with ease and inexhaustible capacity.

Consequently, all officials diligently attend to their duties without flagging, and all offices discharge their functions together, with none neglected. Harmonizing and assisting: the Three Dukes and Three Junior Guardians have already undertaken these tasks. Leading their subordinates and bringing prosperity: the ministers have already undertaken these. Extending the ruler’s influence and serving as his bulwarks: the regional governors have already undertaken these. Apportioning manifold business and managing difficult affairs: the various offices have already undertaken these. Thus rites and music are cultivated and clarified; punishments and administration are put into effective operation; the common people are governed and secure; the Nine Yi and Eight Man peoples turn toward his civilizing influence; Heaven and Earth attain balance and fulfillment; ghosts and spirits draw near and accept the offerings; and plants, trees, birds, and beasts all flourish in due order. The sage king alone enjoys the completed achievement. Those who perform the work are the ministers, yet they do not claim it as their own; the one to whom the credit belongs is the ruler, yet he does not perform the work himself. Why must he exhaust his spirit and strength, toiling in mind and body? With hands folded and robes hanging down, his transforming influence is already wondrous, and all within the seas have already submitted…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
矣譬則天之運於冲漠之上也四序調六氣順
而物之生成者已遂矣是故聖人在上巍乎其
莫與京蕩乎其無能名昭乎其光而燭極六合
無所不通沛乎其順而變化萬物無所不行則
明之至也盖古稱恭己而治者莫如舜今觀其
任九官任十二牧而又任禹以總之舜於諸臣
之事有弗爲也而各爲之爲乃其所以爲也而
曰俾予從欲以治四方風動此所以爲舜也書
曰庶獄庶愼文王罔敢知於兹而詩則曰濟濟
===
多士文王以寧夫文王豈不欲知諸獄愼者哉
誠不敢以委瑣之故爲吾累也而曰有疏附有

矣。譬則天之運於冲漠之上也，四序調，六氣順，而物之生成者已遂矣。是故聖人在上，巍乎其莫與京，蕩乎其無能名，昭乎其光而燭極六合，無所不通；沛乎其順而變化萬物，無所不行，則明之至也。盖古稱恭己而治者莫如舜，今觀其任九官，任十二牧，而又任禹以總之。舜於諸臣之事有弗爲也，而各爲之，爲乃其所以爲也。而曰：「俾予從欲以治，四方風動。」此所以爲舜也。《書》曰：「庶獄庶愼，文王罔敢知於兹。」而《詩》則曰：「濟濟多士，文王以寧。」夫文王豈不欲知諸獄愼者哉？誠不敢以委瑣之故爲吾累也。而曰：「有疏附，有先後，有奔走，有禦侮。」則固可以寧矣，此所以爲文也。後世乃有衡石程書者焉，有衛士傳餐者焉，非不勞且苦也。不知所務，而獨以其身殉之，亦徒自敝已爾，而何治之能爲？故曰：「善治者逸而有成，不善治者勞而無功。」則體要所在，得與不得之說也。

translation_en:
… It is like Heaven’s movement in the heights of empty stillness: the four seasons are regulated, the six vital forces flow harmoniously, and all things duly come into being and grow. Thus, when the sage occupies the highest position, his loftiness admits no equal, and his vastness defies description. His radiance shines to the limits of the six directions, penetrating everywhere; his abundant accord with the natural order transforms the myriad things, operating everywhere. This is the utmost illumination.

Among those of antiquity praised for governing simply by maintaining a reverent bearing, none equaled Shun. Consider how he appointed the nine officials and the twelve regional governors, and further appointed Yu to oversee them all. Shun refrained from performing the duties of his ministers, while each performed his own; their action was thus the means by which he acted. He said: “Enable me to govern in accordance with my wishes, and the four quarters will respond as though moved by the wind.” This was what made Shun who he was. The Book of Documents says: “As for the many lawsuits and matters requiring care, King Wen did not presume to take cognizance of them.” And the Book of Odes says: “Numerous were the worthy officers; through them King Wen enjoyed repose.” Could King Wen really have had no wish to know about lawsuits and matters requiring care? He simply did not presume to burden himself with petty details. The Odes further says: “There were those who drew others close, those who guided and assisted, those who hurried about on his business, and those who resisted aggression.” With such men, he could indeed enjoy repose. This was what made Wen who he was.

In later ages there were rulers who weighed documents to set their daily quota of work, and rulers whose guards passed meals to them. It was certainly not that they failed to toil and suffer. Yet, unaware of what they should attend to, they devoted their own persons to the work and merely exhausted themselves. What effective government could they accomplish? Thus it is said: “Those skilled in governing achieve results at ease; those unskilled in governing labor without accomplishment.” This speaks to whether or not one grasps the essential principles of government.

Even so, employing people is also difficult. The affairs of the realm are inexhaustible, and its need for people to carry them out is endless. If one must diligently seek out talent every day and employ…

translation_en:
…them, even then one could not keep pace. Thus there is something still more essential. In this world there are talented men who can be employed, and talented men who can employ talent. Talent that can be employed is the lesser talent; talent that can employ talent is the greater. Obtaining a hundred fine horses is not as good as obtaining one Bole; obtaining a hundred fine swords is not as good as obtaining one Ouye; obtaining a hundred men whose talents can be employed is not as good as obtaining one man who can employ talent. Obtain one Bole, and there will be more fine horses than one can use; obtain one Ouye, and there will be more fine swords than one can use; obtain one man who can employ talent, and there will be more employable talent than one can use. The “Oath of Qin” says: “If there were a minister, sincere and generous, seemingly able to embrace others; when another possessed a skill, he would regard it as though he possessed it himself; the worthy and wise he would love in his heart. Thereby he could protect my common people—would this not be beneficial?” Such is a man with the talent to employ talent. To employ men and entrust this responsibility to such a person is indeed the most essential thing of all.

Associate Examiner Lu, Compiler, comments: Substantial and refined, precise and meticulous; throughout this expression of thanks, his loyal sincerity is fully apparent.

Associate Examiner Wang, Left Instructor, comments: The language and ideas are classically elegant, perfectly capturing the style of a Song writer.

Examiner Hu, Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: Classically elegant, harmonious, and substantial, it brings out the intention to restrain superficiality. It should be recorded as a model.

Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: The language has no florid ornament, and the ideas concern matters of consequence. Record it to influence the many scholars.

On a day in the third month of the second year of Jiayou [1057], I humbly received your sagely favor appointing me, your servant Xiu, to oversee the tribute examinations. Attached to the palace precincts, I have long unworthily occupied a position devoted to deliberation and reflection; now, reverently undertaking service within the examination compound, I have undeservedly been entrusted with selection and assessment. The advancement and rejection of talented men bear upon the rise and decline of the age’s moral order. Could someone so empty of ability and so mediocre as I presume to fulfill this commission? Your servant Xiu, truly trembling and truly fearful, bows his head to the ground and repeatedly kowtows.

I humbly reflect that when the court of Yu rewarded service with carriages and robes, it invariably began by receiving and examining men’s words; when the house of Zhou appointed men of ability to office, it generally first discussed and distinguished their qualifications. Thus regional overseers and governors were assigned their places, and worthy men, established in office, filled the court. Once selection from local communities ceased to operate, the tribute examination system arose. …as ruler and teacher, with schools in households and district schools, rites and music fill the realm; writing is uniform and carriage tracks are standardized, and your civilizing influence reaches north and south. You open the gates on all four sides, selecting the worthy and good through policy questions after the Han precedent; you exalt the Six Classics, curbing the emphasis on lyric poetry and rhapsodies found in the Tang examinations. Thus you recover the flourishing simplicity of antiquity, and all share the blessings of an enlightened sovereign.

Now the triennial examination comes round again, and the established regulations are once more put into effect. Promoted as honored guests on the basis of the three categories of qualification, the candidates all accompany the officials bringing accounts to the capital; worthy men from throughout the realm await the imperial summons at the Directorate of Palace Gate Reception. This is an auspicious occasion for drawing out talent together, like pulling up interconnected roots of couch grass, and the time has come to assess their accomplishments. Yet can those who judge victory and defeat merely peer through a crack? Those who determine right and wrong must themselves occupy the judgment hall.

Your servant’s learning falls short of the exemplary teachings of our predecessors, and his writing does not accord with current tastes. I am no Bole: could I empty the plains of Ji of their herds by identifying every fine horse? My discernment falls shamefully short of Bian He’s: how could I distinguish the jade of Mount Jing? Yet in recommending worthy men for the state, I cherish something of Di Renjie’s loyalty; and in rescuing what is submerged and reviving what has declined, I privately share the aspiration of Han Yu of Changli. How could I fail reverently to obey your illustrious command and strive to fulfill my original purpose?

I shall esteem mastery of the Classics and study of antiquity, and guard against elaborately ornamented compositions and sentences. Listening to each player individually, how could I allow an incompetent performer to pass among the players of the yu pipes? Let the various accomplishments each be displayed: why should my preferences discriminate against a skilled player of the se zither? If a man’s name is accepted onto the path of advancement for the worthy, his words must not depart from the Way of the sages. Although ridgepoles, beams, and rafters differ, catalpa, lacquer tree, yi tree, and paulownia must each be put to suitable use. If candidates still follow debased old tracks, however, I shall not shrink from leaving pearls uncollected.

Advancing together with Wen Zi, how could I dare cultivate private interests among the men I recommend, my ‘peach and plum trees’? If I judge Jia Dao inadequate and decline to admit him, let slander arise over the ‘roses.’ In this way I hope to arrest the declining literary fashion and lend some small assistance to…

天眷，受符命，超越隆古，尤有不偶然者。此作能推本敷揚其盛，殆涵濡聖化而有得於觀感之深者。

同考試官都給事中邢批：我二祖、皇上，功德並隆，禎符相契，邁五超三。凡子孰不思一揚厲其盛？顧摹寫天地，有難爲容者。今子獨能敭賛洪庥，炳炳烺烺，可以占邃養矣。

同考試官編修李批：帝王受命，咸叶貞符。惟我二祖、皇上，峻德神功，昭受鴻祉，視昔尤烈。子能鋪張揚厲，藻思蔚如，是可與頌盛美者，錄之。

同考試官修撰丁批：我二祖、皇上，禎符鴻茂，未易揄揚。以經生能摹擬其盛，殆雍容聖化而獲觀其深者，取之。

同考試官右中允陳批：我
translation_en:
…Heaven’s favor and received auspicious tokens of the Mandate, surpassing even high antiquity: this above all was no mere coincidence. This essay traces the underlying causes and fully expounds that magnificence. Its author must have been steeped in the sage’s transforming influence and gained a profound understanding through observing and being moved by it.

Associate Examiner Xing, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: Our two ancestral emperors and His Majesty alike possess exalted achievements and virtue, and their auspicious tokens correspond with one another, surpassing the Five Emperors and the Three Sovereigns. Who among you would not wish to extol their magnificence? Yet portraying Heaven and Earth is difficult indeed. You alone have been able to celebrate these immense blessings with brilliant clarity; from this one can discern the depth of your cultivation.

Associate Examiner Li, Compiler, comments: When emperors and kings receive the Mandate, authentic auspicious tokens invariably accord with it. Our two ancestral emperors and His Majesty, through lofty virtue and wondrous achievements, have manifestly received great blessings, still more splendid than those of former times. You have expounded and extolled these with abundant literary imagination. Here is someone with whom one may celebrate this flourishing excellence. Enter this essay in the record.

Associate Examiner Ding, Senior Compiler, comments: The auspicious tokens of our two ancestral emperors and His Majesty are grand and abundant, and are not easily extolled. That a student of the Classics can portray their magnificence suggests that he has dwelt at ease within the sage’s transforming influence and attained insight into its depths. Accept this essay.

二祖、皇上聖德神功，昭揭上下；禎符瑞應，炳燿古今。蕩蕩乎，無能名焉！子能以閎麗之詞發之，其必素懷忠愛而思以自効者歟！

考試官侍讀學士胡批：我二祖、皇上受命永命之符，超越古今。子能揄揚其盛，而仰頌皇上欽承天眷之隆，忠敬溢於言表，宜錄以傳。

考試官學士高批：我二祖□□皇上功德隆茂，逈超千古，故瑞應紛燿，亦為獨盛。而我皇上緝熙纂命者，又獨至焉，則所以迓景祐於無疆者，端在於是。子能仰窺而贊述之，是亦沐浴泰和而能識其大者，特表出之。
translation_en:
…the sage virtue and divine achievements of our Two Founding Emperors and His Majesty shine forth throughout Heaven and earth; their auspicious tokens and propitious signs blaze across past and present. So vast are they that no words can name them! You have expressed them in grand and splendid language. Surely you have long cherished loyalty and devotion and wished to offer your service!

Examiner Hu, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: The tokens of our Two Founding Emperors’ and His Majesty’s receipt and perpetuation of the Mandate surpass all those of past and present. You have extolled their magnificence and reverently praised His Majesty’s respectful reception of Heaven’s abundant favor. Loyalty and reverence overflow your words. This answer deserves to be recorded and transmitted.

Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: The achievements and virtue of our Two Founding Emperors [two illegible characters] and His Majesty [?] are lofty and abundant, far surpassing those of all previous ages. Thus the propitious signs shine forth in profusion, likewise flourishing as never before. Moreover, His Majesty’s continuation of their luminous accomplishments and succession to the Mandate are uniquely consummate. Herein lies precisely the means of welcoming great blessings without limit. You have reverently discerned this and set it forth in praise. You are indeed one who, bathed in supreme harmony, can recognize its greatness. I single out this answer for distinction.

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
執事以帝王符命發策承學將以闡曠世
之
鴻禎表
至聖之駿烈颺頌金石光之罔極心至忠也顧
隙光無以議日月之明斗水無以評滄海
之量愚生何足與知之哉雖然
玄貺集而弗彰則神心弗恱
洪業成而弗賛則闓澤弗騰是掩
天庥而盖
===
===
聖德也愚竊惡焉敢不攄厥所聞恭述以對夫
受命之說莫詳於詩如曰有命自天曰天
有成命者不一而足固未嘗言符命也永
命之說莫詳於書如曰祈天永命曰受天
永命者不一而足亦未嘗言符命也然觀
玄鳥之詠歸禾之篇非符命而何故知天
鑒孔昭聖生非偶若乃貞元既會光嶽載
完運合豐隆聖當首出將以旋轉乾坤綏
定大業則必有俶儻非常之瑞預發其兆

完運合豐隆聖當首出將以旋轉乾坤綏
定大業則必有俶儻非常之瑞預發其兆
punctuated: 執事以帝王符命發策，承學將以闡曠世之鴻禎，表至聖之駿烈，颺頌金石，光之罔極，心至忠也。顧隙光無以議日月之明，斗水無以評滄海之量，愚生何足與知之哉？雖然，玄貺集而弗彰，則神心弗恱；洪業成而弗賛，則闓澤弗騰。是掩天庥而盖聖德也，愚竊惡焉，敢不攄厥所聞，恭述以對？夫受命之說，莫詳於詩，如曰「有命自天」，曰「天有成命」者，不一而足，固未嘗言符命也。永命之說，莫詳於書，如曰「祈天永命」，曰「受天永命」者，不一而足，亦未嘗言符命也。然觀玄鳥之詠、歸禾之篇，非符命而何？故知天鑒孔昭，聖生非偶。若乃貞元既會，光嶽載完，運合豐隆，聖當首出，將以旋轉乾坤，綏定大業，則必有俶儻非常之瑞，預發其兆。
translation_en:
You, honored Examiner, have set a policy question on the auspicious tokens of imperial mandate. We students are thereby to elucidate blessings unmatched through the ages, proclaim the mighty achievements of the utmost sage, and raise praises in metal and stone, making his glory shine without limit: the intention is supremely loyal. Yet light through a crack cannot judge the brightness of the sun and moon, nor a dipperful of water measure the vast ocean. How could an ignorant student such as I be qualified to understand these matters? Nevertheless, if heavenly gifts gather but are not made manifest, the divine heart will be displeased; if a great enterprise is accomplished but receives no praise, its generous beneficence will not spread abroad. This would conceal Heaven’s favor and obscure the sage’s virtue. I privately abhor this: how could I dare not set forth what I have learned and respectfully present it in reply?
No account of receiving the mandate is more detailed than that in the Book of Odes. Statements such as “There is a mandate from Heaven” and “Heaven has an established mandate” are too numerous to enumerate, yet they never speak of auspicious tokens of the mandate. No account of perpetuating the mandate is more detailed than that in the Book of Documents. Statements such as “Pray to Heaven for an enduring mandate” and “Receive Heaven’s enduring mandate” are likewise too numerous to enumerate, yet they too never speak of auspicious tokens of the mandate. But consider the ode “Dark Bird” and the chapter “The Presentation of Grain”: what are these if not auspicious tokens of the mandate? Thus we know that Heaven’s scrutiny is exceedingly clear and that the birth of a sage is no accident. When the end of one cycle joins the beginning of another, the vital splendor of the mountains is once more complete, and the movement of destiny converges upon flourishing abundance, a sage is due to arise foremost among men. As he is about to turn Heaven and Earth about and establish the great enterprise in peace, extraordinary and unprecedented auspicious signs must appear to announce its coming beforehand…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
譬則時雨將降山川出雲非故爲之也其
理既動其機自形不得而祕也及其紹天
闡繹克懋厥勛馨德昭升眷懷濃渥將俾
之昌熾祚以靈長則又必有俶儻非常之
瑞明示其意譬則愛深於心喜見於色亦
非故為之也其理已動其機自形不得而
祕也故曰國家將興必有禎祥又曰聖人
達順則天不愛道地不愛寶吁天人之際
其昭灼弗僭顧若此歟巢燧遠矣迨夫書
===
契而後羲農軒堯虞夏殷周之際則粲然
矣其迹瞑瑶鈴事傳金簡維風可覩也是
故虹流龍見羲炎寔生樞電龍圖軒堯用
誕玉曆神珠啟舜禹之興巨跡玉璜開商
周之祚其炳耀於先者固若此也謂之受
命之符非歟若夫出河之圖涌泉之醴熊
洛之書赤文之籙華琯龜疇狼鈞鳳書所
以鏗鈞於後者又若此也謂之永命之符
非歟卒之濬發既長保定且固以履位則

誕玉曆神珠啓舜禹之興巨跡玉璜開商

命之符非歟若夫出河之圖涌泉之醴熊
洛之書赤文之籙華珣龜疇狼鈎鳳書所
以鑒鍧於後者又若此也謂之永命之符
非歟卒之濬發既長保定且固以履位則
punctuated:
譬則時雨將降，山川出雲，非故爲之也。其理既動，其機自形，不得而祕也。及其紹天闡繹，克懋厥勛，馨德昭升，眷懷濃渥，將俾之昌熾，祚以靈長，則又必有俶儻非常之瑞，明示其意。譬則愛深於心，喜見於色，亦非故為之也。其理已動，其機自形，不得而祕也。故曰：「國家將興，必有禎祥。」又曰：「聖人達順，則天不愛道，地不愛寶。」吁！天人之際，其昭灼弗僭，顧若此歟！
巢燧遠矣，迨夫書契而後，羲農軒堯虞夏殷周之際，則粲然矣。其迹瞑瑶鈴，事傳金簡，維風可覩也。是故虹流龍見，羲炎寔生；樞電龍圖，軒堯用誕；玉曆神珠，啟舜禹之興；巨跡玉璜，開商周之祚。其炳耀於先者，固若此也。謂之受命之符，非歟？若夫出河之圖，涌泉之醴，熊洛之書，赤文之籙，華琯龜疇，狼鈞鳳書，所以鏗鈞於後者，又若此也。謂之永命之符，非歟？卒之濬發既長，保定且固，以履位則
translation_en:
…It is like clouds rising from mountains and rivers when timely rain is about to fall: this is not done deliberately. Once the underlying principle is set in motion, its workings manifest themselves and cannot be concealed. When the ruler carries forward and unfolds Heaven’s purposes, greatly advances his achievements, and his fragrant virtue rises resplendently on high, Heaven’s regard becomes deep and generous. Wishing to make him flourish and grant him enduring blessedness, Heaven must again send extraordinary and exceptional auspicious signs to reveal its intention plainly. It is like love deep within the heart appearing as joy upon the face: this, too, is not done deliberately. Once the underlying principle has been set in motion, its workings manifest themselves and cannot be concealed. Thus it is said: “When a state is about to flourish, there must be auspicious signs.” It is also said: “When the sage fully accords with the proper order, Heaven does not withhold its Way, nor Earth its treasures.” Ah! Can the connection between Heaven and humanity indeed be so clear and unfailing?
The ages of Youchao and Suiren are remote. But from the advent of writing onward, in the times of Fuxi, Shennong, Xuanyuan, Yao, Yu, Xia, Yin, and Zhou, these signs became brilliantly evident. Their traces were obscured amid jade bells [?], their deeds transmitted on golden tablets, and their legacy can still be discerned [?]. Thus, a streaming rainbow and an appearing dragon attended the births of Fuxi and Yandi; lightning at the Pivot star and a dragon chart attended the births of Xuanyuan and Yao. A jade calendar and a divine pearl heralded the rise of Shun and Yu; a giant footprint and a jade pendant inaugurated the dynastic fortunes of Shang and Zhou. Such were the brilliant manifestations that preceded them. Is it not right to call these tokens of receiving the Mandate? As for the chart emerging from the Yellow River, sweet liquor welling up from a spring, the writing of the bear and the Luo River [?], the register with red inscriptions, the ornate jade pitch pipes and the tortoise’s categories, the wolf’s bell [?] and the phoenix’s writing—such, again, were the signs that resounded afterward [?]. Is it not right to call these tokens of perpetuating the Mandate? In the end, their profound flourishing was enduring, and their preservation and stability were secure. As for the duration of their tenure upon the throne…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
或百九十年或百十有五年或百年八九
十年以奠基則或四百年或六百年或八
百年據其始各有明徴驗諸終如持左劵
信豈偶然者哉所以載在詩書傳諸信史
萬代而下猶班班如見者也後代英誼之
辟非無氣珎物異垂諸簡策第其德謝淳
精治歉洪暢偶於一至之應即謂興王之
兆猶且君臣動色紀元升歌封泰山禪梁
父昭揭發揚圖所不朽者矣然其視古帝
===
王何如哉若乃
峻德神功作述相暎玄珎黃瑞圖牒交輝則未

translation_en:
…some for one hundred and ninety years, some for one hundred and fifteen, and some for a hundred, eighty, or ninety years; as for establishing a dynastic foundation, some endured four hundred years, some six hundred, and some eight hundred. At their beginnings, each had clear portents; checked against their eventual outcomes, these were as reliable as holding the matching half of a tally. Could this truly have been mere chance? Thus they were recorded in the Odes and the Documents and transmitted in trustworthy histories, remaining so distinct even ten thousand generations later that one seems to see them.
The illustrious rulers of later ages were not without wondrous vapors and extraordinary objects recorded in their annals. Yet their virtue fell short of purity and refinement, and their governance lacked breadth and unobstructed efficacy. When some auspicious sign happened to appear just once, they immediately called it a portent of a king’s rise. Ruler and ministers would show their excitement, inaugurate an era and raise songs of praise, perform the feng sacrifice on Mount Tai and the shan sacrifice at Liangfu, and proclaim and magnify the event, seeking to make it imperishable. Yet how did they compare with the emperors and kings of antiquity?
As for lofty virtue and divine achievements, the work of founding and carrying forward the dynasty illuminating one another, heavenly treasures and earthly auspicious signs, charts and records shining together—never has there been magnificence like that of our dynasty. Its extraordinary and unparalleled manifestations could not easily be recounted to the end even with relays of attendants; nevertheless, some examples may be cited. When the fortunes of the barbarians were collapsing and the Chinese realm was in disorder, without a master, Heaven was about to wash away the foul, rank defilement and restore the old domain of divine civilization. Then our Emperor Taizu arose. Before this, there had been an ivory tablet and the presentation of a pellet [?], and red light had filled the chamber. A divine dragon leaped upright to announce the marvel, while Qingtian gazed at the clouds and recognized the portentous vapors. When, through a single military campaign…

translation_en:
…he expanded his dominion, and the six zones of allegiance accepted his influence. Then rosy clouds took the form of phoenixes, auspicious clouds gathered like embroidery, and such marvels as single-horned rhinoceroses, fire-eating birds, auspicious grain, propitious lotuses, red crows, and white rabbits arrived in succession. How magnificent, how resplendent! Were not these tokens of receiving Heaven’s mandate and perpetuating it equal in grandeur to those of the ancient emperors and kings?

When the royal path had only just been made smooth and the juncture of the era’s abrogation arrived, Heaven intended to sweep away treacherous wielders of power and secure the great imperial enterprise. Thus arose our Emperor Chengzu. Before this, divine light had illuminated the palace and filled its chambers with a five-colored radiance. His heavenly countenance grew more illustrious each day, and diviners marveled at his appearance, which betokened supreme peace. When the bestowal of the jade tablet marked the completion of his achievement, and he spread transforming influence while ruling with robes hanging down, auspicious stars, felicitous clouds, sweet dew, and sweet springs appeared brightly in heaven and on earth; auspicious grain, propitious wheat, qilin, and zouyu abounded far and near. How magnificent, how resplendent! Were not these tokens of receiving Heaven’s mandate and perpetuating it equal in grandeur to those of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors?

Why was this so? To establish the boundaries and restore order in the Chinese realm was a mighty achievement; to carry forward the accomplishments of his august deceased father was exalted filial piety; to order the enduring norms of the people was to establish constant institutions; to bathe the four distant corners in beneficence was far-reaching favor; to offer sacrifice…

punctuated:
帝，假廟，崇釐也；垂裕無疆，昌緒也。其建茲大業，天寔使之，是故必有開也；其既建茲大業，天寔鑒之，是故必有應也。而我二祖方且志操兢業，躬勵儉勤，審察機祥，綏懷窮困，抑抑乎其弗遑焉。此所以丕冒之治蟠極於無垠，聿懷之福昭受而勿替者也。
列聖嗣服，重熙累洽，及百五十年餘，維紀稍弛，海内多故。天佑邦家，聿求至聖，於是中興大命遂集於我皇上。先是，慶雲炫采，當翼軫之分；黃流澄派，協震育之年；神芝滿山，赤光燭漢，野老獻蟠龍之
translation_en:
…the Lord on High and entering the ancestral temple exalted their blessings; bequeathing abundance without limit made their dynastic succession flourish. When they established this great enterprise, Heaven indeed enabled them to do so; thus there necessarily were signs heralding its inception. Once they had established this great enterprise, Heaven indeed watched over them; thus there necessarily were auspicious responses. Yet our two founding ancestors continued to maintain reverent vigilance in their resolve, personally striving for frugality and diligence, carefully examining subtle signs and portents, and comforting and cherishing those in poverty and distress. Humbly and earnestly, they allowed themselves no respite. This is why their all-embracing governance extended to the utmost bounds of the limitless realm, and why they manifestly received enduring blessings that never ceased.
Successive sage sovereigns inherited the throne, adding brilliance to brilliance and prosperity to prosperity. After more than a hundred and fifty years, the bonds of order grew somewhat slack, and troubles multiplied within the realm. Heaven protected the dynasty and sought out a supreme sage. Thus the great mandate to restore the dynasty came to rest upon our Emperor. Before this, auspicious clouds displayed their brilliant colors in the celestial region of the Wings and Chariot Crossboard constellations; the Yellow River’s waters ran clear in the year of his birth. Divine numinous mushrooms covered the mountains, and a red radiance illuminated the Milky Way. An old man of the countryside presented a portent of a coiled dragon…

punctuated: 兆，靈崗著天子之稱。其受命之符，紛呈疊見，亦既超古今而獨盛矣。乃我皇上體睿含幾，窮神達化，於是踐玉斗，握金鏡，振乾綱，肅坤紀，宣鬱達幽，敕憲申度，懲奸遏惡，起滯亨屯，盖一日而天下改觀焉。乃於是崇孝尊親，敦有本之至化；議禮制度，定無前之大猷。以禮百神，則四郊秩分祀之儀，明堂隆大享之制，春秋重其祈報，水旱切其禱祠，是炎黃之肇祀也。以惠萬姓，則勸農蠲租，開衣食之源；發帑施藥，軫煢獨之慮；憫矜庶獄，屢頒欽恤之條。
translation_en:
…an omen; the auspicious ridge displayed the designation “Son of Heaven.” The signs of his receiving Heaven’s mandate appeared in profusion and repeated succession, surpassing those of ancient and recent times in their unrivaled abundance. Our Emperor, embodying sagacity and comprehending the subtle beginnings of events, fathomed the workings of the spirits and understood transformation. He thereupon ascended to the Jade Dipper and grasped the Golden Mirror—the emblems of sovereign rule—strengthened Heaven’s guiding bonds and set Earth’s ordering principles in proper array. He gave expression to what had been pent up and brought to light what had been obscure, enforced statutes and reaffirmed standards, punished treachery and checked evil, raised up those who had languished and relieved adversity. In a single day, the realm took on a new aspect.
He then exalted filial piety and honored his parents, deepening the supreme moral transformation rooted in these foundations. He deliberated on rites and established institutions, settling a grand plan without precedent. In honoring the many spirits, he ordered the ceremonies of separate sacrifices in the four suburban quarters and exalted the institution of the great offering in the Hall of Light. In spring and autumn he emphasized prayers and thanksgiving; in floods and droughts he earnestly offered supplications and sacrifices. Such was the founding of sacrificial worship by the Yan and Huang Emperors. In bestowing benefits upon the people, he encouraged agriculture and remitted land taxes, opening the sources of clothing and food; disbursed treasury funds and distributed medicines, showing concern for the bereft and solitary; and treated those involved in criminal cases with compassion, repeatedly promulgating provisions enjoining reverent care and mercy…

translation_en:
…He carefully evaluates the various officials and imposes especially severe punishments for corruption and cruelty: this is the concern for the people shown by Shun and Yu. To manifest his sagely cultural accomplishments, his admonitions and instructions reveal the essentials of transmitting the mind; his records and eulogies express his sincere reverence for Heaven; his canon proclaims the clarification of human relationships, and his record commemorates the Great Hunt. These are the cultural patterns of Fuxi and Yao. To display his divine martial prowess, he sends his fleet southward, stilling the waves of the whale-filled seas; he arrays his banners in defense of the north, extinguishing the beacon fires of the desert frontier. Among the Man streams and Tong mountain settlements, those who relied on mountain strongholds and mustered bands in the wilderness all turn their hearts toward righteousness or surrender their heads and submit to punishment. From the regions of the sun to the caverns of the moon, chiefs with braided hair and pierced chests all bring precious offerings in acknowledgment of his sovereignty, present maps, and request officials. These are the martial achievements of Tang and King Wu.

Thus his profound benevolence spreads in vast abundance, and harmonious energies flow everywhere, reaching upward throughout the nine regions of heaven and downward to the eight limits of the earth, surging like a wellspring, pouring forth and spreading without bounds. How lofty! How expansive! Enduring and far-reaching, hence broad and substantial; broad and substantial, hence lofty and luminous.

Accordingly, all Heaven’s auspicious tokens descend: auspicious stars appear from time to time, sweet dew falls repeatedly, propitious snow spreads its blossoms, and numinous rain abundantly moistens the earth. 以復明問云爾。

第二問
陳經邦

同考試官給事中周批：權不離經以為用，漢儒以下鮮有窺斯義者。此對獨得孔孟宗㫖，有根據，有體驗，必通方之士，録之。

同考試官編修萬批：孔子之心矩，《中庸》之時中，斯足盡權之義。而子能發明至此，豈經生所易及哉？

同考試官修撰諸批：發揮權義，精深詳盡，是可與權者也。録之以為學聖人者之的，豈惟以其文哉？

考試官侍讀學士胡批：議論精確明暢，是知聖人之權者。

…merely to reply to your illuminating question.

Second Question
Chen Jingbang

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Supervising Secretary: “Discretion in practice does not depart from constant principles. From the Han Confucians onward, few have discerned this meaning. This answer alone grasps the essential teaching of Confucius and Mencius. It has a firm foundation and reflects personal understanding gained through experience. Its author must be a scholar who comprehends how principles apply in varying circumstances. Select it.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Compiler: “The meaning of discretion is exceedingly difficult to comprehend. This essay analyzes it clearly and exhaustively, bringing out what earlier Confucians had not brought out. Only someone with a refined understanding of moral principles could offer such an explanation. It should be selected to serve as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wan, Compiler: “The moral measure within Confucius’s heart and the Doctrine of the Mean’s teaching of attaining the mean as circumstances require suffice to express fully the meaning of discretion. That you have elucidated it to this extent—could an ordinary student of the Classics readily achieve this?”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhu, Senior Compiler: “Its exposition of the meaning of discretion is profound, precise, detailed, and exhaustive. Here is someone with whom one may exercise discretion. Select it as a target for those who would learn from the sages. Could this be merely for its literary qualities?”

Comment by Examiner Hu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: “The argument is precise, sound, clear, and fluent. Here is someone who understands the sages’ exercise of discretion.”

Comment by Examiner Gao, Academician: “He appears capable of probing the learning of the sages to its depths. Select it.”

text:
學聖人者必知其道之所在而求以至焉
可也譬則射然儀的在前躍如而有見也
於是運其巧力則有能中者矣苟儀的之
不知而漫焉以射則用力愈多而去儀的
也愈遠苟知之而力弗至猶弗知也夫學
亦有儀的焉孔子云可與共學未可與適
道可與適道未可與立可與立未可與權
夫權也者圓而通者也是聖人之事而學
之儀的也聖人圓而學聖人者以方始而
===

通而學聖人者以一隅始而一隅可也終
而止一隅焉則遂失其通也夫學不至於
聖人非成也不能權非聖人也非圓非通
不可以與權也而不知所以求不求所以

錘也稱之為物有衡有權衡也者為銖為

自為用也權也者銖則為之銖兩則為之

punctuated:
學聖人者必知其道之所在，而求以至焉可也。譬則射然，儀的在前，躍如而有見也，於是運其巧力，則有能中者矣。苟儀的之不知，而漫焉以射，則用力愈多，而去儀的也愈遠。苟知之而力弗至，猶弗知也。夫學亦有儀的焉。孔子云：「可與共學，未可與適道；可與適道，未可與立；可與立，未可與權。」夫權也者，圓而通者也，是聖人之事，而學之儀的也。聖人圓，而學聖人者以方，始而方可也，終而愈方焉，則遂失其圓也。聖人通，而學聖人者以一隅，始而一隅可也，終而止一隅焉，則遂失其通也。夫學不至於聖人，非成也；不能權，非聖人也；非圓非通，不可以與權也。而不知所以求，不求所以至，非學也。

請先言權之義。夫權者何也？稱錘也。稱之為物，有衡有權。衡也者，為銖，為兩，為斤，為鈞，為石，其體無弗具也，然不能自為用也。權也者，銖則為之銖，兩則為之
translation_en:
Those who seek to learn from the sage must know where his Way lies and strive to reach it. It is like archery: the target stands ahead, vividly apparent to the eye. By applying skill and strength, one can then hit it. If one does not know where the target is and shoots at random, the greater the effort, the farther one strays from the target. If one knows where it is but lacks the strength to reach it, this is still like not knowing. Learning, too, has a target. Confucius said: “Those with whom one can study may not yet be able to advance along the Way; those with whom one can advance along the Way may not yet be able to stand firm; those with whom one can stand firm may not yet be able to exercise discretion.” Discretion (quan) is rounded and adaptable. It is the work of the sage and the target of learning. The sage is rounded, while those learning from him proceed by being square. To be square at the outset is acceptable, but if in the end they become ever more square, they lose his roundness altogether. The sage comprehends all sides, while those learning from him begin with a single corner. To begin with a single corner is acceptable, but if in the end they remain confined to that corner, they lose his comprehensive understanding altogether. Learning that does not attain sagehood is incomplete; one who cannot exercise discretion is no sage. Without roundness and adaptability, one cannot participate in the exercise of discretion. Not to know how to seek it, or not to seek the means of attaining it, is no learning at all.

Let me first explain the meaning of quan. What is quan? It is the counterweight of a balance. A balance consists of a beam and a counterweight. The beam accommodates zhu, liang, jin, jun, and shi: its structure provides for all these units of weight. Yet it cannot function on its own. 往来取中至於千億而不窮其用無弗周
也然必有衡而後可用也故謂衡即是權
權即是衡不可也然使衡離於權權離於
衡亦不可也盖衡以權為用權非用於衡
無所用之分之則二物而合之則一事也
故有言衡而不言權者焉如曰律度量衡
是也然而權在其中也有言權而不言衡

權必不得其正也斯權之義也知權則知

…liang; for jin, it serves to weigh jin; for jun, it serves to weigh jun; and for shi, it serves to weigh shi. Moving back and forth to find the balance, it can accommodate even hundreds of billions without exhausting its capacity: its application encompasses everything. Yet it can function only if there is a balance beam. Thus one cannot say that the beam is simply the sliding weight, or that the sliding weight is simply the beam. Neither, however, can the beam be separated from the weight, or the weight from the beam. The beam functions by means of the weight; unless the weight is applied to the beam, it has no use. Considered separately, they are two objects; brought together, they perform one operation. Thus sometimes the beam is mentioned without the weight, as in the phrase “pitch standards, measures of length and capacity, and balances”; yet the weight is included within it. Sometimes the weight—or weighing—is mentioned without the beam, as in “Only after weighing does one know what is light and what is heavy”; yet the beam is included within it. Why? Because these are two objects performing one operation.
Now, since quan—both the sliding weight and discretionary judgment—is discussed in terms of lightness and heaviness, it adjusts up or down in every case, whether ordinary or changing, great or small. It is not something used only when there is no alternative and dispensable when there is. If discretionary judgment is absent at any moment, the proper balance cannot be attained. Nor is it used only for jun and shi and dispensable for zhu and liang. If discretionary judgment is absent in any matter, the proper balance cannot be attained. This is the meaning of quan. To understand discretionary judgment is to understand the sage.
How, then, does the sage exercise discretionary judgment? Consider the Book of Changes. That odd numbers constitute yang and even numbers constitute yin, that yang bestows through vigor and yin receives through compliance—these things people know. title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄

化而之陽剛或推而爲柔柔或往而從剛
其理不可定也是故事以位異則易事以
當位法以時遷則更法以趨時故曰變動
不居周流六虛不可爲典要惟變所適聖
人以此神明其德定天下之吉凶而成天
下之亹亹者也故曰巽以行權夫巽風也
風之爲物至動而不拘至速而不滯至徹
而不隔故稱巽焉謂其委順而周至也故
可以行權焉是故以決是非以定可否以

六合莫之能違也權之用大矣哉非聖人
其孰能與於此柰何後儒之不達也於是
有反經合道之說夫物各有則經之謂也
稱物而使當其則權之謂也聖人言權不
言經非遺之也言權而經在其中也聖人
以權行經而漢儒以權反經其謬無足辯
也獨謂處常則守經遇變則行權而其說
至今因之信斯言也是經權之異用也彼

translation_en: …transforms and becomes yang; the firm may shift and become yielding, and the yielding may move and follow the firm. The principles governing these cannot be fixed. Thus, when affairs differ according to position, one changes one's conduct to suit the position; when laws shift with the times, one revises the laws to accord with the times. Hence it is said in the Book of Changes: “Changing and moving without rest, circulating through the six empty positions, it cannot be made into a fixed standard: it follows change alone.” Through this the sage makes his virtue spiritually luminous, determines good and ill fortune throughout the world, and brings the world's endeavors to completion. Hence it is said: “Through Xun, one exercises discretion.” Now Xun is wind. Wind is utterly mobile, without constraint; utterly swift, without obstruction; utterly penetrating, without separation. Thus it is called Xun, meaning that it follows compliantly and reaches everywhere. It can therefore serve to exercise discretion (quan). By this one decides right and wrong, determines what is permissible and what is not, accomplishes transformations, and communicates with ghosts and spirits. Beginning in a single mind and extending throughout the six directions, it encounters nothing that can resist it. Great indeed is the efficacy of discretion! Who but a sage could participate in this? How could later Confucian scholars have failed to understand it! Thus arose the doctrine of departing from constant norms in order to accord with the Way. That each thing has its own standard is what is meant by constant norms (jing); weighing things so that they accord with their proper standards is what is meant by discretion. When the sage speaks of discretion without speaking of constant norms, he has not omitted them: in speaking of discretion, the constant norms are already included. The sage uses discretion to put constant norms into practice, whereas Han Confucian scholars use discretion to depart from them. Their error scarcely merits refutation. Yet they say that in ordinary circumstances one should uphold constant norms, while on encountering changed circumstances one should exercise discretion; and their doctrine has continued to be followed down to the present. If these words are accepted as true, then constant norms and discretion have distinct applications. Those…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
所謂經也者非子思大經孟子反經之經
歟其為經固也而乃為之經綸焉類聚羣
分而各得其理焉反焉而得其正焉非權
孰為之者而獨謂為處變之物哉故程子
曰權即是經自漢以来無人識權字為此
也雖然經也者立本者也猶之衡也權也
者趨時者也經以權為用權非用於經無
所用之者也故謂權不離經也則可而曰
權即是經是曰權即是衡也此朱子所以
===
===
又有經權亦當有辨之說也但猶謂權為
處變之物故引孟子嫂溺援之以手為証
夫嫂溺援之以手權之易見者故直謂之
權也若夫男女授受不親禮也而亦非離
權也何則人之授受未有不親者也而獨
男女則不親焉何也嫌也不嫌則授受親
嫌則授受不親非權而何是禮之正者亦
由權而正也而曰權而得中是為禮也是
徒以權之得中者為禮而不以禮之得中

translation_en: …what they call constant norms (jing): are these not the norms meant by Zisi’s “great constant norms” and Mengzi’s “returning to constant norms”? That these are constant norms is certain. Yet to order and arrange them, so that things gather by kind and divide into groups, each attaining its proper principle, and to return to them and attain what is correct—what but situational judgment (quan) accomplishes this? How, then, can it be called something used solely to deal with exceptional circumstances? Thus Master Cheng said, “Situational judgment is itself constant norms.” This is why he said that, since the Han, no one had understood the word quan. Nevertheless, constant norms establish the foundation: they are like the beam of a balance. Situational judgment responds to the occasion. Constant norms operate through situational judgment; unless situational judgment is applied to constant norms, it has no application. Thus it is permissible to say that situational judgment does not depart from constant norms. But to say that situational judgment is itself constant norms is to say that the sliding weight is itself the balance beam. This is why Master Zhu also said, “Constant norms and situational judgment must also be distinguished.” Yet he still regarded situational judgment as something for dealing with exceptional circumstances, and therefore cited Mengzi’s “reaching out a hand to rescue one’s drowning sister-in-law” as evidence. Reaching out a hand to rescue one’s drowning sister-in-law is an easily recognizable instance of situational judgment, and so it is directly called such. As for men and women not making physical contact when handing things to one another, this is ritual propriety, yet it too is inseparable from situational judgment. Why? People ordinarily make contact when handing things to one another; why is contact avoided only between men and women? Because it invites suspicion. Where there is no suspicion, they make contact when handing things over; where there is suspicion, they do not. What is this if not situational judgment? Thus even what is correct in ritual propriety owes its correctness to situational judgment. But to say, “Exercising situational judgment and attaining the proper mean constitutes ritual propriety,” is merely to regard situational judgment that attains the proper mean as ritual propriety, without regarding ritual propriety’s attainment of the proper mean…
