一事然而非一物也朱則言其二物然而
非二事也以盡其義合二子而後可者也
斯義不明而世之言權者大抵皆稱古人
不得已之事如舜不告而娶之類夫不得
已而為處者易見者也權固也然而天下
之事豈皆不得已而後為處者乎其日用

易之則使非權以稱之果能各中其則而

誾誾而侃侃者乎此猶可指言者也其曰

translation_en:
…the canonical norm as discretionary judgment [?]; it thus seems that something still remains unexplained. Cheng speaks of them as one activity, though they are not one thing; Zhu speaks of them as two things, though they are not two activities. To exhaust their meaning, one must bring the two masters’ accounts together. Because this meaning is not understood, those who discuss discretionary judgment generally cite cases in which the ancients had no alternative, such as Shun’s marrying without informing his parents. Decisions made under such necessity are readily recognizable instances of discretionary judgment, certainly. Yet can all affairs under Heaven be matters addressed only when there is no alternative? In everyday life and the enduring human relationships, even the smallest and most minute matters each have an appropriate, unchanging standard. Without discretionary judgment to weigh them, could one truly meet the standard in every case, without erring through excess or deficiency? No. How, then, can one say that discretionary judgment is employed in exceptional circumstances but may be dispensed with in ordinary ones?

Moreover, the teaching concerning discretionary judgment comes from Kongzi. Let us therefore discuss it through Kongzi himself. His demolition of the fortifications of the three capitals and execution of the dwarfs were exercises of discretionary judgment, certainly responses to exceptional circumstances. But when he served when it was right to serve, withdrew when it was right to withdraw, remained long when it was right to remain long, and departed promptly when it was right to depart promptly—was this not discretionary judgment? Otherwise, might he not have withdrawn when he could properly have served, or departed promptly when he could properly have remained long? These are still only the major instances. When he entered with his body bent respectfully and emerged at ease, spoke with respectful frankness to his superiors and with ease and assurance to his inferiors—was this not discretionary judgment? Otherwise, might he not have appeared at ease when he should have bent respectfully, or spoken with ease and assurance when he should have shown respectful frankness? These are still instances that can be pointed out and described. As for the statements concerning him: …

則無時無處無非權也是日用而飲食者
也由是觀之權之為用常耶變耶無不有
者耶固可得而識也而世之君子徒曰權

從箕子者以比干為愚從伯夷者以柳惠

千里謬以無筭而大人之事不復見於天

無意無必，無可無不可，從心所欲不踰矩，則無時無處無非權也，是日用而飲食者也。由是觀之，權之為用，常耶？變耶？無不有者耶？固可得而識也。而世之君子徒曰：「權者，濟一時之急，非悠久之用。」居常無事，則置諸空虛之地，遂使聖人大中至正之極、旁行順應之方、虛靈洞達之機、精邃淵微之旨，晦塞不明。於是大道隱，曲學興，膠柱一偏之說，守株一節之行，東嚮望不見西墻，南嚮望不見北方，而不知其合之圓也。從箕子者以比干為愚，從伯夷者以柳惠為䙝，而不知其會之通也。雖稱有道術者，亦不過下守局士之軌，非不為貞，然不免於諒也；非不為禮為義，然不免於非禮之禮、非義之義也。差之毫釐，謬以千里；差之千里，謬以無筭，而大人之事不復見於天下矣。

雖然，權可易言哉？察之幽渺，定之纖忽，非至明弗能也；為一為兩，叅伍錯綜，非
translation_en:
…having no preconceived ideas and no insistence on a predetermined outcome, holding that nothing is invariably permissible or impermissible, and following the heart’s desires without overstepping the bounds: there is then no time or place in which discretionary judgment is not exercised. It is as everyday a practice as eating and drinking. Viewed in this light, whether discretionary judgment serves ordinary circumstances, exceptional circumstances, or all circumstances can surely be understood. Yet the gentlemen of the world merely say: “Discretionary judgment remedies a momentary emergency; it is not something for enduring use.” In ordinary, uneventful times, they consign it to oblivion. Thus they obscure the sages’ utmost centrality and correctness, their methods of adapting to circumstances in every direction, their capacity for receptive and penetrating understanding, and their profound and subtle purport. Consequently, the Great Way falls into obscurity and distorted learning flourishes. They cling to one-sided doctrines as though gluing the tuning bridges of a zither in place, and adhere to a single pattern of conduct as though watching a tree stump for another hare. Looking east, they cannot see the western wall; looking south, they cannot see the north. They do not understand the rounded completeness of these things when brought together. Followers of Jizi regard Bi Gan as foolish; followers of Bo Yi regard Liu Hui as disrespectful. They do not understand the coherence achieved by bringing these ways together. Even those reputed to possess the arts of the Way do no more than follow the tracks of narrowly confined scholars [?]. They are not without steadfastness, yet they cannot escape petty insistence on keeping their word. They are not without ritual propriety and righteousness, yet they cannot escape a propriety that is not true propriety and a righteousness that is not true righteousness. A deviation of a hair’s breadth leads to an error of a thousand li; a deviation of a thousand li leads to an error beyond reckoning. The deeds of the great man are then no longer seen anywhere under Heaven.

Even so, can discretionary judgment be spoken of lightly? To discern what is obscure and elusive, and to decide matters at the finest degree of subtlety, requires the utmost clarity of understanding. To treat things as one or as two, comparing and interweaving them in varied combinations, cannot be accomplished without…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
至變弗能也觸幾而應倏彼倏此非至熟
弗能也效越人游者殘其軀代大匠斲者
傷其手是可與下學道乎然越人之游不
可效也而遂謂世無越人不可也大匠之
斲不可代也而遂謂世無大匠不可也適
道難於學非謂學可不適道也立難於適
道非謂適道可不立也權難於立非謂立
可無權也夫學至於立可不謂有得歟然
而成心未化終有翳於鑑空圭角尚存終
===
有礙於圜轉明非先物何以制變於未形
智不通方何以當機於猝至以之行己則
精義之用窒以之經世則彌綸之道乖聖
人之德業謂若是乎哉是故不可以無權
也夫誠者不勉而中不思而得從容中道
聖人也權之至也誠之者明善而誠身者
也所以求為聖人也明善貴乎虛心心虛
則理融理融則識達誠身在於克己己克
則氣順氣順則德弘求之以問學練之以

至變弗能也。觸幾而應，倏彼倏此，非至熟弗能也。效越人游者殘其軀，代大匠斲者傷其手，是可與下學道乎？然越人之游不可效也，而遂謂世無越人，不可也；大匠之斲不可代也，而遂謂世無大匠，不可也。適道難於學，非謂學可不適道也；立難於適道，非謂適道可不立也；權難於立，非謂立可無權也。夫學至於立，可不謂有得歟？然而成心未化，終有翳於鑑空；圭角尚存，終有礙於圜轉。明非先物，何以制變於未形？智不通方，何以當機於猝至？以之行己，則精義之用窒；以之經世，則彌綸之道乖。聖人之德業，謂若是乎哉？是故不可以無權也。
夫誠者，不勉而中，不思而得，從容中道，聖人也，權之至也。誠之者，明善而誠身者也，所以求為聖人也。明善貴乎虛心，心虛則理融，理融則識達；誠身在於克己，己克則氣順，氣順則德弘。求之以問學，練之以
translation_en:
…cannot be accomplished without the utmost adaptability. To respond at the first stirrings of change, now in one direction, now in another, requires the utmost mastery. Those who imitate the swimmers of Yue injure their bodies; those who hew in place of a master carpenter injure their hands. Can such things be discussed with those at the elementary stages of learning? Yet although the swimming of the people of Yue cannot be imitated, it would be wrong to conclude that no such swimmers exist in the world. Although one cannot hew in place of a master carpenter, it would be wrong to conclude that no master carpenters exist in the world. Advancing toward the Way is harder than learning, but this does not mean that learning need not advance toward the Way. Taking a firm stand is harder than advancing toward the Way, but this does not mean that one who advances toward the Way need not take a firm stand. Exercising discretionary judgment is harder than taking a firm stand, but this does not mean that one who stands firm can dispense with such judgment. When learning reaches the point of taking a firm stand, can one deny that something has been attained? Yet if fixed preconceptions have not been transformed, they will ultimately cloud the mind’s empty mirror; if sharp corners remain, they will ultimately impede its smooth turning. Unless one’s discernment anticipates events, how can one govern changes before they take shape? Unless one’s wisdom comprehends every direction, how can one meet a critical moment when it suddenly arrives? If one conducts oneself in this fashion, the application of finely discerned righteousness is obstructed; if one orders the world in this fashion, the way of comprehensively bringing things into order goes awry. Could the sage’s virtue and achievements be said to be like this? Thus discretionary judgment cannot be dispensed with.
One who is sincere hits the mark without effort, apprehends without deliberation, and effortlessly accords with the Way: such a person is a sage, and this is discretionary judgment at its highest. One who strives to become sincere clarifies what is good and makes his own person sincere; this is how one seeks to become a sage. In clarifying what is good, an open mind is essential. When the mind is open, principles become integrated; when principles become integrated, understanding becomes far-reaching. Making one’s person sincere depends on overcoming the self. When the self is overcome, vital energy becomes harmonious; when vital energy becomes harmonious, virtue becomes expansive. Seek this through inquiry and learning; refine it through…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
事行會之以深思涵之以積養查滓既盡
自圓自通繇是為仁義之宰攝為禮樂之
宗正無不可矣化不可為始諸可為神不
可知始諸可知惟所適者正而不已其功
未有不幾者也中庸一書為下學而作其
言無過不及隨時取中皆權說也而特未
揭乎權之名學者襲口耳昧心識言中庸
而不言權不知中庸之即權也非謂誠之
者不可以至也雖然權亦不同焉有用之
===
於謀也者則為權謀有用之於術也者則
為權術彼其竊變通之似以濟其揣摩之
私而競逐於功利之間則能使天下多事
故有惡於權也雖然弓矢戈矛天下之利
器也良民以之禦寇而奸民以之為寇苟
徒以良民之禦寇也而遂縱於奸民可乎
苟徒以奸民之為寇也而遂禁於良民可
乎顧視所用何如耳奸民之權既任之而
不知擇聖人之權又畏之而不敢求是常

徒以良民之禦寇也而遂縱於奸民可乎
苟徒以奸民之爲寇也而遂禁於良民可
乎顧視所用何如耳奸民之權既任之而
不知擇聖人之權又畏之而不敢求是常
punctuated:
事行，會之以深思，涵之以積養，查滓既盡，自圓自通。繇是為仁義之宰攝，為禮樂之宗正，無不可矣。化不可為，始諸可為；神不可知，始諸可知。惟所適者正而不已，其功未有不幾者也。《中庸》一書，為下學而作，其言無過不及、隨時取中，皆權說也，而特未揭乎權之名。學者襲口耳，昧心識，言中庸而不言權，不知中庸之即權也，非謂誠之者不可以至也。
雖然，權亦不同焉。有用之於謀也者，則為權謀；有用之於術也者，則為權術。彼其竊變通之似，以濟其揣摩之私，而競逐於功利之間，則能使天下多事，故有惡於權也。雖然，弓矢戈矛，天下之利器也。良民以之禦寇，而奸民以之為寇。苟徒以良民之禦寇也，而遂縱於奸民，可乎？苟徒以奸民之為寇也，而遂禁於良民，可乎？顧視所用何如耳。奸民之權，既任之而不知擇；聖人之權，又畏之而不敢求，是常
translation_en:
…practical conduct; bring it together through deep reflection and nurture it through sustained cultivation. Once the dregs are entirely removed, it will naturally become rounded and unobstructed. From this point, one may preside over benevolence and righteousness and serve as the guiding authority for rites and music: nothing will be beyond one’s capacity. Transformation cannot be deliberately produced, but begins with what can be done; spiritual efficacy cannot be known, but begins with what can be known. Provided that one’s course is correct and one does not cease, one’s efforts cannot fail to approach the goal. The Doctrine of the Mean was written for those engaged in elementary learning. Its statements about neither going too far nor falling short, and about finding the mean as circumstances change, all concern discretionary judgment, though they do not explicitly give it that name. Students repeat what passes between mouth and ear, while remaining obscure in their own understanding. They speak of the mean but not of discretionary judgment, unaware that the mean itself is discretionary judgment. This does not mean that those striving to make themselves sincere cannot attain it.
Nevertheless, discretionary judgment also takes different forms. Applied to plotting, it becomes stratagem; applied to techniques, it becomes manipulation. Those who steal the semblance of adaptability to advance their private, calculating designs and compete for achievement and profit can embroil the world in troubles. This is why some detest discretionary judgment. Yet bows, arrows, dagger-axes, and spears are the world’s effective weapons. Law-abiding people use them to resist bandits, while malefactors use them to commit banditry. Would it be acceptable, merely because law-abiding people use them to resist bandits, to give malefactors free rein with them? Would it be acceptable, merely because malefactors use them to commit banditry, to prohibit law-abiding people from having them? One need only consider how they are used. People allow malefactors’ discretionary judgment to operate without knowing how to discriminate, yet fear the sages’ discretionary judgment and dare not seek it. This constantly…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
使禦寇無具而為寇有資也是故天下鮮
通儒而竊之者則肆矣孟子云所惡於智
者為其鑿也如智者行其所無事則智亦
大矣夫所惡於權者為其竊也如權者皆
出乎所學之正則權亦大矣夫是則可與
語權也已矣
第三問
伊在庭
同考試官署郎中林批〔古人任事而能成事者〕
===

使禦寇無具，而為寇有資也。是故天下鮮通儒，而竊之者則肆矣。孟子云：「所惡於智者，為其鑿也。如智者行其所無事，則智亦大矣。」夫所惡於權者，為其竊也。如權者皆出乎所學之正，則權亦大矣。夫是則可與語權也已矣。

第三問

伊在庭

同考試官署郎中林批〔古人任事而能成事者，誠與才合也。此作揣度往迹，而得其深謀遠慮之微，末復嚴夫似是之辨，尤有卓見。子殆豪傑之士者耶？〕

同考試官編修張批〔豪傑所以匡時濟務，類非守方之士所可窺測。此篇陳說往初，辨别機應，歷歷然若在指掌，斯亦足竒矣。〕

同考試官修撰陸批〔古人任天下重務，其裁酌區畫，自有機宜，未易想度。子獨能闡發之，推見至隱，使面質諸公，當亦心服。〕

同考試官左諭德汪批〔古豪傑處事，其妙用機〕
translation_en:
…leaves those who resist bandits without the means to do so, while supplying resources to those who become bandits. Thus there are few broadly learned Confucian scholars in the world, while those who misappropriate discretionary judgment act without restraint. Mencius says: “What we dislike in cleverness is its forced contrivance. If the clever acted without contrivance, their wisdom would indeed be great.” What we dislike in discretionary judgment is its misappropriation. If all such judgment proceeded from the correctness of what one has learned, then discretionary judgment too would be great. Only then could one be considered fit to discuss it.

Third Policy Question

Yi Zaiting

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Acting Director: 〔When men of antiquity undertook affairs and brought them to completion, it was because sincerity and ability were united in them. This essay examines past deeds and grasps the subtleties of their profound plans and far-reaching deliberations. At the end, it further draws rigorous distinctions concerning what merely appears correct, displaying especially outstanding insight. Are you perhaps a man of heroic talent?〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Compiler: 〔The means by which men of heroic talent set their age right and accomplish its affairs are generally beyond the understanding of those who adhere to fixed rules. This essay recounts earlier events and distinguishes the critical circumstances and the responses to them, with everything as clear as though displayed in the palm of one's hand. This too is worthy of admiration.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Senior Compiler: 〔When men of antiquity assumed weighty responsibilities for the realm, their deliberations and arrangements had their own fitness to the circumstances, which is not readily imagined or fathomed. You alone can elucidate this, reasoning your way to what is most deeply hidden. Were you to question those gentlemen face to face, they too would surely be convinced at heart.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Left Mentor: 〔When men of heroic talent in antiquity handled affairs, their subtle use of opportunities…〕

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
宜自有成算要皆不詭於大道而非形迹所能拘
者子能紬繹其旨而以古雅之詞發之足以觀所
蘊矣
考試官侍讀學士胡批豪傑成務非形迹可知此作
能發之而辨析似是之非尤卓有見佳士也
考試官學士高批人臣為國當求實濟若徒務
形迹何裨於用子能據古人之事而明其意是亦
可用之士矣特錄之
夫豪傑之士所以能成天下之務者以心
===
為主以才為用而無與乎形迹之間者也
豪傑何心也忠可貫金石誠可質神明大
罔弗容虛罔弗受無欲而恒清無著而恒

治忽之幾斷足以剖糾結之惑強足以勝
艱大之任權足以酌變通之宜密足以藏
機敏足以應卒斯豪傑之才也若夫人有
所為者吾弗敢違人未有所為者吾弗敢
起言欲人皆聞也而使不吾疑事欲人皆

…in adapting to circumstances, they have settled plans of their own. In essence, none departs from the Great Way, and none can be constrained by outward forms. You have unraveled their meaning and expressed it in language of classical elegance, revealing the understanding you possess.

Comment by Examiner Hu, Academician Reader-in-waiting: How outstanding men accomplish their tasks cannot be understood from outward forms. This essay brings this out; its discrimination of errors that appear correct shows particularly remarkable insight. Here is a fine scholar.

Comment by Examiner Gao, Academician: A minister serving his state should seek practical results. If he merely concerns himself with outward forms, what use is that? You have drawn upon the deeds of men of antiquity and clarified their intentions. You too are a man fit for service. I have selected this essay for special inclusion.

Outstanding men can accomplish the affairs of the world because they take the heart as their guide and employ their abilities as their instruments, without becoming entangled in outward forms. What sort of heart does an outstanding man possess? His loyalty can penetrate metal and stone; his sincerity can stand scrutiny before the spirits. So capacious that it excludes nothing, so open that it receives everything, it is free of desire and thus always clear, free of attachment and thus always impartial. Such is the heart of an outstanding man. What sort of abilities does he possess? Such are the abilities of an outstanding man. text:
見也而使不吾議名之所繫則周旋而不
舍嫌之所在則遠避而不居斯世所謂形
迹者也嗟乎事各有迹亦各有情使情之
於迹若符節之相合則事可直行心得徑
遂夫人而能之矣奚俟豪傑為也惟夫正
變同塗翕張殊用或類之而非或不類而
是或逆而實順或益而實損或就之而適
以背或避之而適以招猶之至長反短至
短反長其理難以執也吾得其是而人謂
===
非吾得其可而人謂否語之則機露而僨
事不以語之則事秘而衆疑有可見有弗
可見其意難以明也先合後違則有譽而
無成孰與先違後合有成而無譽事起後
救則有其功已有其患孰與使事不起則
無其患寧無其功或為之而不以為或不
為而乃以為作事在此取效在彼有既事
而始可知者焉有當時不知後世乃知者
焉有終古而卒無有知之者焉其實難以

…to see one's actions, while ensuring that they do not criticize one. Wherever reputation is at stake, one attends to it and will not let it go; wherever suspicion might arise, one keeps far away and will not remain. These are what the world calls outward appearances. Alas! Every affair has its outward manifestations, but also its underlying circumstances. If those circumstances matched the outward manifestations as the two halves of a tally fit together, affairs could be carried out directly and the heart's intentions readily fulfilled. Anyone could do this: why would outstanding men be needed?

Yet the regular and the exceptional follow the same path, while contraction and expansion serve different purposes. Something may resemble what is right yet be wrong, or fail to resemble it yet be right; it may seem contrary yet actually accord, or beneficial yet actually cause harm. Pursuing something may serve only to turn away from it; avoiding it may serve only to invite it. It is as though the longest became short and the shortest became long: the underlying principles are difficult to grasp. I arrive at what is right, but others call it wrong; I arrive at what is practicable, but others say it is not. Explain it to them, and the crucial plan is exposed and the affair ruined; leave it unexplained, and secrecy breeds suspicion among the multitude. Some things can be shown, while others cannot: the intention is difficult to make clear.

To agree at first but diverge in the end brings praise without accomplishment. How can this compare with diverging at first but agreeing in the end, achieving success without praise? To remedy trouble after it has arisen brings credit, but harm has already occurred. How can this compare with preventing the trouble from arising, so that there is no harm, even if one receives no credit? Sometimes one acts but is not thought to have acted; sometimes one does not act but is nevertheless thought to have done so. Action is taken here, while its effect is obtained there. title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
究也若此者可爲常人言乎豈惟常人雖
有其心苟無其才則亦無以破拘攣之見
必且膠固而不移雖有其才苟無其心則
亦無以黜顧忌之私必且遷就而無定故
必心以主才不役於才才以從心克副其
心然後可以時贏時縮隨詘隨伸歷百折
而不回濟萬變而不匱者也若昔周公聖
人也其相成王制禮作樂所可知者也乃
管蔡懿親也而東征之舉曾不少貸此豈
===
人之所能爲亦豈所肯爲者而周公則爲
之孔子聖人也其攝相事強公弱私所可
知者也乃少正卯聞人也而兩觀之事曾
不後時此豈人之所能爲亦豈所肯爲者
而孔子則爲之蓋大義攸重無寧滅親大
偽是除無寧拂眾安有所圖於國故不計
其身之危化有所要於終故不恤其始之
謗此大聖之作為真萬世之師表也而後
代諸賢如何如勃如傑如瑋又何足以辱

translation_en:
…to fathom. Can matters such as these be explained to ordinary people? And why speak only of ordinary people? Even someone with the requisite resolve, if lacking the requisite ability, cannot break free of constricted views and will surely remain rigidly attached to them. Even someone with the requisite ability, if lacking the requisite resolve, cannot cast aside selfish apprehensions and will surely temporize without any settled direction. Thus resolve must govern ability, without being enslaved by it; ability must follow resolve and fully measure up to it. Only then can one expand or contract as circumstances require, bend or straighten accordingly, endure a hundred setbacks without turning back, and cope with myriad changes without exhausting one’s resources.
Take the Duke of Zhou, a sage of antiquity. That he assisted King Cheng, established rites, and created music is readily understandable. Yet Guan and Cai were his close kinsmen, and in his eastern campaign he showed them not the slightest leniency. Could others have done this, or even been willing to do it? Yet the Duke of Zhou did so. Confucius was a sage. That he acted as chief minister, strengthening public authority and weakening private power, is readily understandable. Yet Shaozheng Mao was a renowned man, and in the affair at the two gate towers [his execution], Confucius did not delay. Could others have done this, or even been willing to do it? Yet Confucius did so. For when great moral duty was at stake, they would sooner destroy their own kin; when great deceit had to be eliminated, they would sooner go against the multitude. They sought security for the state and therefore took no account of danger to themselves; they sought moral transformation in the end and therefore disregarded slander at the outset. Such deeds of the great sages truly set an example for all ages. As for the worthy men of later generations—such as He, Bo, Jie, and Wei—how could they deserve to trouble…

明問哉雖然事變無窮而周孔不常有如
必周孔而後可將天下之事終無濟乎則
四子者固亦一時之傑胡可少也請各為
之明其意炎祚肇興酇侯佐命非與民休
息時歟乃即為之治未央極其壯麗非無
說也夫帝居所必建也若草創於今必且
改拓於後若田賦既定而取以為用必且
賈怨於民況自我為則用半而功倍自後
人為則用倍而功半故當財無定主之時

…your discerning question? Nevertheless, circumstances change endlessly, while men like the Duke of Zhou and Confucius do not always appear. If only a Duke of Zhou or a Confucius could act acceptably, would the affairs of the world never be brought to a successful conclusion? These four men were certainly outstanding figures of their times; how could they be belittled? Allow me to explain the intentions of each.
When the Han dynasty, endowed with the virtue of Fire, first arose, the Marquis of Zan assisted in its founding. Was this not a time to let the people rest and recuperate? Yet he immediately built Weiyang Palace, making it supremely magnificent. This was not without reason. An imperial residence had to be built. If it were built roughly at first, it would inevitably have to be altered and enlarged later. If, once land taxes had been fixed, revenues were drawn upon for this purpose, it would inevitably incur the people’s resentment. Moreover, if we undertake it ourselves, the expenditure is halved and the achievement doubled; if later generations undertake it, the expenditure is doubled and the achievement halved. Thus, while wealth had no fixed owners, he undertook a single labor that would secure lasting ease. This benefited a hundred generations—but who recognized it?
When the Lü clan’s plot was exposed, the Defender-in-Chief led troops against them. Was this not a time to make righteousness manifest and enforce the law? Yet he first tested the troops by having them bare their left arms, and only then took action. This was not without reason. The armies had long been associated with the Lü clan. Once the plot was exposed, they would all fear for themselves; if I then acted together with them, there might be other unforeseen dangers. He therefore specifically offered them the means of baring their left arms, allowing all of them to display a visible sign of allegiance to the Liu house. On the strength of that sign, I could then trust them, and their minds would naturally be at ease. Thus, not only could the execution of the Lü clan be successfully accomplished, but those who were fearful and wavering would already have been reassured. This was wisdom in quelling disorder—but who recognized it?

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
張亂政宜有以制之矣乃非惟無以制也
而至與之博陸者豈無除惡之志歟意固
以為幾未協也幾未協而遽動殆也有謀
人之心而使之知拙也是故不虞其人而
亦使之不虞乎我迨唐社既還僞僭無據
而廡下之事付諸張桓等矣是其弗制乃
所以制也曹瑋鎭秦州時叛卒數十投虜
中宜有以處之矣乃非惟無以處也報至
弗答且以為吾固遣之者豈無討賊之義
===
歟意固以為彼方來合也使我疑則彼信
是堅其合也使我信則彼疑是假手也是
故以疑為信而使之以信為疑曁偵卒歸
報虜果盡殄其人而邊境迄無事是其弗
處乃所以處也若此者皆其有確然自信
之衷有超然獨運之畧見本而知末故計
出必審覩指而識歸故機發必中名不必
有諸已斯能就天下之實樂不必享諸已
斯能袪天下之憂是故以費為省以奇為

張亂政，宜有以制之矣。乃非惟無以制也，而至與之博陸者，豈無除惡之志歟？意固以為幾未協也。幾未協而遽動，殆也；有謀人之心而使之知，拙也。是故不虞其人，而亦使之不虞乎我。迨唐社既還，僞僭無據，而廡下之事付諸張桓等矣。是其弗制，乃所以制也。

To act precipitately before the circumstances were favorable would be perilous; to harbor a plan against someone and let him discover it would be clumsy. Thus he showed no suspicion of them and likewise kept them from suspecting him. Thus he treated the suspicious as trustworthy and induced the enemy to treat the trustworthy as suspicious. When the scouts returned with their report, the enemy had indeed exterminated all those men, and the frontier remained free of trouble. 正以禍為福以敗為功當時藉其休而不
見後世受其庇而不知者也傳曰有非常
之人然後有非常之事有非常之事然後
有非常之功又曰非常之原黎民懼焉及
臻厥成天下晏如也兹四子者豈不亦近
之乎向使其循襲故常假托標表徒較計
於形迹之末則吾據其易而以難遺於君
吾潔其躬而以患貽於國固非志士之所
忍為貞臣之所屑就者也雖然形迹固非

者多富而富者未必盜廉者多貧而貧者

…the orthodox, turning calamity into blessing and defeat into achievement. Their contemporaries enjoyed their beneficence without seeing it; later generations received their protection without knowing it. The tradition says: “Only when there are extraordinary men can there be extraordinary deeds; only when there are extraordinary deeds can there be extraordinary achievements.” It also says: “At the outset of an extraordinary undertaking, the common people are afraid; once it reaches completion, all under Heaven are at ease.” Were these four men not close to this ideal? Had they merely followed established practice, sheltered behind outward displays, and concerned themselves only with superficial appearances, their attitude would have been: “I take the easy part and leave the difficulties to my ruler; I keep my own person unsullied and bequeath trouble to the state.” Such conduct is certainly something that a man of resolve could not bear to undertake, nor a steadfast minister deign to pursue. Nevertheless, outward appearances are assuredly not the concern of outstanding men, and the world likewise must not judge them by appearances.
Thieves are often rich, but the rich are not necessarily thieves; incorruptible men are often poor, but the poor are not necessarily incorruptible. Thus, surrender should not be feigned; yet Zhangzi defeated Qin through surrender, so it is proper to approve his defeat of Qin. Falsehood should not be practised; yet Xian Gao preserved Zheng through falsehood, so it is proper to approve his preservation of Zheng. …their failure [?]. How could they vindicate their intentions? Where could they put their talents to use? If even these four men could not escape such treatment, on whom could the affairs of state depend? And why speak only of these four? Had Duke Dan been abruptly cast aside by Zhou when slander was raging, and had Confucius been expelled from Lu when the song about the coarse fur robe was circulating, even these great sages would have had their hands tied, scarcely able to withdraw quickly enough. Thus, when men of talent and wisdom live in the world, those above them who recognize their worth must entrust them with responsibility without wavering. Otherwise, the wise devise plans and the foolish are allowed to disrupt them; the worthy undertake tasks and the unworthy are allowed to undo them. If the wise must have their strategies decided by fools, and worthy men must have their conduct assessed by the unworthy, it is impossible to obtain results.

Those below them who recognize their worth must help them bring their endeavors to completion. Otherwise, when they achieve nothing and fail to win the people’s support, they are criticized for achieving nothing and failing to win that support; when they achieve success and win the people’s support, they are again criticized for achieving success and winning that support. Before instruction has begun, a clamor is already raised; just as something is planted, it is already uprooted. It is impossible to obtain results this way. 各當其時也子能論析明盡而末復取其有裨
punctuated:
才於不善，下也。本善矣，而托之乎善，假豪傑之似，以眩時俗、亂名實，下之下也。而下之下者恒取類乎上，是故不可弗辨也。人有得燕石者，藏以為玉。或告之曰：「此燕石，非玉也。」棄之。他日見玉，則以為燕石也。有聞鬻朴者，慕以為璞。或告之曰：「彼朴，非璞也。」色之。他日聞鬻璞，則以為朴也。何者？似故也。故良工之目，不可欺以玉石；良賈之耳，不可亂以朴璞。匪耳目也，神識在心，獨見獨聞，難以語人者也。斯又傑之傑也。
第四問
韓楫
同考試官署員外郎常批：「古人建白不同，凡以濟時也。子能一一發其□，而末復有取於賈范所陳，信亦識時務而忠者歟！敬服。」
同考試官修撰馬批：「治無定體，因時為體，故漢宋諸臣所陳說不同，而均之有裨於國是，蓋各當其時也。子能論析明盡，而末復取其有裨
translation_en:
…to employ one’s talents for evil is inferior. Being originally good, yet sheltering behind goodness [?], and assuming the semblance of an outstanding man to dazzle contemporaries and confound names and realities, is the lowest of the low. Yet the lowest of the low constantly resemble the highest; therefore one must distinguish between them.
A man obtained a stone from Yan and treasured it as jade. Someone told him, “This is a stone from Yan, not jade.” He discarded it. Later, when he saw jade, he took it for a stone from Yan. Another heard someone selling plain wood (pu), and coveted it, taking it for unworked jade (pu). Someone told him, “That is plain wood, not unworked jade.” He showed displeasure [?]. Later, when he heard someone selling unworked jade, he took it for plain wood. Why? Because of their resemblance. Thus a skilled craftsman’s eyes cannot be deceived about jade and stone, nor can an experienced merchant’s ears be confused by the words for plain wood and unworked jade. It is not a matter of ears and eyes: discerning awareness resides in the mind. What one alone sees and hears is difficult to convey to others. Such a person is outstanding even among outstanding men.
Fourth Policy Question
Han Ji
Comment by Associate Examiner Chang, Acting Vice Director: “The proposals made by men of antiquity differed, but all aimed to meet the needs of their times. You have brought out their □ one by one, and at the end you also draw upon the proposals of Jia and Fan. Surely you too understand the affairs of the times and are loyal! I respectfully admire this.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Senior Compiler: “Government has no fixed form; it takes its form according to the times. Thus the proposals of the various ministers of the Han and Song differed, yet all contributed to sound state policy, for each suited its own time. Your discussion and analysis are clear and thorough, and at the end you also select what may be beneficial …”

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
於今者致望焉識治體而達時宜有能踰于
者耶
考試官侍讀學士胡批子能善發前賢濟時之忠可
以觀識矣
考試官學士高批言古人濟時事甚詳悉而人
皆得其意非可以經生目也
古之人臣之事其君也欲以陳濟時之猷
而成善守之治也時不同而其志同道不
同而其忠同時也者言乎其所遇也道也
===
者所以濟時而致治也而定之於志行之
以忠夫然後能佐其君成善守之治而太
平之業可建矣是故不知時者不可與言
道不定志者不可與言忠忠以行志道以
濟時此漢宋諸臣所以為識治體而善謀
國故其名于今炳然烈也愚嘗觀於古之
治天下者其體有三沉幾周慮立法貽謀
創業之治體也率舊章而遵法守成之治
體也抹敝政而飭法中興之治體也然亦

體也捄敝政而飭法中興之治體也然亦
punctuated:
於今者致望焉。識治體而達時宜，有能踰于者耶？

考試官侍讀學士胡批：子能善發前賢濟時之忠，可以觀識矣。

考試官學士高批：言古人濟時事甚詳悉，而人皆得其意，非可以經生目也。

古之人臣之事其君也，欲以陳濟時之猷，而成善守之治也。時不同而其志同，道不同而其忠同。時也者，言乎其所遇也；道也者，所以濟時而致治也。而定之於志，行之以忠，夫然後能佐其君成善守之治，而太平之業可建矣。是故不知時者，不可與言道；不定志者，不可與言忠。忠以行志，道以濟時，此漢宋諸臣所以為識治體而善謀國，故其名于今炳然烈也。愚嘗觀於古之治天下者，其體有三：沉幾周慮，立法貽謀，創業之治體也；率舊章而遵法，守成之治體也；抹敝政而飭法，中興之治體也。然亦
translation_en:
…placing your hopes in those proposals that are useful today. In understanding the principles of governance and comprehending what the times require, can anyone surpass you [?]?

Examiner Hu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: You have ably brought out the loyalty with which earlier worthies sought to meet the needs of their times. This reveals your discernment.

Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: You discuss in considerable detail how men of antiquity met the needs of their times, capturing each man's intentions. You cannot be regarded as merely a student of the Classics.

When ministers of antiquity served their rulers, they wished to present plans for meeting the needs of their times and thereby establish a government capable of preserving what had been achieved. Their times differed, but their aspirations were the same; their methods differed, but their loyalty was the same. By “times” I mean the circumstances they encountered; by “methods,” the means by which they met contemporary needs and brought about good government. They grounded these in firm purpose and put them into practice with loyalty. Only then could they assist their rulers in establishing a government that preserved their achievements well, and lay the foundations of an age of great peace. Thus, one cannot discuss methods with someone who does not understand the times, nor loyalty with someone whose purpose is not firmly set. Loyalty puts purpose into practice; methods meet the needs of the times. This is why the ministers of the Han and Song understood the principles of governance and planned well for the state, and why their names remain illustrious today.

I have observed that among those who governed the realm in antiquity, there were three forms of governance. Deep consideration of subtle developments and comprehensive deliberation, establishing laws and bequeathing plans to posterity: this was the form of governance for founding a dynasty. Following established institutions and observing the laws: this was the form for preserving inherited achievements. Eliminating defective policies and putting the laws in order: this was the form for restoring a dynasty's fortunes. Yet there are also…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
有不可泥焉者賢哲之佐直亮之臣欲以
輔其君建太平之業則雖守成之時曷嘗
不以飭法濟時為保泰持盈之道哉漢之
文帝玄默恭儉以德化民庶幾成康而賈
誼上疏多欲改建因陳治安之策曰諸侯
彊大匈奴嫚侮侵掠威令不伸與夫風俗
僭侈薄惡經制不定取舎不審凡數事焉
是其志以濟時為忠故其為策皆濟時之
道也夫文帝繼高惠之後海內固稱富庶
矣然制度疏闊諸侯王僭擬匈奴侵邊秦
習不變非飭法不可也故誼為帝陳之而
劉向稱其通達國體雖伊管未能遠過豈
溢美哉宋之仁宗恭儉慈孝深仁厚澤同
於漢文而范仲淹奉答手詔上條陳之疏
曰明黜陟抑僥倖精貢舉擇長官均公田
厚農桑修武備推恩信重命令減徭役凡
十事焉是其志以濟時為忠故其為疏皆
濟時之道也夫仁宗紹三世之業國運可

十事焉是其志以濟時爲忠故其爲疏皆
濟時之道也夫仁宗紹三世之業國運可
punctuated:
有不可泥焉者。賢哲之佐、直亮之臣，欲以輔其君建太平之業，則雖守成之時，曷嘗不以飭法濟時為保泰持盈之道哉？漢之文帝，玄默恭儉，以德化民，庶幾成康，而賈誼上疏，多欲改建，因陳治安之策曰：「諸侯彊大，匈奴嫚侮侵掠，威令不伸，與夫風俗僭侈薄惡，經制不定，取舎不審。」凡數事焉。是其志以濟時為忠，故其為策皆濟時之道也。夫文帝繼高惠之後，海內固稱富庶矣，然制度疏闊，諸侯王僭擬，匈奴侵邊，秦習不變，非飭法不可也。故誼為帝陳之，而劉向稱其通達國體，雖伊管未能遠過，豈溢美哉？
宋之仁宗，恭儉慈孝，深仁厚澤，同於漢文，而范仲淹奉答手詔，上條陳之疏曰：「明黜陟，抑僥倖，精貢舉，擇長官，均公田，厚農桑，修武備，推恩信，重命令，減徭役。」凡十事焉。是其志以濟時為忠，故其為疏皆濟時之道也。夫仁宗紹三世之業，國運可
translation_en:
…there are nevertheless circumstances in which one must not adhere rigidly to these distinctions. If wise assistants and upright, trustworthy ministers wish to help their ruler establish an age of Great Peace, even when preserving an inherited achievement, how could they fail to regard putting the laws in order and meeting the needs of the times as the means to safeguard peace and sustain prosperity? Emperor Wen of the Han was quietly restrained, reverent, and frugal. He transformed the people through virtue, nearly matching Kings Cheng and Kang. Yet Jia Yi submitted memorials advocating many reforms, presenting proposals for good government and security: “The feudal lords are powerful; the Xiongnu behave with insolence and raid and plunder; imperial authority and commands do not prevail. Moreover, customs are marked by violations of rank, extravagance, meanness, and depravity; governing institutions are unsettled; and decisions about what to adopt or discard are insufficiently considered.” These were the several matters he addressed. His intent was to express loyalty by meeting the needs of the times, and thus all his proposals offered ways to do so. Emperor Wen succeeded Emperors Gao and Hui, and the realm was indeed reputed to be prosperous and populous. Nevertheless, its institutions were lax and incomplete, the feudatory kings presumptuously emulated the emperor, the Xiongnu invaded the frontiers, and the habits of Qin remained unchanged. Putting the laws in order was indispensable. Thus Jia Yi laid these matters before the emperor, and Liu Xiang praised him for thoroughly understanding the essentials of governing the state, saying that even Yi Yin and Guan Zhong could not far surpass him. Was this excessive praise?
Emperor Renzong of the Song was reverent, frugal, compassionate, and filial. His profound benevolence and abundant beneficence matched those of Emperor Wen of the Han. Yet Fan Zhongyan, respectfully answering an edict in the emperor’s own hand, submitted a memorial setting out proposals item by item: “Make demotions and promotions judicious; curb advancement through undeserved favor; improve selection through the examinations; choose chief local officials carefully; equalize allocations of public land; strengthen agriculture and sericulture; put military preparations in order; extend benevolence and good faith; give due weight to commands; and reduce corvée service.” These were ten matters in all. His intent was to express loyalty by meeting the needs of the times, and thus all the proposals in his memorial offered ways to do so. Renzong inherited the achievement of three reigns, and the fortunes of the dynasty could…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
謂盈成矣然紀綱寢隳夷狄寇盜驕橫恩
賞不節賦斂無度非飭法不可也故仲淹
為帝陳之而歐陽脩謂其老練世事所陳
志在遠大誠知言哉乃若漢自武帝好大
喜功百姓疲敝宣帝繼之若可以議飭法
矣魏相總領衆職以為方今務在奉行故
事數條漢興以來國家便宜行事及賈誼
鼂錯董仲舒所言奏請施行之蓋以宣帝
勵精圖治而德教不純故佐之遵法以捄
===
其失維時吏稱民安孰非相之功乎宋自
神宗任用非人變壞舊政哲宗繼之飭法
所必先矣司馬光復起為相毅然以身殉
社稷上言新法之當改如捄焚拯溺乃於
王安石呂惠卿之所建者悉刬革之蓋以
哲宗虛己倚任天下引領觀政故佐之飭
法以善其治君子稱其旋乾轉坤光無愧
乎此也夫此四臣者之事君也惟君之所
遇異時故道之所急異務語其為志之忠

punctuated: 謂盈成矣。然紀綱寢隳，夷狄寇盜驕橫，恩賞不節，賦斂無度，非飭法不可也。故仲淹為帝陳之，而歐陽脩謂其老練世事，所陳志在遠大，誠知言哉！乃若漢自武帝好大喜功，百姓疲敝，宣帝繼之，若可以議飭法矣。魏相總領衆職，以為方今務在奉行故事，數條漢興以來國家便宜行事及賈誼、鼂錯、董仲舒所言，奏請施行之。蓋以宣帝勵精圖治而德教不純，故佐之遵法以捄其失。維時吏稱民安，孰非相之功乎？宋自神宗任用非人，變壞舊政，哲宗繼之，飭法所必先矣。司馬光復起為相，毅然以身殉社稷，上言新法之當改，如捄焚拯溺，乃於王安石、呂惠卿之所建者悉刬革之。蓋以哲宗虛己倚任，天下引領觀政，故佐之飭法以善其治。君子稱其旋乾轉坤，光無愧乎此也。夫此四臣者之事君也，惟君之所遇異時，故道之所急異務，語其為志之忠
translation_en:
…said to have reached fullness and prosperity. Yet the governing order was gradually falling into ruin; foreign peoples and bandits were arrogant and unruly; favors and rewards were unrestrained, and taxation knew no bounds. Putting the laws in order was indispensable. Thus Fan Zhongyan laid these proposals before the emperor. Ouyang Xiu said that he was seasoned in worldly affairs and that his proposals aimed at far-reaching achievements. These were truly discerning words!

As for the Han, Emperor Wu’s fondness for grand undertakings and military achievements had left the common people exhausted. When Emperor Xuan succeeded him, it might have seemed appropriate to discuss putting the laws in order. Wei Xiang, overseeing the various offices, considered the urgent task of the day to be carrying out established precedents. He repeatedly enumerated measures suited to the state’s circumstances since the founding of the Han, together with proposals by Jia Yi, Chao Cuo, and Dong Zhongshu, and memorialized requesting their implementation. Emperor Xuan devoted himself energetically to good government, but his moral instruction lacked purity; Wei Xiang therefore assisted him in adhering to established laws to remedy this failing. At that time, officials fulfilled their duties and the people lived in peace. What part of this was not due to Wei Xiang’s efforts?

Under the Song, Emperor Shenzong employed unsuitable men, altering and ruining the former administration. When Emperor Zhezong succeeded him, putting the laws in order necessarily took precedence. Sima Guang returned to office as Chief Councilor, resolutely dedicating his life to the state. He submitted that the New Policies must be changed with the urgency of rescuing people from fire or drowning, and accordingly abolished all that Wang Anshi and Lü Huiqing had instituted. Emperor Zhezong humbly entrusted him with responsibility, while all under Heaven craned their necks to observe the government. He therefore assisted the emperor in putting the laws in order to improve his rule. Men of discernment praised him for turning Heaven and Earth around; Sima Guang was worthy of this praise. Now, in these four ministers’ service to their rulers, because their rulers faced different circumstances in their respective times, the most urgent tasks in guiding them differed. As for the loyalty of their intentions…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
則烏有不同者哉救政當革則變熈寧之
法而不病於紛更光於哲宗正始之時惟
欲亟除患害者以飭法為體經也故事可
行則條賢臣之奏而不病於因循相於宣
帝中興之時不欲更張政令者以遵法為
體權也誼於文帝仲淹於仁宗皆當熈洽
之時而誼則欲立經陳紀以求長治乆安
仲淹則欲修理政教與國家盤固基本者
以飭法而守成為體經以濟權也然而誼
===

議以佐精明之治功恒人闇於時權安習

之與光亦非易也時之所遇得行其志也

之疏奏四方異聞災變於宣帝是宜有取

觀其進三劄五規於仁宗則必能為仲淹
之跡奏四方異聞災變於宣帝是宜有取
punctuated: 則烏有不同者哉？救政當革，則變熈寧之法而不病於紛更。光於哲宗正始之時，惟欲亟除患害者，以飭法為體經也。故事可行，則條賢臣之奏而不病於因循。相於宣帝中興之時，不欲更張政令者，以遵法為體權也。誼於文帝，仲淹於仁宗，皆當熈洽之時，而誼則欲立經陳紀，以求長治乆安；仲淹則欲修理政教，與國家盤固基本者，以飭法而守成，為體經以濟權也。然而誼與仲淹則當其難焉。何者？文帝、仁宗皆一代守成之賢君也。顧於其時，陳剴切之論議，以佐精明之治功，恒人闇於時權，安習所見，鮮不病其紛更者，而不知其竭忠極慮，盡責難陳善之敬，欲以致其君於唐虞三代之隆。是其難者，以遇承平之時也。相之與光，亦非易也，時之所遇，得行其志也。觀其進三劄五規於仁宗，則必能為仲淹之疏；奏四方異聞災變於宣帝，是宜有取
translation_en:
…how, then, could they have differed? When rescuing government required reform, changing the laws of the Xining era was no fault of disruptive alteration. At the outset of Zhezong’s reign, Sima Guang sought only to remove harmful measures urgently: he embodied enduring principles by setting the laws in order. When precedents remained practicable, setting out the memorials of worthy ministers was no fault of unthinking adherence to the past. During Xuandi’s restoration of prosperity, Wei Xiang wished to avoid recasting governmental commands: he embodied expedient judgment by following established laws. Jia Yi under Wendi and Fan Zhongyan under Renzong both lived in times of peace and harmony. Yet Jia Yi wished to establish guiding principles and set out rules, seeking lasting good government and enduring peace; Zhongyan wished to put government and moral instruction in order and secure the foundations of the state. By setting the laws in order while preserving inherited achievements, they embodied enduring principles to aid expedient judgment.

Yet Jia Yi and Zhongyan faced particular difficulty. Why? Wendi and Renzong were both worthy rulers of their respective dynasties who preserved inherited achievements. Nevertheless, when these ministers advanced incisive arguments to assist their discerning rulers’ accomplishments in government, ordinary people, ignorant of judgments suited to the times and comfortably accustomed to what they knew, almost invariably blamed them for disruptive alteration. They did not understand that these ministers exhausted their loyalty and deliberation, fulfilling their reverent duty to demand difficult achievements of their rulers and lay good counsel before them, wishing to bring their rulers to the heights attained under Yao and Shun and the Three Dynasties. Their difficulty thus arose from serving in a time of settled peace.

Nor was it easy for Wei Xiang and Sima Guang; the circumstances they encountered allowed them to carry out their aspirations. Considering that Guang submitted three memoranda and five admonitions to Renzong, he surely could have composed Zhongyan’s memorial. Since Xiang reported unusual occurrences and calamitous anomalies from all regions to Xuandi, he surely had reason to draw upon…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
於誼之言所謂易地則皆然者也至於誼
與仲淹所遇又有不同者嘗讀二史而知
其槩矣當仁宗拔擢仲淹之初信嚮方篤
故於其所陳悉采用之而又韓琦富弼之
賢同心輔政致成慶曆之治此非其徵與
文帝亦嘉誼之言畧施行矣使時見用功
化必盛而乃排於絳灌抑欝終身以才見
忌不為甚可悼痛耶况宣室所問非治理
之要而天章引對則銳意太平固已不同
===
矣執事又欲以其所陳可裨於今者言之
而愚生非識治體者也然竊有聞焉今
藩封列屏翰世食祿入固有定額矣而支庶
蕃衍歲供弗給其需求則甚亟夷虜擾邊
疆邇嘗內犯雖已驅逐矣而駐牧窺伺經
春未散其狡詐為可虞制法以範俗非不
令民之崇儉也而因恬故習者鮮淳朴之
風禮教以淑民可謂置天下於安也而奉
行德意者寡仁恕之政豈無類於誼之所

疆邇嘗内犯雖已驅逐矣而駐牧窺伺經
春不散其狡詐爲可虞制法以範俗非不

風禮教以淑民可謂置天下於安也而奉
行德意者寡仁恕之政豈無類於誼之所
punctuated:
於誼之言，所謂易地則皆然者也。至於誼與仲淹所遇，又有不同者，嘗讀二史而知其槩矣。當仁宗拔擢仲淹之初，信嚮方篤，故於其所陳悉采用之，而又韓琦、富弼之賢，同心輔政，致成慶曆之治，此非其徵與？文帝亦嘉誼之言，畧施行矣。使時見用，功化必盛，而乃排於絳灌，抑欝終身，以才見忌，不為甚可悼痛耶？况宣室所問，非治理之要，而天章引對，則銳意太平，固已不同矣。
執事又欲以其所陳可裨於今者言之，而愚生非識治體者也。然竊有聞焉。今藩封列屏翰，世食祿入，固有定額矣，而支庶蕃衍，歲供弗給，其需求則甚亟。夷虜擾邊疆，邇嘗內犯，雖已驅逐矣，而駐牧窺伺，經春未散，其狡詐為可虞。制法以範俗，非不令民之崇儉也，而因恬故習者，鮮淳朴之風。禮教以淑民，可謂置天下於安也，而奉行德意者，寡仁恕之政。豈無類於誼之所
translation_en:
…from Jia Yi’s words. This is what is meant by saying that, had they exchanged places, each would have acted likewise. Yet the circumstances encountered by Jia Yi and Fan Zhongyan also differed. Having read the two histories, I have come to understand their broad outlines. When Emperor Renzong first promoted Zhongyan, his trust and esteem were deep; thus he adopted all that Zhongyan proposed. Moreover, worthy men such as Han Qi and Fu Bi assisted the government with one mind, bringing about the good government of the Qingli era. Is this not evidence of it? Emperor Wen also approved Jia Yi’s words and put some of them into practice. Had Jia Yi been employed at that time, his achievements and transforming influence would surely have been great. Instead, he was excluded by Jiang and Guan, remaining frustrated throughout his life. That his talent should have aroused jealousy—is this not deeply lamentable? Moreover, the questions asked in the Xuanshi Hall did not concern the essentials of government, whereas the audience granted in the Tianzhang Pavilion reflected a keen determination to achieve great peace. The circumstances were indeed different.
You further ask me to discuss which of their proposals might benefit the present day. I, an ignorant student, am no one versed in the essentials of government; nevertheless, I have heard something of these matters. Today, the enfeoffed princes stand arrayed as protective bulwarks, receiving hereditary stipends at established rates. Yet their collateral branches and junior descendants multiply, and the annual provisions are insufficient; their demands are therefore exceedingly urgent. The barbarians trouble the frontier and recently invaded our territory. Although they have been driven out, they remain encamped with their herds, watching for an opportunity; throughout the spring they have not dispersed. Their cunning gives cause for apprehension. Laws are established to regulate customs, and certainly enjoin the people to value frugality. Yet those complacently following their old habits show little of the spirit of simplicity and honesty. Ritual instruction is used to improve the people, and may be said to secure peace for all under Heaven. Yet those charged with carrying out this benevolent intent offer little humane and forbearing government. Are there not circumstances resembling those that Jia Yi…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
陳者乎懲貪肆而絕苞苴仕路其清也亦
或有矯飾以賈譽操切以衒能而欲圖僥
倖者稽戶口以定徭役法令甚善也亦或
有供億之太繁貧富之無等而反貽重困
者安民莫要於擇守令選授之時已審慎
矣而未必其皆能修職武備莫急於實營
伍召募之議嘗舉行矣而未必其盡為精
兵豈無類於仲淹之所陳者乎是皆於今
為切務所當加意焉者而亦未敢遽以為
===
然也惟執事進而教之
第五問
高啟愚
同考試官署員外郎武批財貨之通塞關國用之盈
虛有司往往計之而不得其術子能洞悉弊原而
酌處允當鑿鑿可行必素抱經濟之遠猷者
同考試官侍讀呂批鹽法錢法關于
國計甚大此策獨能究極利弊而區畫周詳是留心於經世務
之不特以其文也

爲切務所當加意焉者而亦未敢遽以爲
然也惟執事進而教之
策五問
===
高啓愚
同考試官署員外郎武　批財貨之通塞關國用之盈
〔虛有司往往計之而不得其術子能洞悉弊原而酌處允當鑿鑿可行必素抱經濟之遠猷者〕
同考試官侍讀呂　批鹽法錢法關于
〔國計甚大此策獨能究極利弊而區畫周詳是留心於經世務之不特以其文也〕
punctuated:
陳者乎？懲貪肆而絕苞苴，仕路其清也，亦或有矯飾以賈譽、操切以衒能而欲圖僥倖者。稽戶口以定徭役，法令甚善也，亦或有供億之太繁、貧富之無等而反貽重困者。安民莫要於擇守令，選授之時已審慎矣，而未必其皆能修職；武備莫急於實營伍，召募之議嘗舉行矣，而未必其盡為精兵。豈無類於仲淹之所陳者乎？是皆於今為切務，所當加意焉者，而亦未敢遽以為然也。惟執事進而教之。

第五問
高啟愚

同考試官署員外郎武批：「財貨之通塞，關國用之盈虛。有司往往計之而不得其術。子能洞悉弊原，而酌處允當，鑿鑿可行，必素抱經濟之遠猷者。」

同考試官侍讀呂批：「鹽法、錢法關于國計甚大。此策獨能究極利弊，而區畫周詳，是留心於經世，務之，不特以其文也。」
translation_en:
…resemble what he set forth? Greed and lawlessness are punished and bribery eradicated, so that official service should be clean; yet there may still be those who put on a false display to win praise, act harshly to show off their ability, and seek advancement through undeserved good fortune. Households and population are checked to determine labor-service obligations: these regulations are excellent, yet excessively burdensome provisioning demands and a failure to differentiate between rich and poor may instead cause severe hardship. Nothing is more essential to keeping the people at peace than choosing prefects and magistrates. Although their selection and appointment are already handled carefully, they may not all fulfill their duties. Nothing is more urgent for military preparedness than filling the ranks. Although proposals for recruitment have been put into effect, the recruits may not all be effective soldiers. Are there not things here resembling what Zhongyan set forth? These are all urgent matters today that deserve particular attention, yet I would not venture hastily to pronounce my views correct. I ask only that you, sir, offer me further instruction.

Fifth Question
Gao Qiyu

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Acting Vice Director: “Whether wealth and goods circulate freely or are obstructed bears on the abundance or scarcity of resources for state expenditure. The responsible officials frequently deliberate on this but fail to find the proper method. You thoroughly understand the sources of the abuses, and your proposed remedies are judicious and appropriate, demonstrably practicable. You must long have cherished far-reaching plans for governing the realm.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Lü, Reader-in-Waiting: “The salt and monetary systems have an immense bearing on state finances. This policy essay is exceptional in thoroughly investigating their benefits and defects and in offering comprehensive, carefully considered arrangements. This shows someone who takes the practical work of governing to heart and pursues it, rather than merely treating it as a literary exercise.”

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
考試官侍讀學士胡批經生而能洞究二法之弊
區處復有酌見適用之才也錄之
考試官學士高批處置二法明悉詳審是知
時務者也取之
經國之道莫先於慎法法者國與民之所
同依也國依於法則令重而體尊民依於
法則觀聽不惑有所恃以殖其業而鼓舞
不倦甚矣法之不可以不慎也故立法者
必慎為經久之規而務在法之可常行法
===
者必慎為通變之權而務不失乎立法之
意猶之持衡然鈞鎰銖兩截然不可以毫
釐假也至其一低一昂一進一退趣物制
平因變濟務則權之用歸焉耳今夫鹽筴
之權也錢幣之興也先王所以阜國足民
兼利上下之大經也唯操之而不得其權
焉斯其弊有不可勝原者矣蓋利與義相
為出入者也經國者導利布民期於兼濟
義莫大焉夫苟見小利而輒易軌以求法

translation_en:
Examiner Hu, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: Though a student of the Classics, he can thoroughly investigate the defects of these two systems. His proposed arrangements also show considered judgment. He has talent suited to practical affairs. Accept his essay.

Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: His treatment of the two systems is clear, comprehensive, detailed, and judicious. He understands the affairs of the day. Select him.

In governing a state, nothing takes precedence over care in matters of law. Law is what the state and the people alike depend upon. When the state relies upon law, its commands carry weight and its dignity is upheld; when the people rely upon law, they are not confused by what they see and hear. They have something dependable on which to build their livelihoods and are encouraged to exert themselves without tiring. How essential it is to exercise care in matters of law! Thus, those who establish laws must carefully devise enduring rules, striving to make the laws lasting; those who administer laws must carefully exercise discretion in adapting to change, striving never to depart from the intent behind their establishment. It is like holding a balance: the weights—jun, yi, zhu, and liang—are precisely defined and admit not the slightest discrepancy. But as one side falls and the other rises, as the weight moves forward or back, adjusting to the object to achieve equilibrium and responding to changes to accomplish the task, the function of the movable counterweight comes into play.

Now, control over salt revenues and the introduction of coinage were fundamental measures by which the former kings enriched the state, provided adequately for the people, and benefited both rulers and subjects. Yet when those administering them fail to exercise appropriate discretion, the resulting abuses are too numerous to trace to their sources. For profit and righteousness may accord with or diverge from one another. Those who govern the state channel benefits and distribute them among the people, seeking to provide for all: no righteousness is greater than this. title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
之通行而無害不可得也則今日之鹽政
是已利與害互爲輕重者也經國者導源
塞隙守於畫一利莫大焉若見小害而輙
自沮焉求法之必行而民信不可得也則
今日之錢法是已愚嘗通覽古今之故錯
綜利害之端而有以得致弊之原與夫捄
弊之要矣且鹽筴何昉乎昉于管仲相齊
伐菑薪煑海以啓富疆之基也嗣後元狩
修其術而禁榷遂與古今相爲終始其烹
===

弊代有變矣求其適時之宜大有裨司農
之經費者吾唯取夫唐之募商給引宋之
入粟實邊之二法者焉錢幣何始乎始于

且鹽筴何昉乎？昉于管仲相齊，伐菑薪，煑海，以啓富疆之基也。嗣後元狩修其術，而禁榷遂與古今相爲終始。其烹煎之制、給予之宜、法禁之張弛、公私之利弊，代有變矣。求其適時之宜，大有裨司農之經費者，吾唯取夫唐之募商給引、宋之入粟實邊之二法者焉。

translation_en:
…it is impossible for the law to operate generally without harm: precisely such is the salt administration today. Benefit and harm must be weighed against one another. Those who govern the state channel the sources of revenue, close off leaks, and maintain uniform rules; no benefit is greater than this. If they let every minor harm discourage them, it will be impossible to ensure that the law is implemented and that the people trust it: precisely such is the currency system today. I have surveyed affairs past and present and considered the interwoven sources of benefit and harm, and have thereby come to understand both the origins of these abuses and the essentials of remedying them.
Now, where did the salt monopoly originate? It originated when Guan Zhong served as chief minister of Qi, cutting brushwood for fuel [?] and boiling seawater, thereby laying the foundations of wealth and strength. Later, during the Yuanshou reign period, these methods were developed, and prohibitions and monopoly controls thereafter persisted through the ages. The procedures for boiling salt, appropriate arrangements for its distribution, the tightening and relaxation of legal prohibitions, and the benefits and harms to public and private interests have changed from dynasty to dynasty. If we seek measures suited to their times that substantially supported the expenditures of the Chamberlain for the National Treasury, I select only these two: the Tang practice of recruiting merchants and issuing salt certificates, and the Song practice of accepting grain deliveries to provision the frontier.
Where did coinage begin? It began when Taigong assisted the Zhou, establishing the currency regulations of the Nine Treasuries to facilitate the use of money. When King Jing of Zhou changed this system, later generations came to adopt or abandon monetary arrangements according to the advantages and problems of their times. Differences in names and denominations, variations in manufacture and use, disparities in weight, and the intermingling of genuine and counterfeit coins have changed from dynasty to dynasty. If we seek a sound standard for valuing goods that remained unchanged despite periodic abolition and restoration, I select only the Han…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
五銖唐開元之二錢者焉夫自太公管仲
而來上下數千年矣而法之可稱述者僅
僅若此法之善誠難矣而持法者不可不
慎察也我
朝于産鹽之地設轉運司者六提舉司者七
鹽課司各有定額行鹽各有分地而淮浙
齊晉之課專給邊餉募商輸芻粟塞垣領
引守支盖倣唐宋之意而規制爲益善矣
然就各運司而論兩淮之課居其十七是
===
以九邊之仰給尤重夫何邇年以來鹽務
積滯邊廩告虛使二百年通濟之法一旦
廢格牴牾交敝於中外是惡可不深求其
故耶盖鹽雖斯民無日可缺要不過食味
之一耳管夷吾計口算賦逮于吾子苛矣
然必有是口乃算是賦非漫加也異日者
淮鹽額課不過七十萬引有奇已爾迨承
平寖久而生齒繁于是每引以餘鹽副之
盖實計一百四十萬有奇矣正課遵舊制

translation_en:
…the two coinages: the Han five-zhu coins and the Tang Kaiyuan coins. Several thousand years have elapsed since Taigong and Guan Zhong, yet the measures worthy of commendation amount to only these few. Sound regulations are indeed difficult to devise, and those who administer them must be scrutinized carefully.
Our dynasty has established six Salt Distribution Commissions and seven Salt Tax Supervisorates in salt-producing areas. Each Salt Tax Office has a fixed quota, and salt distribution has its designated territories. The salt revenues of Huai, Zhe, Qi, and Jin are devoted exclusively to provisioning the frontier. Merchants are recruited to transport fodder and grain to the frontier fortifications, receive salt certificates, and await delivery of their salt. This broadly follows the intent of the Tang and Song arrangements, while improving their institutional provisions. Among the distribution commissions, however, Lianghuai accounts for seven-tenths of the salt revenue, so the Nine Frontier Garrisons depend particularly heavily upon it. Why, then, have salt operations in recent years become clogged with accumulated delays, and frontier granaries been reported empty, causing a system that sustained circulation and supplied needs for two hundred years suddenly to become inoperative, with conflicting arrangements producing distress both at the center and in the provinces? How could we fail to investigate the causes thoroughly? Although the people cannot go a day without salt, it is, after all, merely one seasoning for food. Guan Yiwu assessed the levy by counting mouths, extending it even to “your children” [?]: this was harsh indeed! Yet a person had to exist before the corresponding levy was assessed; it was not imposed arbitrarily. Formerly, the assessed quota for Huai salt amounted to no more than somewhat over seven hundred thousand certificates. As peace endured and the population increased, each certificate was supplemented with additional salt, bringing the actual total to somewhat over one million four hundred thousand certificates. The regular quota followed the old system…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
入粟關塞以實邊儲餘鹽權時宜入鏹運
司以解內帑竈無贏積國有倍利法至善
也頃歲額派之外復加以工本鹽三十五
萬引亦以餘鹽副之準
國初課額固已三倍之矣而羨鹽之割沒不
與也夫行貨之地未嘗加闢食鹽之口豈
能驟倍鹽驟增則壅而不售壅而不售二
歲必有一歲積引矣行之十年則有五歲
之積而引不勝滯矣引滯則商本虧本虧
===
則不樂輸邊轉而營他利矣籌邊者以開
中之無人也必下其估雖下其估而猶有
不至焉此邊供之所以益詘也此上下俱
困術也夫鹺司之給邊者凡四獨淮利稱
饒故兩浙山東長蘆必兩淮帶派而後可
通也淮鹽滯則此三方者均病矣是使
國家全不獲煮海利也然則工本之設增正
課乎損正課乎其效可覩矣而可不求所
以通變之耶我

translation_en:
…grain is delivered to the frontier passes to replenish frontier reserves; for the supplementary salt, an expedient arrangement requires payment in money to the Salt Distribution Commission, for remittance to the imperial treasury. The salt producers have no surplus stocks, and the state receives twice the revenue: an excellent system indeed. In recent years, however, beyond the assigned quota, another 350,000 salt certificates have been added under the heading of production-cost salt, likewise matched with supplementary salt. Compared with the salt revenue quota at the founding of the dynasty, this is already three times as much, excluding the portions of surplus salt appropriated or confiscated. Yet the territory in which the salt is marketed has never been expanded. How could the number of mouths consuming salt suddenly double? When the salt supply suddenly increases, it accumulates unsold. If it accumulates unsold, every two years must leave one year’s worth of certificates outstanding. After ten years, five years’ worth will have accumulated, and the backlog of certificates will become unmanageable. When certificates cannot be redeemed, merchants’ capital is depleted; with their capital depleted, they become unwilling to deliver supplies to the frontier and turn instead to other profitable ventures. Those responsible for frontier provisioning, finding no one participating in the system of exchanging grain deliveries for salt certificates, must lower their assessments. Even after these are lowered, some merchants still fail to come. This is why frontier supplies become ever more inadequate. It is a method that impoverishes both those above and those below.
There are four Salt Distribution Commissions that supply the frontier, but only the Huai salt trade is regarded as abundantly profitable. Thus the salt quotas of Liangzhe, Shandong, and Changlu can be marketed only when assigned in conjunction with those of Lianghuai. When Huai salt is held up, these three regions all suffer as well. This deprives the state altogether of the profits from boiling seawater for salt. Does the establishment of production-cost salt, then, increase the regular salt revenue or diminish it? Its effects are plain to see. Can we fail to seek a way to adapt and reform the system? Our…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
朝錢法自
聖祖未建極之前即創大中通寶混一之後又
鑄洪武通寶迨
成祖
宣宗
孝宗各鑄通寶而冠以年號焉其制一準五銖
開元之度與歷代制錢相兼行使今至便
也私鑄之科處以極典而又懸發覺之賞
格購之法至嚴也是以利孔不分民聽不
===
惑財貨流通而上下俱利矣夫何邇年以
來擅巧者工趨利作奸者輕犯法盜鑄雲
興鉛錫殽雜幾于綖環鵝眼矣我
皇上赫然出令悉索浮僞之弊而刬絕之鑄嘉
靖通寶以復
祖宗之舊與天下更始使數十年沿習之陋廓
然大清不啻快矣迺真工大奸復擬而私
鑄之紛紛然與制錢競流於都市此不可
耐也昔漢令郡國鑄五銖錢吏民之坐盜

也私鑄之科處以極典而又懸發覺之賞
格購之法至嚴也是以利孔不分民聽不

興鉛錫殽雜幾于綖環鵝眼矣我

punctuated:
朝錢法，自聖祖未建極之前，即創大中通寶；混一之後，又鑄洪武通寶。迨成祖、宣宗、孝宗，各鑄通寶而冠以年號焉。其制一準五銖、開元之度，與歷代制錢相兼行使，今至便也。私鑄之科，處以極典，而又懸發覺之賞格購之，法至嚴也。是以利孔不分，民聽不惑，財貨流通，而上下俱利矣。
夫何邇年以來，擅巧者工趨利，作奸者輕犯法，盜鑄雲興，鉛錫殽雜，幾于綖環鵝眼矣！我皇上赫然出令，悉索浮僞之弊而刬絕之，鑄嘉靖通寶，以復祖宗之舊，與天下更始，使數十年沿習之陋廓然大清，不啻快矣！迺真工大奸復擬而私鑄之，紛紛然與制錢競流於都市，此不可耐也！昔漢令郡國鑄五銖錢，吏民之坐盜
translation_en:
…As for our dynasty’s coinage regulations, even before the Sagely Founder assumed the imperial throne, he created the Dazhong tongbao coinage; after unifying the realm, he also cast Hongwu tongbao coins. Subsequently, Chengzu, Xuanzong, and Xiaozong each cast tongbao coins bearing their respective reign titles. Their specifications uniformly followed the standards of the wuzhu and Kaiyuan coins, and they circulated alongside the official coinages of successive dynasties—a most convenient arrangement even today. The offense of private minting carried the ultimate penalty, while published reward schedules offered payment for exposing it. The law was exceedingly strict. Thus the source of profit remained undivided, the people were not confused, wealth and goods circulated freely, and both government and people benefited.
Why, then, in recent years have skilled craftsmen become adept at pursuing profit, and wrongdoers readily broken the law? Counterfeit minting has sprung up like clouds, with lead and tin mixed into the coins, which have become almost like the tiny coins called ‘thread rings’ and ‘goose eyes.’ Our Emperor issued a stern command to seek out and eradicate all abuses involving debased and counterfeit currency. He cast Jiajing tongbao coins to restore the practices of his imperial ancestors and make a fresh beginning with all under Heaven. The corrupt practices that had persisted for decades were swept away completely: this was more than merely gratifying! Yet skilled craftsmen [?] and great malefactors have again imitated these coins and minted them privately. In great numbers, they compete with official coins in circulation in the cities and markets. This is intolerable! Formerly, the Han ordered the commanderies and kingdoms to cast wuzhu coins; officials and commoners convicted of illicit minting…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
鑄金者衆矣而不能半天下大抵皆鑄金
錢矣後罷郡國鑄錢專其事上林三官而
盜鑄遂尠以勢重而威行也今自寶源局
而外造鑄者南京寶慶已爾環京師而邑
者鎔冶之爐相望也此其無忌憚之尤也
漢第五倫一督鑄錢掾耳領長安市而市
遂無姦巧矧今法令詳密百司具職局有
督視之長市有徼巡之吏而使僞錢不惟
公行閭閈且旁緣爲百司俸入焉而司課
===
不察也此有司不能奉法之過也而非錢
之不可鑄也因而廢之是使盜鑄者操其
柄而官爲作止也非所以任長利而杜深
奸也而可不思所以變厲之乎是故興廢
有道視時之屈伸而已取予有方視勢之
向背而已贏縮有宜視機之緩急而已故
今欲捄鹽法之弊莫若復舊額去工本欲
理錢法之弊莫若復公冶禁私鑄夫工本
之爲鹽法害也有識固豫言之而人莫之

理錢法之弊莫若復公冶禁私鑄夫工本

punctuated:
鑄金者衆矣，而不能半天下，大抵皆鑄金錢矣。後罷郡國鑄錢，專其事上林三官，而盜鑄遂尠，以勢重而威行也。今自寶源局而外，造鑄者南京寶慶已爾；環京師而邑者，鎔冶之爐相望也。此其無忌憚之尤也。漢第五倫，一督鑄錢掾耳，領長安市，而市遂無姦巧。矧今法令詳密，百司具職，局有督視之長，市有徼巡之吏，而使僞錢不惟公行閭閈，且旁緣爲百司俸入焉，而司課不察也。此有司不能奉法之過也，而非錢之不可鑄也。因而廢之，是使盜鑄者操其柄，而官爲作止也，非所以任長利而杜深奸也。而可不思所以變厲之乎？
是故興廢有道，視時之屈伸而已；取予有方，視勢之向背而已；贏縮有宜，視機之緩急而已。故今欲捄鹽法之弊，莫若復舊額、去工本；欲理錢法之弊，莫若復公冶、禁私鑄。夫工本之爲鹽法害也，有識固豫言之，而人莫之
translation_en:
…those who cast metal were numerous, yet they could not reach half of all under Heaven [?]; virtually everyone was casting metal coins. Later, the commanderies and kingdoms were prohibited from minting coins, and the work was entrusted exclusively to the Three Offices of Shanglin. Illicit minting consequently became rare, because authority was concentrated and its force could be brought to bear. Today, apart from the Coinage Office, there is already minting at Baoqing in Nanjing [?]; in the towns surrounding the capital, smelting furnaces stand within sight of one another. This is the utmost in brazen disregard for restraint. Under the Han, Diwu Lun was merely a clerk supervising coin casting, yet when he took charge of the markets of Chang’an, fraud and trickery disappeared from them. How much more should this be possible today, when laws and ordinances are detailed and comprehensive, and every office has its assigned duties! The mint has a supervising chief, and the markets have patrolling officers. Yet counterfeit coins are allowed not only to circulate openly in the neighborhoods but also, through indirect channels, to enter the salary payments of the various offices, while those responsible for assessing receipts fail to investigate. This is the fault of the responsible officials’ failure to uphold the law; it does not mean that coins cannot be minted. To abolish minting on this account would place control in the hands of illicit minters and make official activity depend upon them. This is no way to secure lasting benefits and prevent deep-seated fraud. Can we fail to consider how to reform and reinvigorate the system?
Thus, there is a proper way to institute or abolish measures: simply observe whether the times call for contraction or expansion. There is a method for taking and giving: simply observe whether circumstances favor or oppose it. There is a fitting degree of increase or reduction: simply observe whether the situation is relaxed or urgent. Therefore, to remedy the abuses of the salt system today, nothing is better than restoring the former quotas and eliminating the production-cost payments; to remedy the abuses of the coinage system, nothing is better than restoring official minting and prohibiting private casting. As for the harm that production-cost payments would do to the salt system, discerning men certainly foretold it, yet no one…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
省也今其敗端見矣所以隱忍而不除者
以各邊歲例非此無以足其額也而不審
其有虛額而無實惠也豈惟無之且並開
中之額而失之矣其為患不細也故無工
本則引不壅引不壅則鹽利通矣利通則
商不困商不困則樂於報納矣商樂報納
則芻粟叢赴而邊備饒矣時估不下侵而
倍有獲矣一舉而四利集焉歲例雖如數
省之可也必不可省則此工本之增無幾
===
時也前此必有所以給之者獨不可考其
原乎此所謂不以小利貽大害也先王錢
幣之興將以利民而非以自利也然國計
不給則亦取贏焉當今經費廣而蓄積詘
也康俗濟用將冶鑄有小補焉而何可廢
也故莫若復公鑄復公鑄之法在於銅美
而工精使私鑄不能擬然其費鉅矣本息
不相權由無利也其要在於斂銅不下布
宜令郡國俾民得以銅贖罪有貨銅者官

先王錢幣之興，將以利民而非以自利也。然國計不給，則亦取贏焉。當今經費廣而蓄積詘也，康俗濟用，將冶鑄有小補焉，而何可廢也？故莫若復公鑄。復公鑄之法，在於銅美而工精，使私鑄不能擬。然其費鉅矣，本息不相權，由無利也。其要在於斂銅不下布。宜令郡國，俾民得以銅贖罪；有貨銅者，官
translation_en:
…gave it any heed. Now the signs of its failure have appeared. The reason it is tolerated and not abolished is that, without it, the annual allocations for the various frontier regions cannot be met. Yet this overlooks the fact that it yields a nominal quota without actual benefit. And it is not merely without benefit: even the quota under the system of supplying grain in exchange for salt certificates has been lost. The harm it causes is considerable. Thus, without the production-cost charge, salt certificates would not accumulate unused; with no such accumulation, the salt trade would flow freely. With trade flowing freely, merchants would not be distressed; free of distress, they would gladly register and deliver their supplies. With merchants gladly delivering supplies, fodder and grain would arrive in abundance, and frontier stores would be plentiful. Current valuations would not be depressed, and the returns would be doubled. A single measure would bring four benefits together. It would therefore be acceptable to reduce the annual allocations by the corresponding amount. If they absolutely cannot be reduced, this production-cost charge was added only recently: previously there must have been some means of providing these funds. Could its original source not be investigated? This is what is meant by not allowing a small gain to bring great harm.
When the former kings introduced currency, their purpose was to benefit the people, not themselves. Nevertheless, when state revenues were insufficient, they also took a profit from it. Today, expenditures are extensive and reserves depleted. To improve the people's livelihood and meet expenses, minting could offer some modest assistance; how, then, can it be abandoned? Nothing would therefore be better than restoring government minting. The method for restoring it lies in using fine copper and skilled workmanship, so that private minters cannot match it. Yet the expense would be enormous. If capital outlay and returns did not balance, there would still be no profit [?]. The essential point is to collect copper without disbursing cash. Orders should be issued to the local administrations allowing people to redeem criminal penalties with copper. Where there are people selling copper, the authorities…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
以罰鍰易之抵歲解額焉則銅必上湊矣
禁私鑄之法在於收偽錢蓋制錢之初興
也司市者不稽使偽錢得入焉民家有而
戶用之非一日矣卒然斷之則奪民之業
而駭且怨彼豪黠者且日蓄而伺禁之弛
也宜令民以私錢首者除罪仍以官錢一
當三爾之其以車畜販載偽錢者沒其貨
不宥則私鑄無所售必可絕矣私鑄絕則
公錢當益布此所謂不以小害妨大利也
===
嗟夫財用之在世猶水之在地中也立法
者濬其源者也行法者導其流者也水之
所以得其性也引而極之則源竭壅而激
之則衡溢而奔放而水之害大矣是故治
水不可不慎也順其性而已矣制法不可
不慎也審其權而已矣權豈易言哉聖人
所以經物宜御人情之大端也是在司
國計者審之而愚生何足與知焉
alt_text:
以罰鍰易之抵歲解額馬則銅必上湊矣
禁私鑄之法在於收偽錢蓋制錢之初興
也司市者不稽使偽錢得入馬民家有而
戶用之非一日矣卒然斷之則奪民之業
而駭且怨彼豪黠者且日蓄而伺禁之弛
也宜令民以私錢首者除罪仍以官錢一
當三所之其以車畜販載偽錢者沒其貨
不宥則私鑄無所售必可絕矣私鑄絕則
公錢當益布此所謂不以小害妨大利也
===
嗟夫財用之在世猶水之在地中也立法
者濬其源者也行法者導其流者也水之
所以得其性也引而極之則源竭壅而激
之則衡溢而奔放而水之害大矣是故治
水不可不慎也順其性而已矣制法不可
不慎也審其權而已矣權豈易言哉聖人
所以經物宜御人情之大端也是在司
國計者審之而愚生何足與知焉
punctuated:
以罰鍰易之，抵歲解額焉，則銅必上湊矣。禁私鑄之法，在於收偽錢。蓋制錢之初興也，司市者不稽，使偽錢得入焉。民家有而戶用之，非一日矣。卒然斷之，則奪民之業，而駭且怨。彼豪黠者，且日蓄而伺禁之弛也。宜令民以私錢首者除罪，仍以官錢一當三爾之。其以車畜販載偽錢者，沒其貨，不宥，則私鑄無所售，必可絕矣。私鑄絕，則公錢當益布。此所謂不以小害妨大利也。

嗟夫！財用之在世，猶水之在地中也。立法者，濬其源者也；行法者，導其流者也：水之所以得其性也。引而極之，則源竭；壅而激之，則衡溢而奔放，而水之害大矣。是故治水不可不慎也，順其性而已矣；制法不可不慎也，審其權而已矣。權豈易言哉！聖人所以經物宜、御人情之大端也。是在司國計者審之，而愚生何足與知焉？
translation_en:
… purchase it with revenue from fines and count it toward the annual remittance quota; copper will then surely flow to the authorities. The way to prohibit private minting lies in collecting counterfeit coins. When the standard coinage was first introduced, those overseeing the markets failed to inspect it, allowing counterfeit coins to enter circulation. Families possess them and households use them, and have done so for a long time. To cut off their use abruptly would deprive the people of their livelihoods, alarming them and arousing resentment. Powerful and cunning men, meanwhile, would continue stockpiling them daily, waiting for enforcement to slacken. People who voluntarily declare their privately minted coins should be exempted from punishment and given official coins at a rate of one for three [?]. As for those who transport counterfeit coins for sale by cart or pack animal, their goods should be confiscated without pardon. Privately minted coins would then have no outlet and could surely be eliminated. Once private minting has ceased, official coins should circulate more widely. This is what is meant by not allowing a small harm to obstruct a great benefit.

Alas! Financial resources in the world are like water within the earth. Those who establish laws dredge its sources; those who administer laws guide its flow. This is how water is allowed to follow its nature. Draw it off to excess, and its sources run dry; dam it up and force it back, and it overflows and rushes unchecked, causing great harm. Thus one must exercise care in controlling water: it is simply a matter of following its nature. One must exercise care in framing laws: it is simply a matter of weighing what circumstances require. Yet is such judgment easy to discuss? It is the great principle by which sages order affairs appropriately and govern human inclinations. It falls to those responsible for the state’s finances to examine this carefully. How could an ignorant student such as I be worthy to have a part in understanding it?

Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the forty-fourth year of His Majesty’s reign, when the Ministry of Rites was to conduct the Metropolitan Examination for scholars from throughout the realm, His Majesty commanded your servants Gong and Zhengmeng to preside over the examination. At the time, both had been commanded to serve as chief collators of the Great Canon (Dadian). That he again charged them with evaluating examination essays showed the importance he attached to selecting talent. translation_en:
…reverently to serve the Lord on High, thereby bringing about harmonious, prosperous, and enduring government. Looking back to antiquity, to the ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, the many worthy men all served as ministers: the emperors raised them to office; solemn and dignified, they took their appointed places; emulating one another, they exerted themselves in service. All enjoyed Heaven’s abundant favor. Through them, the many undertakings of government were brought to fruition and flourishing rule was achieved. Thus Mencius said: “For all their benevolence, Yao and Shun did not extend their love equally to everyone; they gave priority to drawing worthy men close.” Selecting talent is indeed an urgent task in seeking good government!

Our Emperor’s sagely virtue carries forward the work of Heaven. He has restored flourishing rule and established the supreme standard; his achievements shine lofty and resplendent, matching those of Yao and Shun. For four twelve-year cycles, Heaven’s protection has been exceedingly firm, and Heaven’s mandate abundantly bestowed…

壽考作人
道久化洽科目掄才十有五舉於
兹士之彬彬彙征以效用者
乃
天命純佑篤生俊彥俾之仁民安
國以弼成雍熙悠久之治也曩

===
皇上軫念吏治不修國虧民苦特
諭輔臣維時銓曹課吏簡不肖以
黜惡矣而於掄才重典則
俞禮官之請嚴飭章憲非以掄選
賢才之士皆將有體國長民
之責乎民者國之本而賢才
之士則民之望國之器用也

punctuated:
壽考作人，道久化洽。科目掄才，十有五舉於兹。士之彬彬彙征以效用者，乃天命純佑，篤生俊彥，俾之仁民安國，以弼成雍熙悠久之治也。
曩歲，皇上軫念吏治不修，國虧民苦，特諭輔臣，維時銓曹課吏，簡不肖以黜惡矣。而於掄才重典，則俞禮官之請，嚴飭章憲，非以掄選賢才之士，皆將有體國長民之責乎？民者，國之本；而賢才之士，則民之望，國之器用也。
translation_en:
…Enjoying longevity and nurturing men of talent, his Way has long endured and his transforming influence has spread everywhere. Fifteen examinations for selecting talent have now been held. That accomplished scholars advance together to offer their service is due to Heaven’s unstinting favor: it has brought forth outstanding men so that they may treat the people humanely and secure the state, helping to achieve harmonious, flourishing, and enduring rule.
In a previous year, His Majesty, deeply concerned that official administration was neglected, the state impaired, and the people suffering, issued a special instruction to his assisting ministers. Thereupon the Ministry of Personnel assessed officials and singled out the unworthy to dismiss the wicked. As for the great institution of selecting talent, he approved the request of the ritual officials and ordered strict enforcement of its regulations. Was this not because all the worthy and talented men selected would bear responsibility for serving the interests of the state and governing the people? The people are the foundation of the state; worthy and talented men are those to whom the people look with hope and the instruments through which the state acts.

爲國之器用而不能殫忠於
國或以虧之爲民之望而不
能施仁於民或以苦之至㢠
聖心亦奚取於賢才耶夫
天以仁民爲心故生賢才使之異
於凡民以佐君而圖治君以
承
===
天爲心故舉賢才而用之以别於
凡民俾其仁民安國以敷治
至於凡民出力供賦以養賢
才亦莫不欲其施仁以治之
也乃若賢才之士能以畏天
忠君爲心而施仁於民殫忠
於國以䖍成雍熙悠久之治
punctuated: 爲國之器用，而不能殫忠於國，或以虧之；爲民之望，而不能施仁於民，或以苦之，至厪聖心，亦奚取於賢才耶？夫天以仁民爲心，故生賢才，使之異於凡民，以佐君而圖治。君以承天爲心，故舉賢才而用之，以别於凡民，俾其仁民安國，以敷治。至於凡民，出力供賦以養賢才，亦莫不欲其施仁以治之也。乃若賢才之士，能以畏天忠君爲心，而施仁於民，殫忠於國，以弼成雍熙悠久之治，
translation_en: If, as instruments of service to the state, they cannot devote their utmost loyalty to it and instead perhaps diminish it; if, as those upon whom the people place their hopes, they cannot extend benevolence to the people and instead perhaps cause them suffering, to the point of troubling His Majesty’s sagely heart—then what use is there in worthy and talented men? Heaven takes benevolence toward the people as its purpose. Thus it brings forth worthy and talented men, making them different from the common people so that they may assist the ruler and work toward good government. The ruler takes obedience to Heaven as his purpose. Thus he selects worthy and talented men and employs them, distinguishing them from the common people, so that they may act benevolently toward the people, secure the state, and extend good government. As for the common people, who provide labor and pay taxes to support worthy and talented men, they too all wish these men to govern them with benevolence. Now, if worthy and talented men can take reverence for Heaven and loyalty to the ruler as their purpose, extend benevolence to the people, and devote their utmost loyalty to the state, thereby helping to bring about harmonious, prosperous, and enduring government…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
斯不負天之所生與君之所
舉用矣昔伊尹爲天民先覺
其言曰予弗克俾厥后惟堯
舜其心愧耻而思天下之民
有不被堯舜之澤者若已推
而内之溝中其自任之重如
此今諸士生際
===
昌時上事
堯舜之君可不志伊尹之志而欲
使是民爲堯舜之民哉伊尹
之志在忠君在仁民夫士亦
志乎忠與仁而已矣有忠君
仁民之志則必有讜正溫厚
之言有讜正溫厚之言則必

translation_en: …then they will not fail the purpose for which Heaven brought them into being and their sovereign selected and employed them. In former times, Yi Yin was the first among Heaven’s people to awaken to understanding. He said: “If I cannot make my sovereign a Yao or a Shun, I feel shame in my heart.” When he considered that any of the people under Heaven had not received the blessings of Yao and Shun, he felt as though he himself had pushed them into a ditch. Such was the weight of the responsibility he took upon himself. Now you gentlemen have been born into a flourishing age and serve a sovereign like Yao and Shun. Can you fail to adopt Yi Yin’s aspirations and wish to make these people the people of a Yao or a Shun? Yi Yin’s aspirations lay in loyalty to his sovereign and benevolence toward the people. A scholar, too, need aspire only to loyalty and benevolence. If he aspires to loyalty to his sovereign and benevolence toward the people, his words will assuredly be forthright, upright, gentle, and generous; if his words are forthright, upright, gentle, and generous, then assuredly…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
有祗敬惇惠之行有祗敬惇
惠之行則必有寅亮綏和之
事功建立事功以安
國家斯之謂才而恒本之乎志
才不同科稟於天所賦也志
可自奮而勵也諸士茲以言
進必志伊尹之志而自奮勵
===
焉由此措之於行而忠
君仁民建立事功以安
國家用成雍熙悠久之治則於
臣圖報稱之責庶可少塞矣
如其行不逮言有愧於賢才
之名
國家將何賴焉諸士盍亦思自

translation_en: …there will be reverent, earnest, generous, and benevolent conduct. Where there is such conduct, there will surely be achievements in reverently assisting the ruler and bringing peace and harmony. To accomplish deeds that secure the state—this is what is meant by talent; yet it is always rooted in aspiration. Talents differ in kind, being endowed by Heaven; aspiration, however, can be stirred and strengthened through one’s own efforts. You gentlemen now advance through your words; you must surely take Yi Yin’s aspiration as your own and rouse yourselves to diligent effort. Put this into practice, being loyal to the ruler and benevolent toward the people, and accomplish deeds that secure the state, thereby bringing about a harmonious, flourishing, and enduring reign. Then I, your servant, may hope to discharge in some small measure my duty to repay imperial favor and prove worthy of it. But if your conduct falls short of your words and you belie the name of worthy talent, on what will the state be able to rely? Should you gentlemen not also consider exerting yourselves…

會試錄序

我皇上統天建極，臨照九有，如日月之明，無遠弗徹。恩則雨露霑洽庶類，威則雷霆震耀，罔不讋伏，四十四年於茲。道化洋溢，光天之下，至於海隅，蒼生萬邦黎獻，咸切帝臣之願焉。歲乙丑，復當會試天下士。屆期，禮部尚書臣李春芳、侍郎臣秦鳴雷、臣高儀，以考試官請。
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Our Emperor, ruling in accord with Heaven and establishing the supreme standard, presides over and illuminates the nine domains. Like the brilliance of the sun and moon, his light reaches even the remotest places. His benevolence, like rain and dew, moistens and nourishes all living things; his majesty, like thunder, shakes and dazzles them, leaving none who do not submit in awe. It has now been forty-four years. The transforming influence of his Way flows abundantly everywhere beneath luminous Heaven, reaching even the shores of the seas. The common people and worthies of the myriad lands all fervently desire to serve as the Emperor’s subjects.

In the year yichou [1565], the time came once again to hold the Metropolitan Examination for scholars throughout the realm. As the appointed time approached, your servants Li Chunfang, Minister of Rites, and Qin Minglei and Gao Yi, Vice Ministers of Rites, requested the appointment of Examiners.

上命臣拱暨侍讀學士臣正蒙典
厥事臣方總校
大典乃輟館事
陛辭以往臣伏自思念經術淺
薄行能無異乃數蒙

punctuated: 上命臣拱暨侍讀學士臣正蒙典厥事。臣方總校《大典》，乃輟館事，陛辭以往。臣伏自思念：經術淺薄，行能無異，乃數蒙拔擢，超躐恒格，以至今兹。臣受皇上恩至弘厚，踰涯分，多思所可竭力報稱者，其道無繇也。乃今承乏，辱校文之命，既懼弗勝已，又自喜曰：「庶哉！可藉是圖萬一之報矣。其敢弗殫精盡慎，思所自効者乎？」既入院，臣乃諗諸衆曰：「兹舉也，為求賢也。今即以賢進，後或……」
translation_en:
His Majesty commanded your servant Gong and your servant Zhengmeng, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, to take charge of the examination. I was then overseeing the collation of the Great Canon (Dadian), so I suspended my work at the compilation office, took leave of His Majesty in audience, and proceeded to my assignment. I humbly reflected: my learning in the Classics is shallow, and my conduct and abilities are unremarkable. Yet I have repeatedly received promotion, advancing beyond the ordinary rules, until reaching my present position. The favor I have received from His Majesty is exceedingly great and generous, exceeding what befits my station. I have often considered how I might exert all my strength to repay it, but have had no means of doing so.
Now, serving for want of someone better, I have been honored with the command to assess examination essays. Though fearful that I could not discharge the task, I also rejoiced inwardly, saying: “Perhaps through this I may seek to repay even one ten-thousandth of that favor! How could I dare fail to devote all my energy and utmost care, considering how best to render service?” After entering the examination compound, I addressed the assembled officials: “This examination is held to seek worthy men. Even if we now recommend worthy men, what comes afterward may…”

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
未可知也乃即以不肖進後
其謂何是故代者有罰挾冊
者有罰羣聚而通者有罰兹
惟我
聖天子明命諸執事敬之哉罔或
弗覈俾我校文者罔攸據既
入簾臣又諗諸衆曰兹試言
===

或未可知也乃即弗良於言
存其謂何是故浮夸者黜險
僻者黜曼衍而無當者黜兹

聖天子明命我諸執事敬之哉罔
