既入簾，臣又諗諸衆曰：「兹試言也，焉覘所存也。即良於言，存或未可知也；乃即弗良於言，存其謂何？是故浮夸者黜，險僻者黜，曼衍而無當者黜。兹亦惟我聖天子明命，我諸執事敬之哉！罔固舊見，俾或售於淫辭。」於是，
translation_en:
…what they may become remains unknown. But if we recommend the unworthy to begin with, what can be said of their future conduct? Thus, those who sit the examination for others are punished; those who conceal books are punished; and those who gather together and communicate answers are punished. These are the express commands of our sagely Son of Heaven. All you officials charged with these duties, heed them reverently! Let nothing go unexamined, leaving us who assess the essays without a reliable basis for judgment.”
After entering the inner examination enclosure, your servant again addressed the assembled officials: “Here we examine words, through which we discern what lies within the mind. Even when the words are good, what lies within may remain unknown; but if the words themselves are not good, what can be said of what lies within? Thus, the inflated and boastful are rejected; the abstruse and eccentric are rejected; and the rambling and irrelevant are rejected. These too are the express commands of our sagely Son of Heaven. Let all of us charged with these duties heed them reverently! Do not cling to established opinions and thereby allow anyone to win acceptance through extravagant language.” Thereupon…

報本弗可以已也夫

translation_en: …The candidates who took the three sessions numbered more than four thousand six hundred. In accordance with the imperial decision, four hundred were selected as successful candidates. Their names and the finest of their compositions were compiled into a record for presentation to the throne. I, your servant, then addressed the candidates: “Ah! Your going forth to serve the sovereign begins today. But do you also know how to serve him? The sovereign is as exalted as Heaven; the distance separating your positions is immense. Yet those who hold office generally understand their duty but fail to recognize his gracious bounty. They fail to understand that Heaven, though supremely exalted and distant, is nevertheless spoken of thus: ‘Heaven is the father and mother of all things.’ Such is its bounty. Thus it is said: Heaven must not be deceived, and repaying the source of our blessings must never cease. Now, …”

說萬物者，莫說乎澤。

書

簫韶九成，鳳凰來儀。

夾右碣石，入于河。

文王惟克厥宅心，乃克立茲常事司牧人
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Comfort them, and they will come; stir them to action, and they will be harmonious.

The way of human beings makes government flourish readily; the way of the earth makes trees grow readily. Government is like reeds, which grow quickly.

The Book of Poetry says: “Heaven gives birth to the multitude of people; wherever there is a thing, there is a rule. The people hold fast to their constant nature and love this admirable virtue.” Confucius said: “The author of this poem surely understood the Way! Wherever there is a thing, there must be a rule. Because the people hold fast to their constant nature, they love this admirable virtue.”

Book of Changes

Topmost nine: Examine your conduct and consider its auspices. On its completion, there is supreme good fortune. The Image says: “Supreme good fortune in the topmost position: there is great cause for celebration.”

Great Strength means that the great is strong. Firmness joined with movement produces strength. “Great Strength: constancy is beneficial” means that the great is correct. Through correctness and greatness, the true character of Heaven and Earth can be seen.

It resembles Heaven and Earth and therefore does not run counter to them.

Among things that gladden the myriad beings, nothing brings greater delight than the marsh.

Book of Documents

When the Shao music on the panpipes had been performed nine times, phoenixes came to dance in stately harmony.

Passing Jieshi on their right, they entered the Yellow River.

King Wen was able to discern where their hearts were set; thus he could establish these regular officers and those charged with shepherding the people…

…and thus was able to employ men of outstanding virtue. King Wen did not take upon himself all matters of pronouncements, legal cases, and affairs requiring care; King Wen did not presume to manage these himself.
Duke, now establish here at Chengzhou a foundation that will endure without end.

The Odes
They dye some dark, some yellow; our vermilion is brilliantly bright.
The multitudes became fish; the tortoise-and-serpent banners became falcon banners. The diviner interpreted this: “The multitudes becoming fish means a year of abundant harvests; the tortoise-and-serpent banners becoming falcon banners means households will multiply.”
At the Biyong ceremonial school in Haojing, from west and east, from south and north, none failed to submit.
Profoundly wise was Shang; long had its auspicious signs been manifest.

The Spring and Autumn Annals
“Autumn, the seventh month.” Sixth year of Duke Yin.
“The army of Song attacked Chen; the men of Wei came to Chen’s aid.” Twelfth year of Duke Xuan.
“Spring. The Marquis of Jin sent Han Chuan to come and say that the lands of Wenyang should be returned to Qi.” Eighth year of Duke Cheng.
“Jin attacked Xianyu.” Twelfth year of Duke Zhao. “Autumn. Xun Wu of Jin led an army to attack Xianyu.” Fifteenth year of Duke Zhao.

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
者夫數子者皆當時所謂豪傑也而所
爲若是初蓋有疑之者焉然卒以濟事
而天下賴之豈倖成歟抑豪傑所見自
有異乎人者歟傳云非常之原黎民懼
焉及臻厥成天下晏如也夫臻厥成焉
固可自表著矣不知黎民懼焉之際果
何以用之歟且未用之先靡所嘗試或
有假之者焉抑何以辨歟夫今茲之舉
誠願得豪傑爲世用也諸士無有因而
===
自見者乎其各以意對無徒勦說焉也
問昔人有言立治有體論治者貴識體則
夫人臣欲以佐太平之業者不可不審
也嘗觀漢宋二史所紀載佐元祐者於
新法之害民而更張之可謂得善治之
體矣而佐元康者則好觀故事數條奏
請施行之何歟乃若當以德化民之君
而陳治安之策輔深仁厚澤之主而答

punctuated:
者。夫數子者，皆當時所謂豪傑也，而所爲若是，初蓋有疑之者焉。然卒以濟事，而天下賴之，豈倖成歟？抑豪傑所見，自有異乎人者歟？傳云：「非常之原，黎民懼焉；及臻厥成，天下晏如也。」夫臻厥成焉，固可自表著矣；不知黎民懼焉之際，果何以用之歟？且未用之先，靡所嘗試，或有假之者焉，抑何以辨歟？夫今茲之舉，誠願得豪傑爲世用也。諸士無有因而自見者乎？其各以意對，無徒勦說焉也。

問：昔人有言：「立治有體，論治者貴識體。」則夫人臣欲以佐太平之業者，不可不審也。嘗觀漢宋二史所紀載，佐元祐者，於新法之害民而更張之，可謂得善治之體矣；而佐元康者，則好觀故事，數條奏請施行之，何歟？乃若當以德化民之君，而陳治安之策；輔深仁厚澤之主，而答手詔條陳十事，其果論治而識體，如所
translation_en:
… Those several men were all regarded as outstanding figures in their day, yet they acted in this way, and at first there were doubtless those who questioned them. Nevertheless, they ultimately accomplished their tasks, and all under Heaven benefited from them. Was their success merely good fortune? Or do outstanding men possess insights different from those of others? A transmitted text says: “At the inception of extraordinary undertakings, the common people are afraid; once success is achieved, all under Heaven is at ease.” Once they have achieved success, their merits can certainly become evident of themselves. But while the common people are still afraid, on what grounds should such men be employed? Moreover, before they have been employed, when they have never been put to the test, some may falsely claim such qualities. How are they to be distinguished? In holding this examination, we sincerely hope to obtain outstanding men for service to the age. Are there none among you candidates who will take this opportunity to make yourselves known? Let each answer according to his own understanding, without merely borrowing the arguments of others.

Question: Someone of old said: “Establishing good government has its essential principles; those who discuss government must above all recognize those principles.” Thus, a minister who wishes to assist in the achievement of great peace must examine them carefully. Reading the accounts in the histories of the Han and Song, we find that those who served during the Yuanyou era changed the New Policies because they harmed the people. They may be said to have grasped the essential principles of good government. Yet one who served during the Yuankang era delighted in examining precedents and repeatedly submitted itemized memorials requesting their implementation. Why was this? Then there was one who, serving a ruler who transformed the people through virtue, presented proposals for good order and security; and another who, assisting a sovereign of profound benevolence and abundant beneficence, responded to an imperial edict in the ruler’s own hand by setting forth ten matters. Did they truly recognize the essential principles when discussing government, as …

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
賢者擬聖人之治有神於得民者有神於化民
者蓋民心難得而尤難以化也聖人有以感之
而效可立致焉非至神其孰能如此哉子貢曉
子禽之意如此蓋謂有德者必有業然德之未
至者以形用而德之至者以神用夫子天下之
至聖也設見諸行事豈但所謂立斯立道斯行
而已乎民罔常懷固必綏之而後來也然有未
必來者况斯來耶夫子弗綏則已苟於既立而
加惠焉亦為之懷保云爾而非若是其幾也然
===
有是懷保之仁即有是歸附之義近孰與被己
相招矣遠孰與聞已相應矣有不疾而自速者
焉何也綏之神故也所以潛為之格者非惟天
下弗知而聖人亦弗知也民心罔中固必動之
而後和也然有未必和者况斯和耶夫子弗動
則已苟於既道而振德焉亦為之鼓舞云爾而
非若是其幾也然有是鼓舞之機即有是變化
之妙以章百姓既昭明矣以協萬邦既時雍矣
有不行而自至者焉何也動之神故也所以黙

punctuated:
賢者擬聖人之治，有神於得民者，有神於化民者。蓋民心難得，而尤難以化也。聖人有以感之，而效可立致焉，非至神，其孰能如此哉？子貢曉子禽之意如此。蓋謂有德者必有業，然德之未至者以形用，而德之至者以神用。夫子，天下之至聖也，設見諸行事，豈但所謂「立斯立，道斯行」而已乎？民罔常懷，固必綏之而後來也。然有未必來者，况斯來耶？夫子弗綏則已，苟於既立而加惠焉，亦為之懷保云爾，而非若是其幾也。然有是懷保之仁，即有是歸附之義。近孰與被己相招矣，遠孰與聞已相應矣。有不疾而自速者焉，何也？綏之神故也。所以潛為之格者，非惟天下弗知，而聖人亦弗知也。

民心罔中，固必動之而後和也。然有未必和者，况斯和耶？夫子弗動則已，苟於既道而振德焉，亦為之鼓舞云爾，而非若是其幾也。然有是鼓舞之機，即有是變化之妙。「以章百姓」，既昭明矣；「以協萬邦」，既時雍矣。有不行而自至者焉，何也？動之神故也。所以黙

When a worthy man envisages the governance of a sage, he sees a spiritual efficacy in winning the people and a spiritual efficacy in transforming them. For the people’s hearts are difficult to win and still more difficult to transform. Yet the sage has the means to move them, and the results can be achieved at once. Who could accomplish this without the utmost spiritual efficacy? Such was the meaning of Zigong’s explanation to Ziqin. His point was that those possessing virtue must also have accomplishments. Yet virtue that has not reached perfection operates through outward forms, whereas perfected virtue operates through spiritual efficacy. The Master is the supreme sage of the world. Were his virtue expressed in the conduct of government, would it amount merely to what is called, “Establish them, and they stand established; guide them, and they proceed”?

The people’s allegiance is not constant; one must therefore bring them peace before they will come. Yet even then they may not come—how much less can one expect them to come immediately? If the Master did not bring them peace, there would be nothing further to say. But if, having established them, he bestowed benefits upon them, he would merely be cherishing and protecting them, without looking for such an outcome. Yet wherever there is this benevolence in cherishing and protecting, there is a corresponding sense of rightness in coming over and submitting. Those nearby, receiving his benefits, summon one another; those far away, hearing of him, respond to one another [?]. There is a swiftness that comes of itself, without haste. Why? Because of the spiritual efficacy of bringing them peace. The means by which he imperceptibly reaches their hearts are unknown not only to all under Heaven but even to the sage himself.

The people’s hearts do not hold to the mean; one must therefore stir them before they become harmonious. Yet even then they may not become harmonious—how much less can one expect them to become harmonious immediately? If the Master did not stir them, there would be nothing further to say. But if, having guided them, he roused them through virtue, he would merely be encouraging and inspiring them, without looking for such an outcome. Yet wherever there is this impulse of encouragement and inspiration, there is the corresponding wonder of transformation. In “making the people illustrious,” they are already enlightened; in “bringing the myriad states into concord,” they are already in harmony. □而性立其有情效其動亦未始不相符也使
有物而無則是器之離乎道也而何以為器乎
使秉彛而不好德是情之拂其性也而何以為
情乎所以天之生人有是物必具是則乃其所
為主者也有是則斯成是物乃其所主者也盖
天非此無以生人而賦則惟均人非此無以為
人而分則有定其謂民之秉彛非與夫秉彛即
物則也以在民而謂之彛然懿德即秉彛也以
可好而謂之懿惟為秉彛所以根於心者悅諸
===

容自己者也勉強云乎哉所同具者所同然而
好此懿德者揆之百世而如一焉盖有不能自
知者也矯飾云乎哉信乎有物之必有則也秉

之乎夫知有物之有則則吾所謂仁義禮知者
可識也知秉彛之好德則吾所謂惻隱羞惡辭
讓是非者可識也而情之可為善也不既明乎
情善則性可知矣彼三說者奚待辯焉大抵孔

If there were things without their governing principles, this would mean that concrete objects were severed from the Way. How, then, could they be concrete objects? If people possessed the constant moral norm but did not love virtue, this would mean that their feelings ran counter to their nature. How, then, could they be feelings? Thus, when Heaven brings human beings into existence, wherever there is a thing, it necessarily possesses a principle: this is what governs it. With this principle, the thing takes form: it is what the principle governs. Without this, Heaven could not bring human beings into existence, and its endowment is bestowed equally; without this, human beings could not be human, and their allotted constitution is fixed. Is this not what is meant by the people’s possession of the constant moral norm? This constant norm is precisely the principle inherent in things. Because it resides in the people, it is called “constant”; and excellent virtue is precisely this constant norm. Because it is worthy of love, it is called “excellent.” Precisely because it is the constant norm they possess, what is rooted in their hearts delights their hearts. Love of this excellent virtue extends throughout the world without exception: it is something people cannot help themselves from feeling. How could it be called forced? What all alike possess is what all alike affirm. Measured across a hundred generations, love of this excellent virtue remains the same: it operates even without their awareness. How could it be called pretence? Truly, wherever there is a thing, there must be a principle; whoever possesses the constant norm must love virtue! Such indeed is the Way. Did the poet understand this? If we understand that things have their principles, we can recognize what we call benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom. If we understand that possessing the constant norm entails loving virtue, we can recognize what we call compassion, shame and aversion, deference and yielding, and the sense of right and wrong. title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
乎時則覽德輝而下焉翩韆可覩於以呈盛世
之光華來者鳳凰也而胡為乎來鳳凰弗得而
知也固有感之者也感者簫韶也而所以為感
簫韶弗得而與也猶有本之者也則夫神人之
胥懌不益可知而鳥獸之蹌蹌又何待言矣乎
吁帝之德其可為至德也已矣大抵咸章而下
作者亦多而古今獨稱舜樂何歟盖其得位於
揖遜而致治於無為樂以象之故若此其盛也
厥後孔子在齊聞之至於三月不知肉味千載
===
而下所感且若此矣而況后夔之親典其事者
乎雖然聖人之樂亦惟聖人能知之否則端冕
而聽古樂惟恐臥者豈謂其不能感哉
公其惟時成周建無窮之基

…at that time, beholding the radiance of virtue, they descend, their fluttering flight visible, thereby displaying the splendor of a flourishing age. Those that come are phoenixes; but why do they come? The phoenixes themselves cannot know: surely something moves them. What moves them is the Xiaoshao music; yet the reason it moves them cannot be attributed to the music itself. There is still an underlying source. Is it not then all the more understandable that spirits and human beings alike rejoice? And what need is there to speak of the birds and beasts dancing in measured steps? Ah! The emperor’s virtue may indeed be called the highest virtue. From the Xianzhang music onward, there have been many composers; why, then, have people throughout the ages singled out Shun’s music for praise? Because he obtained the throne through courteous yielding and brought about good government through nonaction. His music embodied this, and hence attained such magnificence. Later, when Confucius heard it in Qi, he went so far as to lose awareness of the taste of meat for three months. If its moving power was still such a thousand years later, how much more must this have been so for Kui, who personally directed its performance? Nevertheless, only a sage can understand a sage’s music. Otherwise, when someone listens to ancient music in ceremonial robes and cap, fearing only that he will fall asleep, can one really say that the music lacks the power to move him?

“Duke, establish for this Chengzhou a foundation that will endure without end.”
Zhou Ziyi

What a worthy king expects of a great minister lies solely in establishing achievements that can endure. In establishing achievements, nothing is greater than ensuring their endurance. When the Duke of Bi governed Chengzhou, King Kang set this expectation for him: the respect and esteem he thereby showed him were of the highest order. His meaning was as though he said: A great minister takes concern for the state as his loyalty, and must therefore make provision for what follows his chief task. In your government of Chengzhou, my lord, I have certainly expected you to bring the undertaking to completion. Yet this place lies very close to the royal house, and what depends upon it is no small matter. You bear responsibility for the moral order of the age, so your concerns must extend far into the future; you shoulder the weight of the state, so your plans must be far-reaching. In this Chengzhou, reverently uphold the intention of the command entrusted to you and attend to far-reaching counsels, leaving plans for those who will carry on your work. Deepen still further your loyalty in assisting the sovereign, and cherish enduring designs, enlarging your achievements in securing peace and order. Promote the Way to bring about good government, striving to ensure that all virtues are cultivated and that accomplished work continues without cease. Transform the people and change their customs, striving to eradicate every lingering pernicious influence, so that the great undertaking may extend without limit. Employ firmness and gentleness together, implementing measures that distinguish the worthy from the unworthy. Seek not merely the felicity of today, but lasting results sufficient to extend the grand design through a hundred generations. Provide both protection and orderly government, spreading instruction in virtue and righteousness. Let its reach extend beyond the brief span of a single age into the future, sufficient to establish magnificent achievements lasting ten thousand years. Set an example…

translation_en:
…As for ritual, whenever archery was practiced, achievement took precedence; whenever the district ceremonies were practiced, age took precedence. These were regularly observed here. Thus the joy of the Biyong, the royal academy, grew still greater here, and the praise and cultivation of these outstanding scholars spread still more widely. Yet how did this secure the hearts of all under Heaven? The capital is the pivot of the four quarters, from which exemplary influence proceeds, while the national school is the foremost seat of goodness, where moral instruction originates. Thus, coming from the east and coming from the west, although their lands were indeed distant, those who looked up to the diffusion of the civilizing commands all devoted their hearts to receiving this transforming influence: those in the east were like those in the west. Coming from the south and coming from the north, although the people were indeed numerous, those who trusted the instruction of the August Ultimate all responded wholeheartedly and awaited the royal will: those in the south were like those in the north. Since nurturing people through goodness does not consist in driving them by force or compelling them through power, their sincere submission to virtue surely cannot be a superficial matter of smiles, appearances, voices, and sounds. Such was the breadth of the sage’s transforming influence and the depth to which it penetrated! Ah! King Wu truly was capable of being a ruler.

Nevertheless, King Wu did not win the people solely through this. He cultivated reverent attentiveness and righteousness together, while the Great Plan and the Cinnabar Writing further supported and assisted him. There was indeed a foundation for his rectification of the root and source. This is what is meant by establishing instruction through the way of the spirits and thereby securing the submission of all under Heaven. Ah! Having quelled disorder through military might, he then brought peace through civil virtue. The eight hundred years allotted to the Ji royal house were truly founded upon this. Thus it is said: employing civil and military means together is the method for enduring peace and lasting good government. Is this not indeed true?

“Profoundly wise was Shang; long had its auspicious signs unfolded.”

Tang Yizhu.

Associate Examiner Xing, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: Its form is balanced and correct, its language ample and unhurried. Moreover, its grasp of the meaning of enduring longevity is especially true and precise. It can serve as a model for all under Heaven.

Associate Examiner Li, Compiler, comments: It develops the idea of receiving the Mandate through virtue without contrived embellishment. Its integrated elegance deserves praise; it should be recorded as a model.

Associate Examiner Ding, Senior Compiler, comments: Its elucidation of the meaning of “long has its auspiciousness unfolded” is exceptionally clear and penetrating. The author is evidently deeply versed in the Book of Poetry.

Associate Examiner Chen, Right Assistant Companion, comments: Its language and meaning are clear and precise. Record it.

Examiner Hu, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: Its language is harmonious and dignified.

Examiner Gao, Academician, comments: Elegant and vigorous.

The people of Shang praised the abundance of their ancestral virtue and traced how far back their reception of the Mandate extended. For wherever virtue resides, there the Mandate of Heaven comes to rest. Since the people of Shang received the Mandate through virtue accumulated over generations, had not their auspicious signs likewise been unfolding for a long time? This is what they recalled at the collective ancestral sacrifice in the ancestral temple. The meaning is this: those who establish a dynasty are human, but the Mandate depends upon Heaven; it is Heaven that renews the Mandate, but the influence that moves it comes from human beings. How was it with our Shang? Profound indeed was its depth, its subtle workings unfathomable; sagacious indeed was its clarity, its illumination reaching everywhere without limit. No ruler’s virtue could surpass this, yet few possess it—how much rarer for it to be possessed generation after generation! It was our Shang alone: Heaven’s Mandate had found its destination, and the destined rise of a king was about to begin. Thus Heaven wholeheartedly bestowed its favor, bringing forth sages endowed with virtue one after another…

記者原樂之所由作著樂之所由盛蓋樂必由
本以及文非徒作也則夫本之盛者其文豈有
不盛哉樂記之意若曰樂之爲道也無本不立
無文不行善觀樂者亦惟於其本焉求之何則
樂所以象德也以言乎德乃性之渾然者呈諸
端緒是樂之本也以言乎樂乃德之粹然者顯
於聲容是德之華也若夫金石絲竹不過其器
焉耳而本豈在是乎何也樂之始而有詩焉志
動於內而情見乎辭所以言其志也言之不足
===
而宣之於歌非咏其聲以成方乎歌之不足而
形之於舞非動其容以盡變乎夫是三者根心
而生詩歌之發舞蹈之容皆無聲無形者爲之
本也然後從之以器被諸八音飾以干羽而有
聲有容樂斯作焉使無是心則將無所謂詩歌
舞者矣而况於器乎此可見情其本也文其著
也是故情之所感者深則文之所著自明不然
未有能明者也猶之天地之氣盛則及物之化
自神不然未有能神者也故夫美在其中而和

punctuated: 記者原樂之所由作，著樂之所由盛。蓋樂必由本以及文，非徒作也。則夫本之盛者，其文豈有不盛哉？樂記之意若曰：樂之爲道也，無本不立，無文不行。善觀樂者，亦惟於其本焉求之。何則？樂所以象德也。以言乎德，乃性之渾然者呈諸端緒，是樂之本也；以言乎樂，乃德之粹然者顯於聲容，是德之華也。若夫金石絲竹，不過其器焉耳，而本豈在是乎？何也？樂之始而有詩焉，志動於內而情見乎辭，所以言其志也。言之不足，而宣之於歌，非咏其聲以成方乎？歌之不足，而形之於舞，非動其容以盡變乎？夫是三者根心而生，詩歌之發、舞蹈之容，皆無聲無形者爲之本也。然後從之以器，被諸八音，飾以干羽，而有聲有容，樂斯作焉。使無是心，則將無所謂詩歌舞者矣，而况於器乎？此可見情其本也，文其著也。是故情之所感者深，則文之所著自明；不然，未有能明者也。猶之天地之氣盛，則及物之化自神；不然，未有能神者也。故夫美在其中而和
translation_en: The author of the Record traces the origins of music’s creation and explains how it comes to flourish. Music must proceed from its foundation to its patterned expression; it does not arise without a basis. Thus, when its foundation flourishes, how could its patterned expression fail to flourish? The meaning of the Record of Music is as if to say: as a Way, music cannot be established without a foundation, nor can it take effect without patterned expression. Those skilled at discerning music seek it in its foundation alone. Why is this? Music gives visible and audible form to virtue. To speak of virtue: it is the undivided wholeness of human nature revealing itself in particular manifestations, and this is music’s foundation. To speak of music: it is the purity of virtue made manifest in sound and movement, and this is virtue’s flowering. As for metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments, these are merely its implements. How could its foundation lie in them? Why is this so? At music’s inception there is poetry: intent stirs within, and feeling appears in words, thereby expressing that intent. When words are insufficient, it is voiced in song—is this not the chanting of sounds to form a pattern? When song is insufficient, it takes shape in dance—is this not the movement of the body to exhaust the possibilities of variation? These three arise from roots in the heart. The utterances of poetry and song and the movements of dance all have as their foundation that which has neither sound nor form. Only then are instruments added, the expression given voice through the eight classes of musical sound, and embellishment supplied by shields and feathers. With sound and movement thus present, music comes into being. Without this heart, there would be nothing that could be called poetry, song, or dance—how much less could there be instrumental music? From this one can see that feeling is its foundation and patterned expression its manifestation. Thus, when feeling is deeply stirred, its manifestation in patterned expression is naturally clear; otherwise, it can never be clear. Likewise, when the vital energy of Heaven and Earth flourishes, its transforming influence upon things is naturally wondrous; otherwise, it can never be wondrous. Thus, when beauty resides within and harmony…

受王明之福茲者復當大比載舉彜章三

於公車利用拔茅方當校藝顧觀勝負者

punctuated: 君作師，家塾黨庠，禮樂彌乎寰宇，書文車軌，聲敎訖於朔南。乃闢四門，舉賢良於漢策；乃崇六籍，抑詞賦於唐科。聿追淳古之隆，並受王明之福。茲者復當大比，載舉彜章。三物賓興，悉預偕於計吏；萬邦黎獻，共待詔於公車。利用拔茅，方當校藝。顧觀勝負者豈隙中之目，而斷屈直者必堂上之身。臣學不逮於先猷，文罔諧乎時尚。人非伯樂，能空冀野之羣；識愧卞和，安辨荊山之玉？第薦賢為國，頗懷仁傑之忠；且濟溺起衰，竊有昌黎之志。敢不恪承明命，勉副初心？以通經學古為高，以繪章繪句為戒。一一而聽吹，寧許其濫竽；種種各陳，好何分於工瑟？名苟見收於賢路，言必不詭於聖塗。雖棟梁榱桷或有不同，然梓漆椅桐要諸適用。倘尚循其陋轍，則無惜於遺珠。與文子同升，敢樹私於桃李；薄賈島不錄，任興謗於薔薇。庶挽頹風，少裨
translation_en:
…as ruler and teacher, with schools in households and district schools, rites and music fill the world; writing is uniform and carriage tracks are standardized, and your civilizing influence reaches north and south. You open the four gates, selecting worthy and capable men through policy questions as under the Han; you exalt the Six Classics, curbing verse and rhapsodies in the examinations as under the Tang. Thus you pursue the flourishing simplicity of antiquity, and all share the blessings of an enlightened sovereign.

Now the triennial examination comes round again, and the established regulations are once more put into effect. Honored and recommended on the basis of the three attainments, the candidates all accompany the officials bringing fiscal accounts to the capital; worthy men from every region await the imperial summons at the office receiving candidates. This is an auspicious occasion for drawing forth talent, like pulling up grass whose roots bring others with it; the time has come to assess their accomplishments. Yet can those who judge victory and defeat merely peer through a crack? Those who determine what is right and wrong must themselves occupy the judgment hall.

Your servant’s learning falls short of the exemplary teachings of our predecessors, and his writing does not accord with contemporary tastes. I am no Bole, able to empty the plains of Ji of their herds by recognizing every fine horse; my discernment falls shamefully short of Bian He’s—how could I distinguish the jade of Mount Jing? Yet in recommending worthy men for the state, I cherish something of Di Renjie’s loyalty; and in rescuing the drowning and reviving what has declined, I privately share the aspiration of Han Yu of Changli. How could I fail reverently to receive your enlightened command and strive to fulfill my original purpose?

I shall prize mastery of the Classics and study of antiquity, and guard against ornate paragraphs and embellished sentences. I shall listen to each man play in turn: how could I permit an incompetent player to pass among the musicians? Let each display his particular accomplishments: why should personal preference distinguish among skilled zither players [?]? If a man’s name is admitted to the path of advancement for the worthy, his words must not depart from the way of the sages. Though ridgepoles, beams, and rafters differ, catalpa, lacquer tree, yi tree, and paulownia must each be suited to its use. If candidates still follow their debased old tracks, I shall not shrink from leaving pearls uncollected.

Ascending together with Wenzi, how could I cultivate private interests among my protégés, my ‘peach and plum trees’? Rejecting Jia Dao as unworthy of selection, I shall let slander arise over the roses [?]. I hope thereby to reverse the declining fashion and contribute a little to…

皇上聖德神功昭揭上下
禎符瑞應炳燿古今蕩蕩乎無能名焉子能以閎麗之詞發之其
必素懷忠愛而思以自効者歟
考試官侍讀學士胡批我

皇上欽承

皇上功德隆茂獨超千古故
瑞應紛燿亦為獨盛而我
皇上緝熙基
命者又獨至焉則所以迓

皇上緝熙基

景祐於無疆者端在於是子能仰窺而賛述之其亦沐浴
泰和而能識其大者特表出之
punctuated:
二祖、皇上聖德神功，昭揭上下；禎符瑞應，炳燿古今。蕩蕩乎，無能名焉！子能以閎麗之詞發之，其必素懷忠愛而思以自効者歟？

考試官侍讀學士胡批：我二祖、皇上受命永命之符，超越古今。子能揄揚其盛，而仰頌皇上欽承天眷之隆，忠敬溢於言表，宜錄以傳。

考試官學士高批：我二祖、皇上功德隆茂，獨超千古，故瑞應紛燿，亦為獨盛。而我皇上緝熙基命者，又獨至焉，則所以迓景祐於無疆者，端在於是。不知子能仰窺而贊述之，是亦沐浴泰和而能識其大者，特表出之。
translation_en:
…The sagely virtue and divine achievements of the two dynastic ancestors and His Majesty shine manifestly above and below; their auspicious tokens and propitious portents illuminate past and present. So vast are they that no words can name them! You have expressed them in grand and splendid language. Surely you have long cherished loyalty and devotion, and sought to give proof of these through your service?

Comment by Examiner Hu, Hanlin Reader-in-waiting: The tokens of our two dynastic ancestors’ and His Majesty’s receipt of the Mandate and its enduring continuance surpass those of every age. You have extolled their magnificence and reverently praised His Majesty’s reverent reception of Heaven’s abundant favor. Loyalty and respect overflow your words. This deserves to be recorded and transmitted.

Comment by Examiner Gao, Academician: The achievements and virtue of our two dynastic ancestors and His Majesty are abundant and flourishing, uniquely surpassing all past ages. Hence the profusion and brilliance of auspicious portents are likewise unrivaled. Moreover, His Majesty’s continuation and illumination of the foundational Mandate have attained an unparalleled perfection. Here precisely lies the means of welcoming great blessings without end. I had not expected that you could discern these lofty matters and celebrate them in writing. You are indeed one who, bathed in supreme harmony, can recognize its greatness. I single this out for special commendation.

punctuated:
或百九十年，或百十有五年，或百年、八九十年，以奠基；則或四百年，或六百年，或八百年。攄其始，各有明徵；驗諸終，如持左券。信豈偶然者哉！所以載在詩書，傳諸信史，萬代而下，猶斑斑如見者也。後代英誼之辟，非無氣珍物異垂諸簡策，第其德謝淳精，治猷洪暢，偶於一至之應，即謂興王之兆，猶且君臣動色，紀元升歌，封泰山，禪梁父，昭揭發揚，圖所不朽者矣。然其視古帝王何如哉？
若乃峻德神功，作述相暎，玄珍黃瑞，圖牒交輝，則未有如我國家之盛者。其卓譎殊尤之迹，更僕未易終也，而其端則可引焉。當夫夷運方傾，華亂無主，天將滌腥羶之汚涅，復神明之舊疆，於是我太祖皇帝出焉。先是象簡薦丸，赤光充室，神蛟躍立以告異，青田望雲而知氣。迨夫一戎
translation_en:
…some one hundred and ninety years, some one hundred and fifteen years, some a hundred or eighty or ninety years to establish their foundations; then some four hundred years, some six hundred years, or some eight hundred years. Unfold their beginnings, and each has clear portents; test these against their eventual outcomes, and it is like holding the left half of a contract as proof. Surely this could not have been mere coincidence! Thus these things were recorded in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents and transmitted in trustworthy histories, remaining vividly discernible ten thousand generations later, as though before our eyes. The valiant and righteous rulers of later ages did not lack wondrous vapors and extraordinary objects recorded in their chronicles. Yet their virtue fell short of pristine purity, and their plans of government of expansive greatness [?]. On encountering even a single auspicious response, they immediately called it a portent of dynastic ascendance. Ruler and ministers would visibly show their excitement, inaugurate an era, perform songs of praise, offer the feng sacrifice on Mount Tai and the shan sacrifice at Liangfu, and conspicuously proclaim and celebrate these things, seeking to make them immortal. Yet how did they compare with the ancient emperors and kings?
As for lofty virtue and divine achievements, with founding and continuation illuminating one another, heavenly marvels and earthly auspicious signs lending mutual splendor to charts and records, nothing has equaled the flourishing of our dynasty. Its extraordinary and incomparable manifestations could not readily be recounted to the end even with relays of attendants; yet some principal instances may be cited. When the fortunes of the barbarians were collapsing and the Chinese realm lay in disorder without a ruler, Heaven was about to wash away the foul, rank contamination and restore the old dominion of the divine powers. Then our Emperor Taizu arose. Before this, an ivory tablet and the presentation of a pellet [?], red light filling the room, and a divine dragon leaping upright announced extraordinary things; the man of Qingtian gazed at the clouds and recognized the portentous vapor. When at last, with a single military campaign…

===

天之於

天眷而敬無斁眷則彌純今幽賛叶矣神告明

睿謨雨暘四時恒禜
punctuated:
鹿、祥兎、玉龜、白鵲，羣遊於宮沼，是不愛其寶也。殊絶竒詭，莫可名狀，紛紜叢委，史不勝書，則其永命之符，又非超古今而獨盛者歟？卽是而言，定命者，天也；時行者，聖也；感通者，機也；達順者，信也。其德神者，其應速；其功鉅者，其效閎。雖云莫致而至，寔則多福之自求者矣。謂無自而然歟？抑猶未也。
天之於君，猶親之於子也。親慈而孝尤加，慈則愈至；天眷而敬無斁，眷則彌純。今幽贊叶矣，神告明矣，億萬年無疆之休，端在是矣。皇上猶穆然淵觀，惕然勤思，上帝之昭事日嚴，下民之陰隲愈厚。徼圍萬里，時厪睿謨；雨暘四時，恆縈宸慮。所以
translation_en:
…deer, auspicious rabbits, jade turtles, and white magpies [?] roam in groups about the palace pools: this is to withhold none of its treasures. These extraordinary and wondrous things defy description; they gather in such profusion that historians cannot record them all. Are these tokens of an enduring mandate not uniquely abundant, surpassing all of ancient and modern times? Speaking on this basis: Heaven determines the mandate; the sage acts in accordance with the times; the subtle impulse brings about sympathetic communication; sincerity brings harmony to fulfillment. When virtue is numinous, its response is swift; when achievement is great, its effects are vast. Though these blessings are said to arrive unbidden, in truth one has sought this manifold good fortune for oneself. Can one say that they occur without a cause? That would still fall short of the truth.
Heaven’s relation to the ruler is like that of a parent to a child. When a parent is loving and the child becomes still more filial, that love grows ever deeper; when Heaven bestows favor and the ruler’s reverence never flags, that favor becomes ever more complete. Now unseen assistance has brought concord, and the divine announcements are clear: here indeed lies boundless felicity for hundreds of millions of years. 一事然而非一物也朱則言其二物然而
非二事也以盡其義合二子而後可者也
斯義不明而世之言權者大抵皆稱古人
不得已之事如舜不告而娶之類夫不得
已而為處者易見者也權固也然而天下

用權而常則可不用也且權之說出諸孔

仕而止可久而速者乎此猶其大者也若
夫入而鞠躬出而與與上而誾誾下而侃

…to call this discretionary weighing seems fitting, yet something still remains unsaid. Thus Cheng speaks of it as one activity, though not one object; Zhu speaks of it as two objects, though not two activities. Only by bringing the two masters together can its meaning be fully expressed. Because this meaning is not understood, those who discuss discretionary weighing generally cite occasions when the ancients had no alternative, such as Shun’s marrying without informing his parents. Cases in which one acts because there is no alternative are readily apparent; these certainly constitute discretionary weighing. Yet can it be that all affairs under Heaven are addressed only when there is no alternative? In everyday life and the enduring human relationships, even the smallest details each have their own unchanging rule of what is right. Without discretionary weighing to assess them, could one really conform to the rule in every case, without erring through excess or deficiency? No. How, then, can one say that discretionary weighing is used in exceptional circumstances but may be dispensed with in ordinary ones?

Moreover, the teaching concerning discretionary weighing comes from Confucius. Let us therefore discuss it through Confucius himself. His dismantling the fortifications of the three cities and executing the dwarfs were instances of discretionary weighing: certainly, he was responding to exceptional circumstances. But what of taking office when it was right to take office, withdrawing when it was right to withdraw, remaining long when it was right to remain long, and departing swiftly when it was right to depart swiftly—was this not discretionary weighing? Otherwise, might he not have withdrawn when he should have taken office, or departed swiftly when he should have remained long? These are still the major instances. As for bowing his body upon entering and appearing relaxed upon leaving, speaking with respectful directness to higher-ranking officials and with ease to lower-ranking officials—was this not discretionary weighing? Otherwise, might he not have appeared relaxed when he should have bowed his body, or spoken with ease when he should have spoken with respectful directness? title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
明問哉雖然事變無窮而周孔不常有如
必周孔而後可將天下之事終無濟乎則
四子者固亦一時之傑胡可少也請各為
之明其意炎祚肇興酇侯佐命非與民休
息時歟乃即為之治未央極其壯麗非無
說也夫帝居所必建也若草創於今必且
改拓於後若田賦既定而取以為用必且
賈怨於民況自我為則用半而功倍自後
人為則用倍而功半故當財無定主之時
===
而為一勞永逸之舉是百世之利也而誰
則識之諸呂事露太尉率軍討之非明義
正法時歟乃先試以左袒而後舉事非無
說也夫諸軍通呂久矣事露且皆自懼而
吾乃與之舉事則或有他虞故特開以左
袒之路使皆得以為劉之迹自見吾於是
遂因其迹而信之而其心當自安蓋不惟
誅呂可以濟事而反側亦已帖然矣是戡
亂之智也而誰則識之狄仁傑為相時二

punctuated:
明問哉！雖然，事變無窮，而周孔不常有。如必周孔而後可，將天下之事終無濟乎？則四子者固亦一時之傑，胡可少也？請各為之明其意。
炎祚肇興，酇侯佐命，非與民休息時歟？乃即為之治未央，極其壯麗，非無說也。夫帝居所必建也，若草創於今，必且改拓於後；若田賦既定而取以為用，必且賈怨於民。況自我為，則用半而功倍；自後人為，則用倍而功半。故當財無定主之時，而為一勞永逸之舉，是百世之利也，而誰則識之？
諸呂事露，太尉率軍討之，非明義正法時歟？乃先試以左袒而後舉事，非無說也。夫諸軍通呂久矣，事露且皆自懼，而吾乃與之舉事，則或有他虞。故特開以左袒之路，使皆得以為劉之迹自見。吾於是遂因其迹而信之，而其心當自安。蓋不惟誅呂可以濟事，而反側亦已帖然矣。是戡亂之智也，而誰則識之？

translation_en:
…An enlightened question indeed! Nevertheless, circumstances change without end, while men like the Duke of Zhou and Confucius do not appear in every age. If nothing could be accomplished without a Duke of Zhou or a Confucius, would the affairs of the world then remain forever unresolved? Those four men were certainly outstanding figures of their time: how could they be dismissed? Allow me to explain the intention of each.
When the Han dynasty, ruling under the virtue of Fire, first arose, the Marquis of Zan assisted in its founding. Was this not a time to give the people rest and recuperation? Yet he immediately undertook the construction of Weiyang Palace, making it magnificent in the extreme. This was not without justification. An imperial residence necessarily had to be built. If it were built roughly now, it would surely have to be altered and enlarged later. If funds were taken for this purpose after the land taxes had been fixed, this would surely incur the people's resentment. Moreover, if we undertook it ourselves, the expense would be halved and the achievement doubled; if later men undertook it, the expense would be doubled and the achievement halved. Thus, while wealth had no settled owners, he undertook a work requiring one great exertion but bringing lasting ease. This benefited a hundred generations—but who understood it?
When the plot of the Lü clan came to light, the Defender-in-Chief led the troops against them. Was this not a time to make righteousness manifest and enforce the law? Yet he first tested the troops by having them bare their left arms, and only then took action. This was not without justification. The troops had long been associated with the Lü clan. Once the plot was exposed, they would all fear for themselves; if he then enlisted them in his undertaking, unforeseen dangers might arise. He therefore expressly offered them the means of baring their left arms, enabling all to display outward evidence of their support for the Liu house. He could then trust them on the strength of that evidence, and their minds would naturally be at ease. Thus, not only could the destruction of the Lü clan be accomplished, but those who were fearful and wavering had already been reassured. Such was his wisdom in suppressing disorder—but who understood it?

text:
才於不善下也不善矣而托之乎善假豪
傑之似以眩時俗亂名實下之下也而下
之下者恒取類乎上是故不可弗辨也人
有得燕石者藏以為玉或告之曰此燕石
非玉也棄之他日見玉則以為燕石也有
聞鬻朴者慕以為璞或告之曰彼朴非璞
也已之他日聞鬻璞則以為朴也何者似
故也故良工之目不可欺以玉石良賈之
耳不可亂以朴璞匪耳目也神識在心獨
===

第四問
韓楫

translation_en:
…To employ talent in wrongdoing is inferior. To do wrong yet cloak it in goodness, borrowing the semblance of outstanding men to dazzle one’s contemporaries and confound names with realities, is the lowest of the low. Yet the lowest of the low constantly liken themselves to the highest; therefore one must distinguish between them. A man obtained a stone from Yan and treasured it as jade. Someone told him, “This is a stone from Yan, not jade.” He discarded it. Later, when he saw jade, he took it for a stone from Yan. Another heard someone selling plain wood (pu) and coveted it, thinking it was uncut jade (pu). Someone told him, “That is plain wood, not uncut jade.” He desisted. Later, when he heard someone selling uncut jade, he took it for plain wood. Why? Because of their resemblance. Thus a skilled craftsman’s eyes cannot be deceived by jade and stone, nor can a skilled merchant’s ears be confused by the words for plain wood and uncut jade. This is not a matter of ears and eyes: discerning understanding resides in the mind. What one alone sees and hears is difficult to convey to others. Such a person is outstanding even among outstanding men.
Fourth Question
Han Ji 韓楫

text:
謂盈成矣然紀綱寢隳夷狄寇盜驕橫恩
賞不節賦斂無度非飭法不可也故仲淹
為帝陳之而歐陽脩謂其老練世事所陳
志在遠大誠知言哉乃若漢自武帝好大
喜功百姓疲敝宣帝繼之若可以議飭法
矣魏相總領眾職以為方今務在奉行故
事數條漢興以來國家便宜行事及賈誼
鼂錯董仲舒所言奏請施行之蓋以宣帝
勵精圖治而德教不純故佐之遵法以捄
===
其失維時吏稱民安孰非相之功乎宋自
神宗任用非人變壞舊政哲宗繼之飭法
所必先矣司馬光復起為相毅然以身殉
社稷上言新法之當改如捄焚拯溺乃於
王安石呂惠卿之所建者盡刬革之蓋以
哲宗虛己倚任天下引領觀政故佐之飭
法以善其治君子稱其旋乾轉坤光無愧
乎此也夫此四臣者之事君也惟君之所
遇異時故道之所急異務語其為志之忠

punctuated:
謂盈成矣，然紀綱寢隳，夷狄寇盜驕橫，恩賞不節，賦斂無度，非飭法不可也。故仲淹為帝陳之，而歐陽脩謂其老練世事，所陳志在遠大，誠知言哉！乃若漢自武帝好大喜功，百姓疲敝，宣帝繼之，若可以議飭法矣。魏相總領眾職，以為方今務在奉行故事，數條漢興以來國家便宜行事及賈誼、鼂錯、董仲舒所言，奏請施行之。蓋以宣帝勵精圖治而德教不純，故佐之遵法以捄其失。維時吏稱民安，孰非相之功乎？

宋自神宗任用非人，變壞舊政，哲宗繼之，飭法所必先矣。司馬光復起為相，毅然以身殉社稷，上言新法之當改，如捄焚拯溺，乃於王安石、呂惠卿之所建者盡刬革之。蓋以哲宗虛己倚任，天下引領觀政，故佐之飭法以善其治。君子稱其旋乾轉坤，光無愧乎此也。夫此四臣者之事君也，惟君之所遇異時，故道之所急異務，語其為志之忠
translation_en:
…said that prosperity and settled order had been attained. Yet the governing framework was gradually collapsing; foreign peoples, raiders, and bandits acted with insolent impunity; favors and rewards were dispensed without restraint, and taxes and levies imposed without limit. It was therefore imperative to put the laws in order. Thus Zhongyan presented these matters to the emperor. Ouyang Xiu said that he was seasoned in worldly affairs and that his proposals embodied far-reaching ambitions. How truly discerning these words were!

As for the Han, Emperor Wu’s fondness for grand undertakings and eagerness for achievement had left the common people exhausted. When Emperor Xuan succeeded him, it might have seemed appropriate to discuss putting the laws in order. Wei Xiang, overseeing the various offices, held that the urgent task was to carry out established precedents. He repeatedly itemized measures expedient for the state since the founding of the Han, together with proposals made by Jia Yi, Chao Cuo, and Dong Zhongshu, and submitted memorials requesting their implementation. Since Emperor Xuan exerted himself diligently in pursuit of good government, yet was not wholehearted in moral instruction, Wei Xiang assisted him in adhering to established laws to remedy this failing. At that time, officials performed their duties capably and the people lived in peace. Was any of this not attributable to Wei Xiang’s efforts?

Under the Song, Emperor Shenzong employed unsuitable men, who altered and ruined the old administration. When Emperor Zhezong succeeded him, putting the laws in order necessarily took priority. Sima Guang returned to office as chief councilor and resolutely devoted his life to the altars of soil and grain. He memorialized that the New Policies must be changed with the urgency of rescuing people from fire or drowning, and accordingly abolished all that Wang Anshi and Lü Huiqing had instituted. Since Emperor Zhezong humbly entrusted him with responsibility, while all under Heaven craned their necks to observe the government, he assisted the emperor in putting the laws in order to improve his rule. Gentlemen praised him for turning Heaven and Earth around; Guang fully deserved this praise. Now, in serving their rulers, these four ministers encountered rulers facing different circumstances in their respective times. Thus, the urgent demands of the Way called for different tasks. As for the loyalty of their intentions…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
五銖唐開元之二錢者焉夫自太公管仲
而來上下數千年矣而法之可稱述者僅
僅若此法之善誠難矣而持法者不可不
慎察也我
朝于産鹽之地設轉運司者六提舉司者七
鹽課司各有定額行鹽各有分地而淮浙
齊晉之課專給邊餉募商輸芻粟塞垣領
引守支盖倣唐宋之意而規制為益善矣
然就各運司而論兩淮之課居其十七是
===
以九邊之仰給尤重夫何邇年以來鹽務
積滯邊廩告虛使二百年通濟之法一旦
廢格牴牾交敝於中外是惡可不深求其
故耶盖鹽雖斯民無日可缺要不過食味
之一耳管夷吾計口筭賦逮于吾子苛矣
然必有是口乃筭是賦非漫加也異日者
淮鹽額課不過七十萬引有奇已爾迨承
平寖久而生齒繁于是每引以餘鹽副之
盖實計一百四十萬有奇矣正課遵舊制

translation_en:
…the two coinages, the wuzhu and the Tang Kaiyuan coins. Now, several thousand years have passed since Taigong and Guan Zhong, yet the methods worthy of recounting amount to only these few. Good methods are indeed difficult to devise, and those who administer them must be scrutinized carefully.

Our dynasty has established six Salt Distribution Commissions and seven Salt Tax Superintendencies in salt-producing regions. Each Salt Tax Office has a fixed quota, and each salt distribution operation has its designated territory. The salt revenues of Huai, Zhe, Qi, and Jin are devoted exclusively to provisioning the frontier. Merchants are recruited to deliver fodder and grain to the frontier fortifications, receive salt certificates, and wait to collect their salt. This broadly follows the intentions of the Tang and Song systems, while improving their regulations. Among the distribution commissions, however, the Lianghuai salt revenue accounts for seven-tenths of the total; hence the Nine Frontier Garrisons depend particularly heavily upon it. Why, then, have salt operations become increasingly backlogged in recent years, while frontier granaries report that they are empty? A system that sustained circulation and supplied needs for two hundred years has suddenly become inoperative; conflicting arrangements have caused exhaustion both at court and in the provinces. How can we fail to investigate the causes thoroughly?

Although these people cannot go a day without salt, it is ultimately only one of the seasonings for food. Guan Yiwu calculated the levy by counting mouths, extending it even to ‘our children’ [?]—a harsh practice indeed. Yet a mouth had to exist before the corresponding levy was assessed; it was not imposed arbitrarily. Formerly, the assessed quota for Huai salt amounted to no more than a little over seven hundred thousand salt certificates. As prolonged peace brought population growth, an additional allotment of salt was attached to each certificate, bringing the actual total to the equivalent of more than one million four hundred thousand certificates. The regular levy followed the old regulations…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
省也今其敗端見矣所以隱忍而不除者
以各邊歲例非此無以足其額也而不審
其有虚額而無實惠也豈惟無之且並開
中之額而失之矣其爲患不細也故無工
本則引不壅引不壅則鹽利通矣利通則
商不困商不困則樂於報納矣商樂報納
則芻粟叢赴而邊備饒矣時估不下侵而
倍有獲矣一舉而四利集焉歲例雖如數
省之可也必不可省則此工本之增無幾
===
時也前此必有所从給之者獨不可考其
原乎此所謂不以小利貽大害也先王錢
幣之興將以利民而非以自利也然國計
不給則亦取贏焉當今經費廣而蓄積詘
也康俗濟用將冶鑄有小補焉而何可廢
也故莫若復公鑄復公鑄之法在於銅美
而工精使私鑄不能擬然其費鉅矣本息
不相權由無利也其要在於斂銅不下布
宜令郡國俾民得以銅贖罪有貨銅者官

punctuated:
省也。今其敗端見矣，所以隱忍而不除者，以各邊歲例非此無以足其額也，而不審其有虚額而無實惠也。豈惟無之？且並開中之額而失之矣，其爲患不細也。故無工本則引不壅，引不壅則鹽利通矣；利通則商不困，商不困則樂於報納矣；商樂報納，則芻粟叢赴而邊備饒矣；時估不下侵而倍有獲矣。一舉而四利集焉，歲例雖如數省之可也。必不可省，則此工本之增無幾時也，前此必有所从給之者，獨不可考其原乎？此所謂不以小利貽大害也。
先王錢幣之興，將以利民，而非以自利也。然國計不給，則亦取贏焉。當今經費廣而蓄積詘也，康俗濟用，將冶鑄有小補焉，而何可廢也？故莫若復公鑄。復公鑄之法，在於銅美而工精，使私鑄不能擬。然其費鉅矣，本息不相權，由無利也。其要在於斂銅不下布，宜令郡國，俾民得以銅贖罪。有貨銅者，官
translation_en:
…be reduced. Now the defects of this practice have become apparent. The reason it is reluctantly tolerated rather than abolished is that, without it, the prescribed annual allocations to the various frontiers cannot be met. Yet this overlooks the fact that these are nominal quotas yielding no actual benefit. Nor is the problem merely a lack of benefit: even the quotas under the system of exchanging grain deliveries for salt certificates are being lost. The harm is considerable. Thus, without the working-capital charge (gongben), salt certificates would not accumulate unredeemed; without that accumulation, the salt trade would flow freely. With trade flowing freely, merchants would not be distressed; free from distress, they would willingly register to make deliveries. With merchants eager to deliver, fodder and grain would pour in, and frontier supplies would be abundant. Current valuations would no longer be depressed [?], and the yield would be doubled. A single measure would bring four benefits together. The annual allocations could therefore be reduced by their full amount. If they absolutely cannot be reduced, this additional working-capital charge has, after all, been in place only a short time. Previously there must have been some other source from which the allocations were supplied. Could that source alone not be investigated? This is what is meant by not allowing a small profit to bring great harm.
When the former kings introduced coinage, their purpose was to benefit the people, not themselves. Nevertheless, when the state's resources were insufficient, they also took a profit from it. Today expenditures are extensive and reserves are depleted. Casting coin could make a small contribution toward improving the people's livelihood and meeting expenditures; how, then, could it be abandoned? Nothing would therefore be better than restoring government minting. The method for restoring it lies in using good copper and fine workmanship, so that privately cast coins cannot match the result. Yet the expense would be enormous. If costs and returns do not balance, there would still be no profit [?]. The essential point is to collect copper without disbursing money. Orders should be issued to the local administrations allowing people to redeem punishments by paying in copper. For those who have copper to sell, the government…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
壽考作人
道久化洽科目掄才十有五舉於
兹士之彬彬彙征以效用者
乃
天命純佑篤生俊彦俾之仁民安
國以弼成雍熈悠久之治也曩
歲
===
皇上軫念吏治不修國虧民苦特
諭輔臣維時銓曹課吏簡不肖以
黜惡矣而於掄才重典則
俞禮官之請嚴飭章憲非以掄選
賢才之士皆將有體國長民
之責乎民者國之本而賢才
之士則民之望國之器用也
alt_text:
壽考作人
道乂化洽科目掄才十有五舉於
茲士之彬彬彙征以效用者
乃
天命純佑篤生俊彥俾之仁民安
國以衍成雍熙悠久之治也曩
歲
===
皇上軫念吏治不修國虧民苦特
諭輔臣維時銓曹課吏簡不肖以
黜惡矣而於掄才重典則
俞禮官之請嚴飭章憲非以掄選
賢才之士皆將有體國長民
之責乎民者國之本而賢才
之士則民之望國之器用也
punctuated:
壽考作人，道久化洽，科目掄才十有五舉於兹。士之彬彬彙征以效用者，乃天命純佑，篤生俊彦，俾之仁民安國，以弼成雍熈悠久之治也。
曩歲，皇上軫念吏治不修，國虧民苦，特諭輔臣。維時銓曹課吏，簡不肖以黜惡矣。而於掄才重典，則俞禮官之請，嚴飭章憲，非以掄選賢才之士，皆將有體國長民之責乎？民者，國之本；而賢才之士，則民之望，國之器用也。
translation_en:
…longevity and the nurturing of men. The Way has long prevailed, and its transforming influence has spread throughout. By now, fifteen examinations have been held to select talented men. That cultivated scholars advance together to offer their services is owing to Heaven’s unstinting favor in abundantly bringing forth outstanding men, that they might treat the people humanely and bring security to the state, helping to establish harmonious, prosperous, and enduring rule.
In a previous year, His Majesty, deeply concerned that official administration was neglected, the state impaired, and the people suffering, issued a special directive to his grand secretaries. Thereupon, the Ministry of Personnel assessed officials and singled out the unworthy to remove the wicked. As for the momentous institution of selecting talent, he approved the request of the ritual officials and ordered strict observance of its regulations. Was this not because all the worthy and talented scholars selected would bear responsibility for serving the state and governing the people? The people are the foundation of the state; worthy and talented scholars are those upon whom the people place their hopes and the instruments through which the state accomplishes its work.

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
斯不負天之所生與君之所
舉用矣昔伊尹爲天民先覺
其言曰予弗克俾厥后惟堯
舜其心愧耻而思天下之民
有不被堯舜之澤者若已推
而內之溝中其自任之重如
此今諸士生際
===
昌時上事
堯舜之君可不志伊尹之志而欲
使是民爲堯舜之民哉伊尹
之志在忠君在仁民夫士亦
志乎忠與仁而已矣有忠君
仁民之志則必有讜正溫厚
之言有讜正溫厚之言則必

translation_en: …Thus one will not fail Heaven, which gave one life, or the ruler, who selected one for service. In former times, Yi Yin was one of Heaven’s people who first attained understanding. He said: “I have not succeeded in making my sovereign a Yao or a Shun.” His heart felt shame, and whenever he thought of people under Heaven who had not received the blessings of Yao and Shun, he felt as though he himself had pushed them into a ditch. Such was the weight of the responsibility he took upon himself. Now you gentlemen have been born into a flourishing age and serve a ruler like Yao and Shun. Can you aspire to make these people the people of a Yao or a Shun without adopting Yi Yin’s aspiration? Yi Yin’s aspiration lay in loyalty to his ruler and benevolence toward the people. A scholar, too, need aspire only to loyalty and benevolence. If one has the aspiration to be loyal to the ruler and benevolent toward the people, one will surely speak with forthright integrity, warmth, and generosity; if one speaks with forthright integrity, warmth, and generosity, then surely…

title: 嘉靖四十四年會試錄
text:
有祗敬惇惠之行有祗敬惇
惠之行則必有寅亮綏和之
事功建立事功以安
國家斯之謂才而恒本之乎志
才不同科稟於天所賦也志
可自奮而勵也諸士兹以言
進必志伊尹之志而自奮勵
===
焉由此措之於行而忠
君仁民建立事功以安
國家用成雍煕悠久之治則於
臣圖報稱之責庶可少塞矣
如其行不逮言有愧於賢才
之名
國家將何賴焉諸士盍亦思自

才不同科禀於天所賦也志
可自奮而勵也諸士茲以言
進必志伊尹之志而自奮勵
===
焉由此措之於行而忠
君仁民建立事功以安
國家用成雍熙悠久之治則於

如其行不逮言有愧於賢才
之名
國家將何賴焉諸士盍亦思自
punctuated: 有祗敬惇惠之行，有祗敬惇惠之行，則必有寅亮綏和之事功。建立事功以安國家，斯之謂才，而恒本之乎志。才不同科，稟於天所賦也；志可自奮而勵也。諸士兹以言進，必志伊尹之志而自奮勵焉。由此措之於行，而忠君仁民，建立事功以安國家，用成雍煕悠久之治，則於臣圖報稱之責，庶可少塞矣。如其行不逮言，有愧於賢才之名，國家將何賴焉？諸士盍亦思自
translation_en: …there will be conduct marked by reverence, earnestness, and benevolence. Where there is such conduct, there will assuredly be accomplishments in reverently assisting the ruler and bringing peace and harmony. To achieve deeds that secure the state: this is what is meant by talent, yet it is always rooted in resolve. Talents differ in kind, being endowed by Heaven; resolve, however, can be roused and strengthened through one’s own efforts. You gentlemen now seek advancement through your words; you must take Yi Yin’s resolve as your own and exert yourselves accordingly. Put this into practice by being loyal to the ruler and benevolent toward the people, achieving deeds that secure the state and thereby bringing about harmonious, flourishing, and enduring government. Then I, your servant, may hope to have fulfilled in some small measure my duty to repay imperial favor fittingly. But if your conduct falls short of your words and you prove unworthy of the name of worthy and talented men, on whom will the state rely? Should you gentlemen not also consider how you yourselves…
